speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Green Paper by the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) as well as the Ministry of Communications and Information highlighted the serious nature of the issues, the significant impact in other countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of the discussions since the Bill has been tabled have not considered what the SC has said or the evidence that had been presented, and the balancing between the different interests that the SC had to do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I hope the discussions in this House will be better informed by reference to the SC's report.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My colleagues Minister S Iswaran and Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong will deal with the key provisions of the Bill and how they implement the SC's recommendations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung will speak on the universities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My colleagues Zaqy Mohamad and Sun Xueling will also speak, in addition to other Members.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, the powers that the Government has under existing legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are wider than what is proposed under this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As we consider the Bill, the first question is: what are the Government's powers under the existing legislation?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What can the Government do about objectionable material now?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In essential respects, existing powers are wider than those proposed under the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We can refer to the Broadcasting Act, Telecoms Act, various other pieces of legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They allow orders to be made for the takedown of any material that is objectionable on grounds of public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The statements do not have to be factual or false.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They can be true, they can be opinions, they can, nevertheless, be ordered to be taken down under the current laws.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Two, current laws also criminalise the transmission of false or fabricated messages, including on the Internet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Licensed newspapers, broadcasters, including on the Internet, can be required to carry clarifications, other content.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Ministers can order to restrict financing, technical support, to offending websites and restrict their reach; can block offending websites and access to objectionable material.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Section 16 of the Broadcasting Act allows the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) to direct a broadcasting licensee to "take such action" with regard to content as it considers necessary to comply with the Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of these powers have existed since the 1960s.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Others were added on subsequently with the development of technology.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Laws had been updated; many of these powers also apply to online material.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Internet revolution took off in the 1990s. 1996 – the Class Licensing Scheme under the Broadcasting Act for Internet Content Providers was put in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Internet Content Providers (ICPs) are automatically licensed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All have to comply with guidelines under the Class Licence Conditions and the Internet Code of Practice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: IMDA has power to take down content that goes against "public interest, public order, national harmony", amongst other grounds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The new regime harmonised the legal framework for online news sites with the framework for traditional news providers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At that point in 2013, Members will recall, some persons created the "Hands Off My Internet" movement; "Free My Internet" Rally in Hong Lim; some painted doomsday scenarios, how there was going to be a "Chilling effect on Free Speech", death of free speech and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Online statements were circulated to take a strong stand against the licensing regime; online petition as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All of that had little to do with the truth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prior to the 2013 regulations, online news sites already had to comply with the same content standards, so there was no change in content standards.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Most people in the street do not even know of the	Broadcasting Act (BA) or other legislation and no impact on what they have been saying.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The powers under the BA have been used judiciously and discussions had carried on as before.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The arguments made in 2013 against the changes are similar to the arguments that are being made now, and I will explain that later.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now make the point that the Bill provides for a narrower set of powers, compared with powers that the Government already has.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is an important point when we make philosophical arguments in this House.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Earlier, I sketched out the existing powers and I have said the Bill is narrower in essential respects because it only applies to false statements of fact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In addition, it must be shown that the falsehoods are against public interest, which is set out in some detail in the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The current position, if Members compare the first point, the BA is broader on the types of material that can be taken down.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has the power to impose further obligations on licensees through their licensing conditions to correct falsehoods or shut down fake accounts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: IMDA can also require a licensee to carry any correction as directed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second point: powers under the BA are exercised by the Minister today, and there is no direct appeal to the Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The definition under the current law is wider, and the grounds for taking action are also broader.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Any statement, whether true or false, factual or opinion, if it is objectionable against public interest, national harmony, can be ordered to be taken down, subject to judicial review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Section 45 of the Telecoms Act criminalises falsehoods transmitted over the Internet and other modes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the Courts have long had to deal with the question of falsehoods in the law of torts, contracts, criminal law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The relevant provision of transmitting falsehoods is now under section 14D of MOA without any change; it has just been transported over.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of the discussions by those opposed to this Bill fail to consider what the SC report has said, and seem to be without an understanding of the existing position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not just narrower in scope but it also gives greater judicial oversight compared with the current law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Existing powers on takedown of objectionable material; the Government responses to be carried; other orders to be made; what oversight does the Court have today?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That was a considered decision by the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The process will be made fast and inexpensive for individuals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Other exercise of Government powers under the Bill, judicial review will be available, as is the law now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, whatever concerns there are about the Bill, they cannot logically be increased by this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Lawyers will know, when you have a narrower Bill and the facts come within the narrower Bill as opposed to the broader law, in general, the narrower Act will apply.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, in fact, that represents the narrowing of the current position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does the current law already criminalise transmission of falsehoods?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, these arguments about definition of fact, these concerns cannot be new.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We had similar provisions all this while with less judicial oversight.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, how does the Bill increase the concerns?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fourth, can a Minister order takedowns on broader grounds than under the Bill?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fifth, does the Bill give greater judicial oversight?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Having said that, Members can then ask, if the powers are narrower in essential respects, why is the Government introducing this legislation?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The existing legislation, with broad powers, have been in place for some time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An alternate approach was entirely possible which would be to rely on existing legislation with slight tweaks and add subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we relied on existing legislation, what we want to achieve under this Bill can be achieved as follows.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, rely on the BA as it is now for correction directions, takedown directions, general correction directions and demonetisation, to some extent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Section 16 of the BA allows IMDA to direct a licensee to "take such action" with regard to content as it considers necessary to comply with the Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, you have subsidiary legislation under the BA which can be passed, with account restriction directions, declaration of online location, advertising levers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then you move on to the existing class licensing scheme which can also be amended through subsidiary legislation to cover provision of content by individual publishers and clarify that Internet intermediaries like Facebook and Google are also covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, all of this could have been done under subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think anybody in this House would say we should not cover Internet intermediaries based outside Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we had taken this alternate approach, the powers would have been broad and there would be less judicial oversight.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Issues that have been raised – facts versus falsehoods, public interest, Ministerial action – there would be no amendments needed for the legislation; can rely on existing legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members can, therefore, see that if we had relied on existing legislation with the appropriate amendments, and if you map that against issues that have been raised in public – facts versus falsehoods, public interest and Ministerial action to take down – there would have been no need to amend.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we had taken that approach, the result would have been a blunt instrument with none of the calibration that the Bill proposes or the extent of judicial oversight, which is also going to be made speedier under the current proposals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the BA was essential at its time to achieve the objective of that Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It provides a balanced framework applicable to all forms of broadcast content.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is the need and the rationale for the Bill?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What are the substantive reasons for the Bill?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To understand that, we need to look at this larger context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Trends around the world affecting the very foundations of democracy, seriously impacting on societies, affecting the free flow of ideas, honest discussions and strangling the marketplace of ideas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that is the true nature of the exercise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the Bill is not a silver bullet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I will ask Members to bear with me as I set this out because it important for both Members and the public to understand the big picture before we can understand why this Bill is necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The SC dealt with a part of the issue, but if Members take one step back, what is the fundamental problem in many countries today?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is really a serious loss of trust in governments, in institutions both public and private, including the political system, the media, the professions, businesses, financial institutions and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is the reason for the loss of trust?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These developments have been aided by at least two other factors: the way traditional media has been behaving; and second, the effect of new media.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This loss of trust, in turn, has led to destructive populism in many countries, with serious consequences for democracies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will ask Members to bear with me as I explain each because what we are facing is a very serious situation across the world, and we will face it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And this is not something to be taken lightly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The very seriousness of what we are facing, what many countries in the world are facing, has to be understood.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not just this legislation, but everything that we are going to do as a Parliament, as a Government, as a society, hereafter, has to be seen in the context of what is happening.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Trust in institutions is important for society’s well-being and prosperity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Institutions deliver public goods for society: the Executive, Parliament, the Courts, the Army, the Police, and other institutions like the media, healthcare system, banks, the professions and universities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Institutions are the building blocks of democratic societies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People depend on institutions to deliver economic and social benefits.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They serve to manage diversity, hold communities together and keep extremist politics at bay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Institutions, in turn, depend on trust and legitimacy to work, to persuade the public to make sacrifices for the common good and to encourage societies to cooperate and come together to solve problems, to implement policies successfully, to take action for society’s benefit, and to steer countries through crises.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When people lose trust in institutions, it creates a vicious cycle.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Studies show, for example, low trust in the medical system has an impact on public health – management of disease outbreaks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Take law enforcement: perceived legitimacy of the Police is crucial to effective law enforcement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We can give examples in all sectors, but the basic point is that when trust in institutions is lost, society suffers, everyone suffers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is the situation in many countries in the West, in many countries?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Western democracies, trust in governments is falling significantly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a decline in nearly all countries in Europe.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the United States (US), a research centre's study shows public trust at "near historic lows".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The percentage of Americans with a great deal of confidence in the courts, 16%; 45% do not have much confidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the presidency, 19%; 54% do not have much confidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Americans have the least confidence in Congress – their parliament. 8% have a great deal of confidence; 71%, not much confidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Trust in other public institutions is also falling – in the media, the medical profession, the legal profession, many others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We were first included in the Edelman Trust Barometer in 2011.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are in the top "Trust" category and the Government is one of the most trusted institutions in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Trust in mainstream media, we are seventh out of 26 countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we cannot ignore the global risks, and we are likely to be impacted by the same forces.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Loss of trust in America has been described by the Wall Street Journal as "not merely a problem, but a crisis".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It speaks to a loss of trust in the political system as a whole and in democracy itself.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What has led to this loss of trust?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, rising inequality and inequity in many parts of the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the UK, on the eve of Brexit, the UK reached its wealthiest position in modern history.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Yet, in the previous two years, the overall wealth of the poorest 20% of UK households declined by 9%.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a very serious issue, and it is an issue in Singapore as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In absolute terms, living standards in most countries have risen, compared with previous generations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But absolute figures are just one part of the picture.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have to look at the reality of people's lives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Three indicators amongst many: social mobility, the quality of public education, jobs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Social mobility in the world's richest countries has stalled since the 1990s.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As of 2018, in the UK, it took five generations, or 150 years, for a child from the bottom 10% in terms of income to reach the average national income.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In France and Germany, it took six generations, 180 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the US, the public education system, the serious deficiencies have been documented.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And low investments in public education is one reason for lower social mobility.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, people lose faith in democracy as a whole.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the US, Australia, the UK, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Sweden and other countries, the percentage of people who say that it is "essential" to live in a democracy has fallen significantly, especially amongst the young.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: From 1995 to 2017, the share of French, Germans and Italians who favoured military rule, went up more than three times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: From 1995 to 2014, the share of Americans who favoured military rule, rose 2.5 times, from one in 16 to one in six.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Imagine that – one in six in America.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the desire for an upending of the status quo has serious consequences – destabilisation, with global effects.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will be very unwise for us to just watch and do nothing because it can sweep us over very quickly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I believe we are at one of those crucial turning points in history.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It may not quite be Gotterdammerung, but a turn for the worse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This weakening of democracy and institutions has been powered by a series of contributing factors, and I will mention two: media and new media.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Media has, in other countries, played a highly corrosive role, in eroding trust in many ways.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Australia, media played a major role in the ousting of former Australian Prime Ministers Kevin Rudd and Malcolm Turnbull.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Media attacked Turnbull savagely and regularly because the media owner did not agree with Turnbull's government policies, in particular, on climate change.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And media became an active participant in politics and decided outcomes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As he was being ousted, Turnbull said, and I quote, "The reality is that a minority in the party room, supported by others outside the Parliament, have sought to bully, intimidate others into making this change of leadership that they are seeking".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Kevin Rudd, another former Prime Minister, was also ousted by the media.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He wrote a scathing article and he said Murdoch ran a campaign to destroy his government in the 2013 elections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Murdoch's papers began to attack Rudd because Rudd planned to build a National Broadband Network that would be good for Australia, but Murdoch's cable monopoly would face greater competition.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Rudd described Murdoch as "the greatest cancer of the Australian democracy".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I quote, "A political bully and a thug who for many years has hired bullies as his editors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The message to Australian politicians is clear: either toe the line on what Murdoch wants or he kills you politically." He described, and I quote, "a cowering, fearful political culture across the country" – fear of personal repercussions, if you have challenged Murdoch's interests, and said that Murdoch's print media had "a disproportionate impact on setting the day's overall agenda", using a "masterful conflation of 'opinion' with 'news'." Such media environment, of course, erodes trust in government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at Britain, the baleful influence of media in British politics is well-documented.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It said: "Blair 'paid court' to Murdoch, securing Murdoch's patronage", Murdoch gave Blair the power to shut out detractors, used his newspapers to help Blair beat down his rival, Brown.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Brown, on the other hand, used the Daily Mail as a platform.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And Murdoch was opposed to the European Union (EU).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When asked why, Murdoch reportedly said, "When I go into Downing Street, they do what I say; when I go to Brussels they take no notice." Murdoch has since denied saying it, but the City Editor of The Times, Hilton, has stood by his account of what Murdoch said to him.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, with your permission, Mr Speaker, may I display slides on the LED screen?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Steven Barnett is a prominent parliamentary advisor and Professor of Communications in the UK.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said, "In the lead up to the June 23 EU referendum, British mainstream media failed spectacularly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Later, it admitted it was inaccurate Government on the one side; people on the other; media is intermediary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the media regularly trade in lies to attack the Government without basis, this happens – trust in government goes down.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An example of a great institution that is being savaged is the UK Courts, among the best in the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have spoken about this in the House previously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not wish to go into it but I have, in the attachment, set out how the British media have severely damaged the British judiciary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has the ability to influence minds and viewpoints.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, in many countries, traditional media has played a big role in the loss of trust.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I spoke about inequality, inequity, political systems not delivering results, media abusing its power, new media being abused.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: New media is the subject of this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will come back to it and deal with it in greater detail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But let me first complete the larger point on the consequences of the four aspects coming together.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members can then see what happens when you do not deal with the very real dangers of these developments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In an active democracy, the foundations include trust, free speech and the infrastructure of fact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The four elements I referred to, have combined, like a battering ram, to damage, destroy these foundations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When people lose trust, when they lose faith, when there is no proper public discourse, when infrastructure of fact is damaged, then democracy, societies are at serious risk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Violence will rise, particularly towards the minorities, the weak.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The ability of countries to face challenges will be weakened.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The crisis of trust in many countries has opened wide the doors to dangerous, destructive politics, populism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Populism both exploits and deepens the loss of faith in the system, making it harder for institutions to correct and to find solutions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Gallup has said, and I quote, when people hold "low trust in government and low or static expectations for their future lives", support for populist, anti-establishment politics increases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A politics that can – and has, in some countries – destroy democracy and replace it with corruption.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The 2017 Edelman Trust Barometer drew a direct link between the lack of trust in public institutions and these populist movements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Populists used these fears as ammunition to feed the crisis of trust in institutions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And 2016 saw populist movements make major gains.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Eurasia Group said populism is a force in US politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And in Europe, populist political parties are getting close to or are in government positions in several countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is the serious situation that faces many countries, and we will face it as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why I referred to Gotterdammerung earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many issues: inequality, inequity, political system failing to deliver, traditional media, new media, the impact leading to loss of trust and to populism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And to try and help support the infrastructure of fact and promote honest speech in public discourse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is an important part, even as we work on the other aspects.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, I turn to falsehoods and new media.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many societies, including ours, are pluralistic and diverse, with competing interests and identities, with religious diversity as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Various interest groups – non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and other associations are there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It can give rise to instability and conflict.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: James Madison, one of America's founding fathers, argues that the "factions" in a diverse society cannot be controlled.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Only the effects of such factions can be countered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And a key foundation of a democracy is public discourse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ideally, public discourse will help citizens understand complex policy issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will guide policymakers to make optimal decisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will shape differing viewpoints and expand common ground.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But public discourse can only take place when there is free and responsible speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The prerequisites for national conversations are a common vocabulary, an underpinning of facts and that provides a platform for accommodation and compromise amongst diverse voices in society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A critical piece of infrastructure in these conversations is fact, and the infrastructure of fact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is necessary so that we can have diversity without conflict, and public participation while still getting decisions made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: William Davies, the English sociologist and political economist has said, and I quote, "The fact that millions of people are able to believe the same things about reality is a remarkable achievement, but one that is more fragile than is often recognised." A critical reason for this remarkable achievement, and I quote Davies again, is "something so ubiquitous, so ordinary, that we scarcely ever stop to notice it: trust.” This is the trust that when public institutions – the Government, the media and other institutions – share a piece of information with the public, they do so honestly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Trust in public institutions is a cornerstone of the infrastructure of fact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The belief in the authenticity of the source, whether it be the media, the Government, experts or other authoritative sources, makes society accept facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Authenticity, of course, has to be earned, maintained.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if a usually trusted source is not telling the truth, there must be avenues to expose and there must be consequences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People will then believe that if it is said, it is likely to be true.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if not true, it will be exposed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are amongst the foundations on which modern societies are based.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are bigger than the government of the day.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is about the basic structure of society New media has been heavily exploited to batter this infrastructure of fact which, in turn, weakens trust in public discourse, in institutions, in democracy itself.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now set out how falsehoods have been weaponised to attack the infrastructure of fact, to destroy trust, and to attack societies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has got many by ways, links to different groups in society, and to everyone.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has now been used to send out on an industrial scale, falsehoods, to mislead people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Broad sections targeted, but also specific groups targeted, and individuals are targeted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, let us look at some sources of falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a military doctrine that has been developed for the Internet age.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Basically, he says, the "rules of war" have changed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Non-military measures, including information operations, they can be harnessed to, in turn, harness what he calls the "protest potential of the population".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Information operations can target and create internal opposition as a "permanently operating front" throughout the target country.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These non-kinetic military measures, in many cases, can exceed, as his doctrine says, the power of force and weapons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even though military or overt violent measures are not being used, the target states’ national sovereignty and security are threatened and violated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this way, the lines between war and peace have now blurred and wars no longer have to be declared.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Security experts gave evidence to the Select Committee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A national security expert from Latvia, Dr Janis Berzins, said that the notion of a broken social contract is the main vulnerability exploited by foreign adversaries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has military superiority in this region – experts said this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That superiority in conventional military forces means it will be futile to start a war with Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, therefore, militarily weaker countries will then focus on other means to weaken Singapore, sap our will from inside, create deep internal divisions and keep us in a permanent state of internal dissension.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The evidence is that this is already happening.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We know it is happening even though we do not come out in public and say it very openly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is happening to sap people’s support for the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF), for defence, to try and shift Singapore’s foreign policy as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are not issues that we should dismiss lightly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just assuming we go on the basis of the evidence that was presented at the SC, it has happened elsewhere and I will give Members some evidence of how it has happened.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It spread online falsehoods about atrocities being carried out against a particular community in Ukraine.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, that Ukrainian soldiers had crucified a child, which was later debunked.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Volunteers who fought against Ukraine said they were motivated because of these supposed atrocities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Loss of sovereignty, part of territory, loss of lives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you take the Czech Republic, disinformation operation by a foreign country was used to turn domestic sentiments in favour of a foreign state’s geopolitical goals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One objective was to make people believe that the US was responsible for the influx of Syrian refugees into Europe and the conflict in Ukraine.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The disinformation appears to have had some impact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it was done to weaken Czech support for NATO and Ukraine.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If it can happen in the UK and if it can happen in Germany, I believe it can easily happen here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A girl fabricated a claim that she had been assaulted by three Middle Eastern migrants.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Foreign media outlets reported on that widely, suggesting it was true, specifically from one country.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Berlin authorities investigated, confirmed the girl’s claim had been fabricated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But falsehoods were circulated online that the police had failed to follow up on the case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A Swedish defence agency said false information about subjects, such as NATO, immigration and terrorism, are spread "on a daily basis in Sweden." In many of these countries, trust is being eroded in institutions, populism is on the rise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Since Russia’s name had come up in the media, the SC invited Russia to help us and the Russian Embassy very helpfully sent us a letter that Russia is also very concerned about fake news and has been a victim of fake news.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we have no doubt that Russia takes this matter very seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Next, apart from foreign state actors, commercial profit is another dimension.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Digital advertising models have turned websites into virtual real estate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, value depends on the attention attracted, with every click, every view, digital ad revenue is earned.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This business model has created an attention economy, content that stokes fear and anger are good for attracting attention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Falsehoods can help people earn large sums of money and have political impact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the US, an American named Paul Horner set up at least 20 fake news websites.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It tricked readers into thinking that they were mainstream sources like ABC News or Cable News Network.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He used his websites to publish fake stories, stoke partisan engagement, claimed that they were satirical, said he assumed people would fact-check.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But many did not, and they were fooled.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some examples of his falsehoods: during a government shutdown, President Obama used his own money to keep open a government-funded Muslim culture museum.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fox News reported the story as a fact, before retracting it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was opposed to President Trump but targeted conservatives with his fake stories because he found it more profitable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A BuzzFeed news investigation found a network of at least 43 websites, which together, published more than 750 fake news articles – a small study.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All of them used Google AdSense to earn digital advertising revenue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Towards the end of the 2016 US presidential elections, a small town in Macedonia became well-known as the registered home of at least 100 pro-Trump websites filled with sensational falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fake stories could gain the most traction amongst Trump supporters, they found.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sometimes they wrote their own articles, but often would just reuse falsehoods from alt-right websites in the US.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For five or six hours of work, he could earn about $1,000 a month.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, as Samanth Subramanian, a reporter with Wired, said, "This is the… disturbing heart of the affair: that the Internet made it so simple for these young men to finance their material whims and that their actions helped deliver such momentous consequences." Third category, deliberate individual actors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You had foreign state actors; you had people doing it for money; now, people who do it deliberately, and groups.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The SC found that in several countries, both local and foreign, civilians had spread falsehoods for political causes, affecting both their own countries and other countries as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Example again – far-right, nationalist groups, promoting more extreme politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Domestic alt-right in the US used falsehoods, drove major false narratives during the 2016 US presidential elections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Populists use lies to attack institutions, invoke divisive rhetoric.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They use conspiracy theories to explain complex issues in simple terms and trying to make people believe them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even the most extreme lies which we might think people will normally dismiss, become believed and it impacts very badly on public life.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: British historian and journalist Anne Applebaum said this about populist movements: "They don’t require belief in a full-blown ideology...most of them don’t deploy propaganda that conflicts with everyday reality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And yet…all of them encourage their followers to engage, at least part of the time, with an alternative reality." In the UK, falsehoods were spread extensively during the EU Referendum.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I spoke earlier about false claims in traditional media about Turks, Turkey and Brexit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Digital advertisements were also run by the Leave EU Campaign that Turkey was joining the EU, 12 million Turks would in that event move to the UK, if it remained in the EU.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A large part of the foreign-linked content related to refugees and immigration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But these falsehoods were used to create an alternative reality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you believed them, you would believe there was a conspiracy by the ruling elite to turn the UK and Europe into a Muslim caliphate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Muslims were campaigning for Sharia law to govern the UK, the Mayor of London, a Muslim, was sponsoring them and, in the UK, there are areas where Sharia law dominates and non-Muslims cannot enter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2018, YouGov did a survey of over 10,000 people, so it was a substantial survey.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Forty-nine percent of those who voted to leave the EU stated that this was true.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It also created a permissive environment for hate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was one of the most important events in their recent history.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A massive falsehood campaign may well have affected the outcome.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An investigative report in The Guardian by a British journalist, Caroline Cadwalladr explained.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She went to a town in Wales that probably received more EU funds than any other town and which still voted to leave the EU.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this town, the EU was funding a £350 million regeneration project, a £33 million college for further education, which had 29,000 apprenticeships for young people to learn a trade, a £77 million road improvement scheme and a £30 million railway line.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The town had one of the lowest immigration rates in the country.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was in Wales, which was a net EU beneficiary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But when Caroline interviewed the people in the town, she discovered the existence of an alternative reality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People believed the town was sending more money to the EU than it was receiving.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The EU had not only done nothing for the town, it had also brought a huge immigration problem, including from Turkey.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Welsh town had been a leftwing Labour stronghold.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Yet, the people were repeating information usually found in rightwing newspapers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She discovered that they were getting their information or misinformation from targeted digital ads on Facebook.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One of the most controversial claims in the UK during the referendum was that the UK sends £350 million a week to the EU.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not only plastered on buses but also run as digital ads aimed at specific groups of voters.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Despite the corrections, a 2018 King's College London study found 42% of the people who had heard this claim believed it to be true and 22% were unsure.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Only 30% correctly believed that it was false.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For a referendum that may have irreversibly altered the course of British history, these are serious consequences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the US as well, falsehoods and lies have been spread on a massive scale.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the false narratives were driven by the people who identified with the homegrown alternate-right movement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They largely sought to denigrate the establishment, attack Mrs Clinton's campaign.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Also at play: sophisticated foreign information campaign that sought to influence the outcome; undermine democratic institutions and the democratic ideals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There was the conspiracy theory that Mrs Clinton and other top Democrats were part of a child paedophilia ring operating out of a Pizza restaurant in Washington DC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The rumours began on Twitter, spread to other websites and online forums.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Claims got louder, hacked emails from Mrs Clinton's campaign were distorted to support the conspiracy theory.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An American man showed up at the Pizza restaurant to "self-investigate" and he brought a gun along with him.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People demonstrated in front of the White House declaring that the theory was real.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The falsehoods helped to create an alternate reality, one where a "deep state" existed within US institutions, which was conspiring against the American people and, if you are a part of this echo chamber, you would be told that then-President Obama was colluding with the UK spy agency to spy on Mr Trump.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mrs Clinton was linked to a mysterious explosion that killed one of her employees.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the 2018 Florida school shooting was really a secret government operation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The foreign agents also infiltrated other social media movements to spread falsehoods on both sides of issues – they were agnostic about that – and to create more divisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They amplified the falsehoods and widened the divides.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the political ground became fragile, fraught and conducive for foreign agents to operate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the experiences of these two countries show how, through a combination of falsehoods and digital technology, the foundations of democratic societies are severely attacked.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Falsehoods are used to undermine public trust, which is the cornerstone of our infrastructure of fact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are used to divide and polarise, tearing the social fabric.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And democratic discourse, accommodation and compromise become very difficult.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In these conditions, the political centre becomes hollowed out and people are driven to extremes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you take France, the Yellow Vest movement, at the centre of the movement are these "Anger Groups" on Facebook.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They appeared almost a year before the street protests began in Paris.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the lead-up to the protests, falsehoods were used to increase the sense that the system was failing and turning against the people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Images were falsely captioned as bleeding Yellow Vest protestors and then they were used to make the claim that media and government were hiding police brutality and violence against these protestors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: During the 2016 US Presidential Election, disinformation came from foreign operatives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in the mid-term elections, such campaigns were more domestic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Americans were targeting other Americans, using the same strategies that are said to have been introduced by the Russians.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The SC Report also mentioned an Asian country, it did not name it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is said to have an online cyber army and volunteers who promote the government’s policies and attack those who criticise those policies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Social media has also enabled hate to thrive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Falsehoods are often centrepieces of hate propaganda and, over the past few years, people have used online falsehoods to promote anti-immigrant, anti-Muslim prejudice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After the terrorist attack in Paris in 2015, a video was posted, described as showing "Moderate Muslims" celebrating the attack.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was actually a video of people celebrating a cricket match victory in Pakistan.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But nearly 500,000 views within a few hours.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Video was spread again after the terrorist attack in Paris in 2017 with the same false caption.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The terror attack at Westminster in London in 2017: it became viral.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a photograph of a Muslim woman walking past victims.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She was on her phone, face hidden from view, was falsely accused of ignoring the victims and treating the attack casually.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Later, it was later discovered that the tweet originated from a fake foreign account.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When moderate Muslims demonstrated against terrorism in London, a false story was spread that the demonstration was staged.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And in April this year, falsehoods were used to turn the Notre Dame fire into an anti-Muslim narrative.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A fabricated quote, ascribed to a Muslim US senator saying "they reap what they sow".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A video of Notre Dame burning with shouts of "Allahu Akbar" edited over.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Indonesia, a "Muslim Cyber Army" used falsehoods and hate speech to inflame sentiments against gays, Chinese.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have also seen this in Germany, Italy and Brazil, and all have rising populism, no coincidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Conspiracy theories harm trust in institutions overall, not just the specific institutions that they relate to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, so, people mistrust the very existence of an infrastructure of fact and disengage from public discourse altogether.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, as William Davies said, "…when trust sinks beneath a certain point, many people may come to view the entire spectacle of politics and public life as a sham…" So, in the digital age, almost anyone can make a falsehood go viral, or run a disinformation campaign.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Harm to public health when falsehoods are spread about healthcare.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No one can disagree that this is a serious threat and that it has to be dealt with head on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will say this to Members of this House on both sides and the Nominated Members of Parliament that even when this happens in Singapore, there will be a deep damage to the institutions which are beyond and above politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are seeing this happen before our very eyes in other countries which normally you could have assumed to be stable, much more stable than Singapore, much bigger than Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if that happens, that will damage society beyond repair.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there is no benefit to anyone, regardless of any political persuasion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is no benefit to see this happen because there is no benefit, whether political or otherwise, in seeing this happen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What are the tools that such actors use and what is the cost of such tools?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Digital technology has given falsehoods a new power.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fake accounts have been described as "foot soldiers" of disinformation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They may be run either by humans known as "trolls", or may be automated, in which case, they are called "bots".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of them cultivate persuasive online personas, gain followers, both real and fake, and used as fictitious leaders of public opinion, using falsehoods to sway minds, create impressions of public sentiment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Bots are used to artificially amplify falsehoods – megaphone for falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They draw attention to falsehoods, affirm them and make them appear to be more believable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Digital advertising tools are used to target falsehoods at susceptible segments of the population.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Search engine results manipulated so that false articles are prioritised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Social media groups and online chats are used to polarise and mobilise people to orchestrate conflict.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Falsehoods today travel easily and widely across multiple platforms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2017, a news article that a Russian aircraft had managed to electronically disable a US warship was posted on a Russian state-controlled news site.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The article used a parody that had been published a few years before and presented it as truth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can see how it is not just the labels that matter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People can be made to believe that parody is, in fact, true.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you need to look at the material objectively.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this slide, designed to glorify Russia, undermine confidence in the US Navy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In two days, it was picked up by mainstream outlets in the US and Europe.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In less than seven days, cross-posted on dozens of news sites and their social media pages, catered to different countries and demographics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fox News' version was shared over 27,000 times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Sun’s version was shared over 10,000 times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of the more prominent examples over the last three years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Facebook’s best estimate from 2015 to 2017, approximately 126 million people may have received content from accounts associated with this troll factory.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the 2017 French Presidential Elections, emails from then-candidate Emmanuel Macron’s campaign were hacked and leaked.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, #Macronleaks hashtag was used to guide Twitter users to false claims that the leaked emails showed evidence of illegal activity by Macron.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hashtag was then amplified through a network of trolls and bots and reached 47,000 tweets in less than four hours after the initial tweet. "Coordinated inauthentic behaviour" by fake accounts was also seen in the US' 2018 mid-term elections; 2018 Brazilian Presidential Elections; the US anti-vaccine debate; and in Indonesia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fake accounts have been used in very sophisticated ways.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A Twitter account belonging to one "Jenna Abrams" was created in 2014.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This appeared to belong to a young American woman.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Once she had built a following, she pushed a divisive set of views on immigration and Mr Trump, especially closer to the 2016 Elections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At one point, she had over 70,000 followers, quoted by dozens of high-profile media outlets, including The Washington Post, the British Broadcasting Corporation and the New York Times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it turned out to be a fake account created by a foreign troll agency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Twitter account impersonating the Tennessee Republican Party, also created by the same agency, spread falsehoods: President Obama had admitted he was Muslim; an employee of Clinton’s was killed in a mysterious explosion in Washington and Clinton was involved.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At one point, it had over 152,000 followers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The real Tennessee Republican Party account had less than 14,000 followers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, trolls, bots, can and have been used in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have noticed these spikes in activity from inauthentic accounts when we have discussions on various issues of public concern.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It manipulates perception, creates the impression that there are many voices, shouts down other viewpoints through fake accounts, shifts public opinion, erodes trust and undermines institutions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Members turn to digital advertising, it is done to sway public opinion used on both sides of the Atlantic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Foreign operatives were using it in a disinformation operation to influence the US Elections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was also used by the Vote Leave campaign in the UK.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These tools allow messages to be micro-targeted with a high degree of precision at specific groups based on a variety of indicators, including people’s fears and prejudices.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are able to do so because the personal data of each user is harvested by platforms like Facebook.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Almost 2,000 ads used interest-based targeting and, of those, 800 were geographically targeted, including at swing states.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Remember, in some swing states, the margin of victory was in the tens of thousands.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Targeted digital advertising was used in these campaigns because it was effective.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Study by network theorists showed that when falsehoods are initially aimed at those predisposed to believe them, they spread further.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another troubling aspect of targeted advertising is that it is hidden from public view.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Others cannot see the falsehoods being spread, they are unable to step in to correct them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And again, as British journalist, Carole Cadwallader, said in a Ted Talk: "…this entire referendum took place in darkness, because it took place on Facebook.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And what happens on Facebook stays on Facebook, because only you see your news feed, and then it vanishes, so it's impossible to research anything.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we have no idea who saw what ads, what impact they had, what data was used to target these people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or even who placed the ads, how much money was spent, even what nationality they were." Third, the algorithms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They can play a big role in promoting falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Roger McNamee, who was an early investor and advisor to Facebook, said this about the 2016 US Elections: "Facebook's algorithms have played a huge role in this election cycle by limiting each member's news feed to 'things they like', which effectively prevents people from seeing posts that contradict their preconceptions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Trolls on both sides have exploited this bug to spread untruths and inflame emotions." Platforms' algorithms have boosted conspiracy theories, false claims to the top of search results, recommendation lists and news feed rankings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: By giving them prominence, the falsehoods are made to seem more credible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This spread of falsehoods is also aided by service providers in a growing commercial disinformation industry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Cybersecurity firm TrendMicro gave evidence before the SC of the going rates for tools and services.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One hundred Twitter followers, likes, or retweets, 34 cents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Make a falsehood appear on a YouTube main page for two minutes, US$621.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Make false content appear on legitimate news sites as if it is real, costs a bit more, US$20,000.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To use online propaganda to instigate a street protest in the US, US$200,000, but you can actually get a street protest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are also "hired guns" who spread disinformation for their clients in return for a reward, a market opportunity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Latin America, you have Andres Sepulveda convicted of rigging elections throughout Latin America in return for payment from clients.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He used the cyberspace to spread falsehoods on key domestic issues and policies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Indonesian authorities uncovered one such syndicate, Saracen Cyber Team.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In a 2018 survey by Ipsos, a global independent market research agency, on Singaporeans, 91% of Singaporean respondents could not correctly identify one or more of five false headlines presented to them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They take advantage of the attention spans, mental shortcuts, cognitive biases of reasonable, rational people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, every day, all of us decide which issues to give our time and attention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A lot of the information we come across, we make quick judgements, based on who it comes from, how aligned it is with what we know and believe.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are the human loopholes that falsehoods seek to exploit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People’s socio-political identities can play a key role in why people believe and share falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is consistent with psychological studies on confirmation bias.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Members can see from all this that in the Digital Age, the conditions supporting a Shared Reality have fundamentally changed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: From a main artery sustained by mainstream newspapers, public discourse is fragmenting into millions of social media groups and conversations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mainstream media was likened by law professor Dr Thio Li-Ann to a public street.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On this street, she said, "you might encounter not only friends, but a … variety of people engaged in a wide array of activities." In this system, people are made to see and show civility towards viewpoints they may not otherwise like and choose to see.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is designed to connect people with whom they want to be connected with, usually people they know or like, or who are like-minded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They allow people to cut themselves off from the views and information they do not like.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The SC heard testimony from Dr Simon Hegelich and Mr Morteza Shahrezaye, the political data scientists.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Hegelich had advised German Chancellor Angela Merkel.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They described the use of social media for public discourse as "an enormous misfit in design".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On social media, communication is guided by private affinity and emotions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A world of likes, emoticons, memes and captions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, as Dr Hegelich put it: "…political discourse should not be convenient.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In democracies, politics should be the result of debates, which are often arduous, because a compromise between legitimate interests has to be found." In the aftermath of the 2016 US Election, a group of academics from America’s leading universities gathered to reflect on the problem of fake news.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One of their key conclusions was this, and I quote: "Current social media systems provide a fertile ground for the spread of misinformation that is particularly dangerous for political debate in a democratic society." For those who favour politics of polarisation, politics of misinformation over one of cohesion and reason, these conditions are ideal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Tech companies play a key role in all of this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They provide the platforms from which falsehoods and other content are spread.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have held themselves out as making the world a better place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The evidence over the years shows clearly, no.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One post, and I quote, only one of many such posts: "Kill all Muslims, don’t even let an infant of the dogs escape." In the midst of ongoing violence, what was Facebook’s response to this? "We have looked over the post.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It doesn’t go against one of our specific community standards." The Sri Lankan Communications Minister highlighted a tweet from this user as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Last year, in London, Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong questioned the Facebook’s representative on this post.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The terrorist leader had made videos to gain thousands of followers, called for attacks against other religious groups, led to several previous attacks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But YouTube and Facebook removed the videos only after the Easter bombings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You see the slides of the photos of the victims.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, what do we say to them? "Sorry, we made a mistake"?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As Mr Allan said to Edwin Tong, "Sorry, we made a mistake"?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Big Tech has continuously refused to take down hate speech, ban groups promoting hate speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As one American journalist put it: "Facebook’s world, Facebook’s rules." The fact is that the more users, more content on their platforms, the more user attention they can sell to advertisers, and the more they can profit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have also created a permissive online environment for hate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Copycat shooting in California in a synagogue where the whole thing was live streamed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Chair of the UK Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee, Damian Collins said, it was a "terror attack designed for social media", demonstrated why there had to be statutory regulation for social networks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Only now, Facebook has banned white nationalism from its platforms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Facebook was questioned by the US Senate on whether they had plans to ban the purchase of ads using payments made in foreign currency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Last year, I asked the same question during the SC hearings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Twitter, two years after the US Election, most of the accounts linked to the foreign disinformation campaign were found to be still active.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The recent Indonesian General Election platforms helped disinformation spread, take root faster.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In November 2016, Mr Zuckerberg said, "It is a pretty crazy idea" to think that fake news on Facebook had influenced the 2016 US Election.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ten months later, when there was clear evidence of serious foreign interference, he apologised for having being dismissive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In November 2017, Facebook was questioned by the US Senate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They promised to do better but said they would prefer to self-regulate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The recent release of internal EU Commission documents showed that over the last four years, Facebook has pushed back against regulation; consistently said regulation will stifle innovation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To our SC in March last year, they took the same line. "Prescriptive legislation" would make it harder for Facebook to find the right solutions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In March this year, one day before we tabled this Bill in Parliament, Mr Zuckerberg said regulation against harmful content is needed, the problem too big for them to handle.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Facebook made this concession because it had no choice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In February 2018, a UK parliamentary committee questioned Facebook on whether it had provided user data to Cambridge Analytica, which had used data mining to help political candidates and groups target potential voters.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Simon Milner, Facebook's representative, said to the UK parliament Facebook had not provided such user data to Cambridge Analytica, did not disclose that the user data had been taken by Cambridge Analytica, and he knew of it at the time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I questioned Mr Milner about this during the SC hearing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He then conceded he should have given a more frank answer to the UK committee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: New Zealand's Prime Minister Ms Jacinda Ardern, has said: "We cannot simply sit back, accept that these platforms just exist and what is said on them is not the responsibility of the place where they are published.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It cannot be a case of all profit and no responsibility." I also read Nominated Member Prof Lim Sun Sun's opinion editorial (op ed) on this point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Her view is that the Government, big tech and consumers should come together and work in a tripartite fashion rather than relying on legislation alone.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have said on this subject as well as other subjects.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: By itself, legislation cannot achieve all the needed objectives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We want them to do well in Singapore and as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we must work with them to solve problems.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But at the same time we need to be quite clear about the dynamics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And there is little incentive for them to do things which will affect their profits.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Singapore, they must know, we must make sure they know there is public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And they know that the Singapore Government cannot be bought.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do not take money from their lobbyists and we mean what we say.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore provides a proper rule of law framework for everyone, but they must also be responsible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Last year's SC proceedings and their dealings with us would have left them in no doubt that they can push back when necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Throughout, in good faith, we have had constructive discussions with them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But let me give Members a recent example.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: AIC is a lobby group for tech companies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And his op ed was full of basic errors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One of the points he made, he referred to clause 61, the exemption clause, and said that this was troubling.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This clause gives the power to exempt and really will help tech companies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because where they cannot comply, they can show reasonable reasons why they cannot comply, exemptions can be given.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am speaking in Parliament on Tuesday and if I do not get any response before I speak, I will assume that tech companies do not want this clause".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because how do I tell the Members of this Parliament that this is primarily to help tech companies when they themselves say they do not want it?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They said they appreciated Senior Minister Edwin Tong's clarification on the exemption clause and they appreciated the Government's efforts to make POFMA technically feasible for tech companies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is what they need to see from us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Tech companies will say many things to try and advocate their position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to show them we are fair but also firm, and then they will deal with us in a business-like way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There cannot be and I do not think there is any serious dispute that legislation is necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This Bill is based on the SC report which explains what outcomes should be achieved.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We think the setting out in the Bill will best achieve the outcomes the SC had identified.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong will go through the specific provisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now deal with some of the criticisms of this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Han Yong May had a good commentary in Lianhe Zaobao some weeks back.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She said: (a) there is nothing wrong with questioning whether the powers under POFMA will be abused; (b) but people should first read the Bill in detail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is part of responsible speech and, if they did, they would understand that certain things people have been saying about it are untrue; and (c) at the same time, she had a piece of advice for the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Please understand that some people may be genuinely concerned and do not see shadows and treat them as being purely antagonistic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The following are some of the points that have been made about the Bill: (a)	it gives too much power to the Government; (b) it will have a "chilling effect" on free speech – that phrase again; (c)	definition of fact and opinion is not clear; (d)	definition of public interest is too wide; (e) difficult to challenge the Minister’s decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If a Minister declares that an article contains falsehoods and asks for a Correction Order to be carried, or in some cases, take down, it is open to challenge in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the Minister is wrong, he gets overruled.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And this inaccurate claim is then sought to be backed up by a series of other inaccurate claims.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, it creates a new crime; spreading of falsehoods is a new crime.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It already exists under section 45 of the Telecoms Act (TA), now under the MOA, and applies to the Internet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: TA criminalises falsehoods; the Bill covers the same ground, falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in terms of intent, it requires the person to have known or had reason to know not only that it was false, but also that spreading it was likely to prejudice public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, in fact, there are two requirements for knowledge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And both requirements have to be satisfied, even though it is based on having reason to know.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whereas under the TA, it is just sending out of falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, it is often said that recourse to judicial review is not available under the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, a judge cannot examine the proportionality of a direction.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fourth, power in clause 61 of the Bill to exempt certain persons from the Act can be used for some unstated sinister purpose.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This exemption power is a common provision in many pieces of legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is found in the Executive Condominium Housing Scheme Act, Postal Services Act, Active Mobility Act, Dangerous Fireworks Act and a wide variety of laws.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I explained, for example, when it is not possible to comply with the Act, due to reasons, such as technical impossibility, then we could rely on this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Next, some academics have said that: (a)	truth is relative; (b) impossible to state what is a "fact" as opposed to what is "false and misleading"; and (c) this will affect academic work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung will respond on matters specific to academia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Their concerns appear to be expressed without an understanding of the existing legal position, how this Bill fits in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I am not sure how many of them are aware of the BA, TA, MOA and other legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just to give Members a couple of examples.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Did they know about the current legal position?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another signatory, in a recent interview with Civicus, an international NGO, made several completely erroneous statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He, unfortunately, seems to conflate the two and says that if it contradicts public interest, then we can declare it as false.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, if you believe that, then you will get very worried.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I read the interview more than once to try and see that is what he really meant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If that is what the Bill states, it will be quite illogical – "it is false because public interest is involved".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If a Singaporean academic can be mistaken on such a basic point or a set of points, then it is understandable that foreign academics would have signed without an understanding of appreciation of the true position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I have said, laws that target false statements of facts have been around for a long time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is no legal or logical basis for the concerns that this Bill will stifle academic research specifically.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, Minister Ong Ye Kung will respond later on some points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is better to rely on existing case law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When there is a dispute, the matter can be dealt with by the Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think this must be one of the most overused phrases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Free speech should not be affected by this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are talking here about falsehoods, we are talking about bots, we are talking about trolls, we are talking about fake accounts and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prof Thio Li Ann gave evidence during the SC hearings on the ambit of free speech and whether falsehoods were free speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She made the following points: not all forms of speech are worthy of equal protection.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, if you falsely cry "fire" in a crowded theatre, that is not protected as valuable speech; UK House of Lords' judgement: "There is no human right to disseminate information that is not true.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No public interest is served by communicating misinformation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The working of a democratic society depends on the members of that society being informed and not misinformed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Misleading people, purveying as facts statements which are not true is destructive of the democratic society".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Where speech does not serve the justifications for free speech, by harming the search for truth or by preventing citizens from becoming informed of issues – that does not warrant protection.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
