text: Those statements must be false statements of fact in the first place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some have said that the definition of what is in the public interest is too wide, and that it should not include clause 4(f), which relates to the diminution of public confidence in the functions of Government institutions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have explained earlier in some detail, maybe too considerable a detail, on how slow-drip, online falsehoods seek to break down trust by attacking institutions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is important to protect institutions from such falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if Members look at the point I made many times, you look at the current definition and you look at the existing definition, you decide for yourself which is wider.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then it is said it is difficult to challenge a Minister's decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have previously said, the process that will be in place, it will be fast, it will be simplified to allow individuals to appear and present arguments on whether it is true or false.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The detailed procedure will be in a subsidiary legislation and that is usual.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I will set out an overview of the process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is consistent with the usual position of exhausting administrative remedies before resorting to the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will provide a standard form online for aggrieved persons to use.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The appeal to Court will be similarly quick.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He can file the very next day if he wants, after the Minister decides on the application to cancel a Direction.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Simple standard forms will be provided for the appeal documents that an appellant can fill out and file in the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts will be asked to fix the hearing within six days of an application being filed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The appellant must attend before the Duty Registrar to request for an expedited hearing, again in the manner prescribed by the rules of the Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The documents will need to be served on the Minister no later than the next day.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, an email address will be provided for the appellant to serve the documents on the Minister, to make it easy for him.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Minister must then file his or her reply in Court no later than three days after the documents are served as prescribed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As stated earlier, meanwhile, the Court would have already fixed the hearing no later than six days after the date on which the Court first received the application.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this includes the time the Minister responds, the time for filing, the time for him to file and the time for the Minister to respond and the hearing, that is, beginning to end.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If he moves very fast, it can be nine days.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court will continue, of course, to have a general discretion to extend timelines where there is good reason to do so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How long the hearing takes and how long the Court takes to decide are matters for the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Parliament and the Executive cannot intervene in that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We can say when it should be heard; we cannot say when it should be decided.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Court fees will be kept very low for individuals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Further days of hearing will be charged at the usual rate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But even then, the Court will have power to waive fees.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But this should not be taken as a licence to abuse the process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Courts will still have the power to deal with parties in the usual manner, including how they conduct themselves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Eugene Tan of Singapore Management University suggested we use illustrations during the Second Reading to explain the difference between fact and opinion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I asked for some illustrations from groups which we met – the Community for Advocacy and Political Education (CAPE) and students from NUS and academics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The list is enclosed and circulated to all Members and will form part of the record.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A Professor of Law states that the death penalty in Singapore does not deter crime, as shown by several studies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is a conclusion drawn from the studies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a statement of opinion not covered by the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if that professor refers to a non-existent study, or non-existent data, then it is a false statement of fact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This example is drawn from a recent incident and was one of the illustrations submitted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A person, say, "A", states that the Government is showing "double standards" by having two different permit regimes to govern public activist events on political issues on the one hand, and a public meet-up by an influencer on the other.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is true that two different permit regimes apply to the two different kinds of events.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Therefore, "A's" statement is an opinion and is not covered by the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, if "A" says or implies that the same permit rules govern both kinds of events and double standards were applied for the granting of permits, essentially suggesting bias, based on the point that the same legislation and rules apply for both, that is a false statement of fact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Forms of clarification will be set out in subsidiary legislation, basically, a link to where the clarification can be found with the statement that the article contains inaccuracies or is false, and reference given to the link to the true facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And people can read both documents and decide for themselves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It actually encourages a more honest and more open discussion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another illustration: an economist states that the home ownership rate in Singapore is only 9% and explains that the definition of "home ownership" used excludes any lease, regardless of whether the lease is nine years or 99 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is a conclusion based on a certain methodology.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He says that and he sets it out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government can, of course, disagree with that view.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If, however, the economist says that the number of persons who own freehold property in Singapore is X, when it is actually Y, then that is a false statement of fact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another illustration: "B" publishes an online article stating that the social welfare system in Singapore has gaps.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That conclusion is drawn from interviews with Government officials and social workers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government can disagree with the conclusion, but it does not come within the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If, however, B's article says that welfare assistance had been denied to a needy elderly person when assistance had, in fact, been given, then it is a false statement of fact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Members can see that it will be clear when you look at examples.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If public interest is affected, then it can come under the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In all of these, it is not enough to show it is false.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a situation where, again, the original article can carry a clarification.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will use another recent incident to illustrate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the illustrations, once you look at them, I think they are quite clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It really ought not to be an issue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we have had this legislation in the books forever.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Next, let me turn to the Notice of Amendment (NOA) put up by the Nominated Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is useful for me to set out our views on the NOA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said elsewhere, there is substantial agreement between the Nominated Members and us on the major points of the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The differences we have on the Directions' regime are mainly on matters of process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, the three Nominated Members have proposed that the Directions provide more specific reasons on falsity and public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I agree with the principle underpinning the first part of this proposal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we intend to set this out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When the Directions are given, there must be a statement as to why it is false.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The legislation is specifically designed for this purpose.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Clause 13 allows for subsidiary legislation to be made to set out the requirements for Directions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When a Minister issues a Direction, what kind of information should be contained in that Direction?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why something is false, as I have explained, should be explained in the Direction.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is difficult to set out upfront.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It must be left in each case what extent of detail should be specified.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is really more appropriate to use subsidiary legislation to set out the requirements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And subsidiary legislation is law and it is public, transparent and open to scrutiny.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Separately, on public interest, again, I am not comfortable requiring a setting out of detailed reasons on how a particular course of action serves public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The level of detail depends on each case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is difficult for Parliament today to envisage what are the types of cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How are you even going to start setting out what level of detail ought to be set out?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You do not even know what the case is about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But you must set out enough detail and, if not, you take the risk of a Court challenge and then you go and explain to the judge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If there is a challenge, the Government will have to show "public interest" and we will have to explain in Court why the information provided is adequate and depends on whether the Court accepts the explanation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is the best way of dealing with these things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You cannot go upfront and try to legislate every detail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second proposal is to set out in the primary legislation that appeals to the Minister must be adjudicated without delay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is just a difference on how it should be implemented.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Timelines are usually set out in the subsidiary legislation and I have set out what the timelines are that we are going to put in place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will be in law, by way of subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we are going further than what the three Nominated Members have proposed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Their amendment proposes the "Minister shall do everything reasonable to ensure that appeals to the Minister are adjudicated without delay.".... "High Court hearings shall commence as soon as practicable, and that costs to the appellant are minimised”.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assuming you put these broad principles in legislation without any specifics, what is "as soon as practicable" and what is "without delay"?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Court hearings today can take anything within 12 to 18 months, sometimes longer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if we had it in six months, is that "as soon as practicable"?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, one should avoid this sort of imprecise language in legislation because the Minister shall respond "as soon as practicable" – is that 12 days, 14 days or 30 days?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How are you going to say, "Well it takes six months for the hearing to take place." The short answer to that will be, "Well, you know, it is "as soon as practicable" compared to the fact that it takes 18 months now." You really do not want to go into that territory.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What you want are precise timelines, the kind of timelines I have given.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: From the time you send the Notice to the Minister to the time you are in Court, very precise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you get your act together, nine days.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I am arguing against the Government being given more time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think it is good enough simply to say do everything reasonable to decide quickly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You must mandate that the Minister decides within a certain time period and it is not enough for the High Court hearings to commence as soon as practicable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We should set out when the hearings should start.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The third proposal made by the Nominated Members is the proposal to insert key principles into the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The three Nominated Members want to insert certain principles.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, frankly, without any disrespect, some of the proposals are unworkable and some others are unsuitable for primary legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I can understand that they are not lawyers, so let me just take them through.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at para (a), it covers the importance of critical thinking to a democracy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is acknowledged by the SC in recommendations 1 and 2.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it is one of the tools that supports the development of a well-informed public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is necessary then to push out the facts to the public by way of correction to inoculate them against the falsehood.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The evidence is set out in the SC Report, if Members look at paras 390 to 396 and 425.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You do not get much by adding this to the legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, there is a group of proposals which target, a sort of negative list about when statements are not false and when statements are not statements of fact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I understand the intent, which is to clarify matters.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if you look at your proposals (b) and (c), they essentially relate to the process of establishing truth and falsehood.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is an entire body of law in this area.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The law of evidence is there to deal with the question of how facts should be established.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The question of how truth or falsity should be established and it should draw from the body of principles that form part of case law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It would not serve the rigour of this process to point out some but not the others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, you go and start putting this thing in, you run the risk of trying to take out or deal with some parts of an existing body of law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts will deal with it where necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Similarly, on principle (g), I have already explained why it is preferable to rely on the existing case law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The third group of statements proposed in (d), (e) and (f) and they essentially relate to proportionality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government has gone one step further, perhaps more than one step further, than what you have proposed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Bill only deals with situations where there is a falsehood which affects public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it would not make sense to suggest that we insist upon non-legislative measures when public interest is at stake because there is a need to respond quickly to counteract the damage.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, does that mean that, by putting this in, that you do not ask for corrections?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I caution Members that it can lead to endless litigation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us say the Minister seeks to act under the Bill and there is a principle here; then it can be argued, "Well, you know, in this case you shouldn't act because it's not necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can take non-legislative measures." Someone argues that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It may fail, but that can take months.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It can create a fair bit of confusion as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we should just be very clear what the Bill provides, what is the framework for the Bill and try not to over-egg the pudding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We should have a robust debate here, explain what the Bill is all about, have it as a matter of record in the Hansard and that is used by the Courts as a matter of interpretation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the Nominated Members' concern about enshrining principles in a manner which would bind future governments, I think really is best served by the debate and by the Courts serving as an oversight mechanism and interpreting the provisions in future.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, you know, a future government can always amend.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a good attempt to ensure that the conversation on this important issue continues both on the nature of the problem and how the legislation is implemented.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government agrees that these conversations should continue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The question is, is establishing another council the best way?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On accountability, Ministers, the Executive, are responsible to Members of this House, to Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Every time there is an exercise of power which seems to Members to be not clear, you ask questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You just look at the questions that have been filed since you became Nominated Members, every major issue, anything that happens, from NUS to other areas, you do not need to wait for one year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is raised immediately and answers are given.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Singapore public must know this institution works and, if there is a question, it will be answered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There has got to be the trust as well and, where the trust is not merited, that has got to be exposed as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is meant to work in a democracy in this way where Members of Parliament hold the Ministers accountable and check and ask questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I think I have covered most of the major arguments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have set out the nature of the philosophical reasons for the Bill at some length – perhaps too considerable a length, for which I apologise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I will take Members through the key provisions in the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members who have read the SC report will notice that the Bill tracks closely the SC's findings and recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The measures in the Bill are designed to address, firstly, the impact of falsehoods; and secondly, the reasons underlying why falsehoods have had a severe impact.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On the impact of falsehoods, the SC made the following findings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But low-level falsehoods that have no immediate visible impact can be just as dangerous.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is found in paragraphs 105 to 107 of the SC report.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Minister has explained in detail how falsehoods harm democratic institutions and free speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The SC goes into this in some detail at paragraphs 121 to 138 of its report.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Falsehoods can also cause serious and sometimes fatal consequences for individuals and for businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is covered in paragraphs 139 to 151 of the SC report.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To understand why falsehoods have had such a serious impact, the SC heard extensive expert evidence on the psychology and mechanisms of how falsehoods work and operate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This can be found at paragraphs 152 to 177 of the SC report.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The core trick of falsehoods lies in their use to arouse anger, fear and negative emotions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There is also a stark power imbalance between facts and falsehoods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is very difficult for facts to overcome falsehoods organically.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Falsehoods move and take effect quickly, long before corrections can be put in motion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Hence, the importance of putting out corrections swiftly and circulating them vigorously.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The social transformations caused by the digital revolution have given falsehoods renewed power.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This was something that the SC also addressed at paragraphs 178 to 185.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is useful to see what this means in the Singapore context.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And on that score, the SC looked at it, evaluated, made its findings at paragraphs 208 to 237.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The SC ultimately concluded that such deliberate online falsehoods are a problem that Singapore has to take action against.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The SC also underscored the importance of having to preserve public trust, something that the Minister spoke about at some length.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It noted at paragraph 311 of the report that loss of faith in public institutions increased the success of disinformation operations significantly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There was very detailed discussion as well on legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Three broad positions emerged from the representations received.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Three, we take a hands-off approach altogether and leave matters to be dealt with organically by the marketplace of ideas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Committee considered these positions in some detail.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Its findings explained why the theory of the unregulated marketplace idea was based on assumptions that are flawed in the digital age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Why the conduct of tech companies – their repeated failures and inadequate responses pointed to a fundamental conflict of interest between their business goals and acting in the public interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Minister has also covered this point in some detail in his speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This Bill reflects the fundamental principle of calibration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Government examined the SC's various findings, some of which I have referred to earlier, and found this approach would, in the long run, be more supportive of encouraging good quality public discourse and increasing public trust.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We thus decided that a new approach is needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will be a shift away from the blunt tools that we already have and which many other jurisdictions are considering.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In considering how powers should be exercised, four decision-making models were discussed and considered by the SC.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is set out at paragraph 364 of the report.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The four models are: one, have Courts, including an expedited process; or two, an Executive, followed by recourse to the Courts; third, an independent body; and fourth, online platforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The SC made the following findings: one, that the BA already relies on Executive action; two, judicial process is not fast enough; three, in situations involving public order, national security and public institutions, only the Executive would hold the facts, and facts should be backed up by the Executive’s authority; judicial oversight could assuage concerns over the abuse of Executive power.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Consistent with the SC's recommendations, this Bill provides a toolbox of Government powers to address the impact of specific individual falsehoods and source of falsehoods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This implements recommendations 15 and 16 of the SC’s report.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I must emphasise that these levers remedy the impact of falsehoods primarily and not punish wrongdoers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, just because one might receive a Direction does not mean that that person has done something illegal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I mentioned earlier how the digital revolution has given falsehoods a new power.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In particular, the proliferation of social media services, content aggregators, blogs, search engines and other intermediary services, has profoundly changed the way we consume information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A large majority of the toolkit is, therefore, designed for platforms, not individual publishers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The tools fall into the following categories, which closely reflect the SC’s recommendations: one, providing access to and increasing the visibility of corrections, which implements recommendation 12 of the SC's report; two, disrupting fake accounts that amplify falsehoods, which also implements recommendation 12.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Likewise, discrediting online sources of falsehoods; and finally, the levers which cut off financial incentives of online sources of falsehoods which implements recommendation 15.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The provisions are divided into two fairly self-contained Parts: Part 3 for individual publishers and Part 4 for the platforms, which are the "persons" covered under this section of the Bill which are the Internet intermediaries, and mass media service providers such as newspapers, broadcasters and telecommunications service providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In line with this new approach, I mentioned earlier that the primary tool that we intend to use is the power to give people direct access to corrections.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: People will then have access to both the falsehood and the corrections, and they can decide for themselves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In such a case, the Directions add to and not remove the discourse.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In general terms, the corrections powers will require a person to "tag" a falsehood with a correction or amplify a correction generally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These powers are needed because of the difficulty of getting corrections to overcome the reach of falsehoods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The SC’s report covers the findings on this issue in great detail, at paragraphs 171 to 177.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, by way of example, the SC cited a 2018 study by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology that false news was 70% more likely to be retweeted than true news.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The SC also cited a very interesting study by a tech startup examining a rumour in 2017 about then-French Presidential candidate Emmanuel Macron.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It found that, on Twitter, there was almost no overlap between the audience of the rumour, which was false, and the audience of the correction of that same rumour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Research shows that corrections tend to be effective when they provide an explanation of the facts and give prior warning about the falsehood to come.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is also mentioned in paragraph 361 of the SC’s report.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As such, the Corrections Directions are designed with this in mind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Corrections will take the form of a notice warning people about the falsehood and the notice can set out the facts or provide a link to the facts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The powers relating to Corrections are set out in clauses 11, 21 and 23 of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are two main types of Corrections possible, both of which are designed in accordance with the recommendations in paragraph 361 of the SC’s report.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The first is set out in clauses 11 and 21.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For convenience, I will call this the Targeted Correction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A Targeted Correction must be made accessible to viewers of the falsehood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It acts as a warning tag on the falsehood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The second type of correction is set out in clause 23 and this correction must be generally amplified on certain platforms, such as news outlets and Internet intermediaries, even if these platforms are not carrying the falsehood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For convenience, I will call this the General Correction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A General Correction is important to inoculate the public before a falsehood reaches them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Psychological research has shown that corrections, used in the same manner as vaccines, can be very effective.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is especially appropriate when a campaign to put out falsehoods is ongoing, or a broad false narrative based on various lies could be developing and gaining traction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A General Correction can also help when a falsehood is serious and persistent, or is moving underground, into less visible spaces on closed platforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These powers are set out at clauses 12 and 22.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There can be a Direction to cease communication of the falsehood to viewers in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There can be a further order to require that a correction be communicated to those who had previously viewed the falsehood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill requires these Directions to be published in the Government Gazette.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Falsehoods, when spread online, may pass through hands and cascade through and move across different platforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To curb dissemination, it will be most effective to issue Directions to key nodes of dissemination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These will mainly be the Internet intermediaries, which almost always play a crucial role in the spread of online falsehoods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Directions could also, in some situations, be issued to those with large followings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It would often not make sense to issue Directions to every single person who shares a falsehood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Corrections must be published to users in a clear and conspicuous manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The phrase "false statement of fact" is, as already explained, a legal term drawn from existing law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It covers statements that a reasonable person would consider to be a representation of fact.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Opinions, comments, criticisms, are not covered by the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A statement is false, if it is false or misleading, whether wholly or in part, and whether on its own or in the context in which it appears.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This definition addresses the various ways in which reality might be distorted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Real words and real actions can also be edited and presented in a way that completely transforms their meaning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In a live interview, Hillary Clinton’s adviser referred to a news article that had blamed Clinton for the death of US diplomats in Afghanistan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A clip of the interview was shown out of context to say that Clinton’s own adviser had blamed Clinton for the deaths.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In Sweden, a real police report listed "vulnerable areas" where police needed to regularly respond to volatile situations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A Swedish newspaper columnist exaggerated the report and claimed that there were 50 "no go" zones in Sweden, areas filled with illegal immigrants that were too dangerous for even the police to enter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This reportedly remains one of the most persistent myths in Sweden, despite repeated attempts to debunk it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Similarly, news reports that omit material facts can be a falsehood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This, as experts told the SC, is a common disinformation tactic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, in Germany, online news websites spread a girl’s claims that she had been raped by refugees, and that the police were covering it up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They showed real interviews but omitted the police’s debunking of the claim.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This led to thousands of people protesting on the streets against the alleged cover-up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This means that Directions can be used against both open and closed platforms and also remain flexible enough to deal with falsehoods spread on platforms that are developed in the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Platform neutrality was, in fact, an important design principle, based on the SC’s own findings at paragraph 362.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In particular, evidence was given to the SC of the serious concerns with falsehoods in closed spaces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As falsehoods can be hidden from view, they are ideal platforms for the deliberate spread of falsehoods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Researchers believe that in closed spaces, people are more susceptible to emotive falsehoods, because these are the spaces inhabited by the familiar and trusted, those they know.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill, therefore, recognises that platforms that are closed are not necessarily private.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They can be used not only for personal and private communications, but also to communicate with hundreds or thousands of strangers at a time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Closed platforms – chat groups, social media groups – can serve as a public megaphone as much as open platforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As regards closed platforms, even those with end-to-end encryption, the legislation also covers them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will also find additional ways of dealing with the harm that can materialise from falsehoods spreading on encrypted closed platforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, in such a case, a General Correction order may be used instead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is not enough, as the Minister mentioned earlier, for there to be a false statement of fact.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It must also be in the public interest for the Direction to be issued.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Government powers recommended by the SC were intended to prevent the public interest from being harmed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 4, therefore, sets out a non-exhaustive list of examples of public interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This list reflects the dangers of deliberate online falsehoods identified by the SC, based on real events around the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Minister had already explained the thinking behind the definition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Select Committee stated, at recommendation 12, "There should be adequate safeguards in place to ensure due process and the proper exercise of power, and give assurance to the public of the integrity of the decision-making process… Measures… should include judicial oversight where appropriate." At the same time, the Committee also stated that "The measures will need to achieve the objective of breaking virality by being effective in a matter of hours." That is a quote from the SC's report.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill thus incorporates both speed and due process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: An appeal can then be brought to the High Court to set aside the Direction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Minister has outlined the procedure in the House earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This, in our view, is the best way to be effective, while ensuring that there is always adequate judicial oversight.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Executive weighs the competing interests and acts decisively to protect society, and the Courts will then have the final say over whether the content in question is false.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: During the SC process, some representors preferred a Court order to an Executive Direction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But even an expedited Court process may not be fast enough to deal with virality, some of which examples Members have seen outlined in the Minister's speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Falsehoods can reach many with great speed, and lead to serious consequences just as quickly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In Indonesia, a falsehood was spread that a pro-communist rally was being held.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In France, false posts were put out claiming that leaked campaign documents showed that Macron was engaging in illegal activity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The claims were posted just hours before an election reporting "black-out" – similar to our own "cooling-off" period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The posts were then amplified by bots, trolls and fake accounts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In 2017, a falsehood was put out that the founder of a cryptocurrency called "Ethereum" had died in a car crash.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill has benefited from the analysis of the relevant issues by the SC who had many representors come forward, many of whom had experience and some of whom are experts in this field.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Since time immemorial, a battle for hearts and minds has taken place among people who host different views and seek to persuade others of their beliefs and causes; among politicians at the hustings; among companies through elaborate public relations exercises and spin; and between countries, most vividly played out during the Cold War between the US and the former Soviet Union, each forwarding the superiority of the capitalist and communist systems respectively.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What we refer to as fake news today, with misinformation and disinformation at its core, has been the domain of propaganda in the days before the Internet.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As framed by Claire Wardle in her submission to the SC, at one end of the spectrum, misinformation has been a method of choice of individuals, politicians, companies and countries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Here, misleading content, false context and imposter content dominate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the other end is aggressive disinformation with falsified or manipulated content which seeks to deceive an audience or a reader.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is usually the domain of sophisticated state and well-endowed non-state actors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The advent of the Internet and, more recently, social media – where communication has been democratised with both positive and negative repercussions – has brought the ease of propagating fake news centrestage.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The political economy of social media companies and their algorithms which are skewed at extracting profits, in some cases regardless of the consequences, accentuate the problem.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Bots and the existence of enterprises that charge for services to manipulate the public discourse, subvert democracy and elections and weaponise information, have become a feature of the online world, with many examples highlighted to the SC.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Over the last few years, Western powers have identified Russia’s employment of hybrid warfare, combining both a hostile information campaign employing both misinformation to disinformation before and during the onset of hostilities as the norm for future conflicts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, it would be a mistake to suggest only Russian involvement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The arc of history has proved that many countries, even those friendly to Singapore, are no less seasoned at subversion and subverting even democratic forces in other countries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And it would be naive to assume that the employment of misinformation and disinformation is not a permanent aspect of the world we live in today, much of which is lived online.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The question is: how should Singapore deal with the problem?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: After spending a long time deliberating the nature of the problem, including forming a SC of Parliament, the Government decided not to consult the public on how it preferred to tackle the problem.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, a lot of the public apprehension over the Bill can be located in its choice of the decision-making authority on matters concerning online falsehoods – the Executive.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The remedies available under the Bill are virtually identical to those individuals and companies can rely on under the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In deciding that the Executive will determine what is an actionable falsehood and what is not, there has been significant disquiet even amongst moderate and politically disengaged members of the public about the potentially wide remit of powers extended to Ministers through this Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: By their very nature, such discussions are also limited and even exaggerated sometimes because of a lack of disclosure by the Government or the absence of any freedom of information regime to equalise the asymmetry between the information and facts available to the Executive as compared to the general public.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Given our unique laws that govern how the press operates in Singapore, the infamously local phrase, "out-of-bound", or OB markers, and our unique political culture steeped in a history of hauling up members of the public and politicians who utter defamatory statements to Court to be slapped with punitive damages, there is a genuine sense amongst the public that this Bill can be easily abused in the wrong hands.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It does not help that the public do not appear to be clear on what can be said and what cannot be said.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, how does a false statement of fact interplay with an opinion or a comment?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe the Minister also recognises this point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the SC Report noted representors raising the prospects of the Executive itself spreading falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This should give all Singaporeans reason to pause and consider whether the Bill that will be passed with the Executive as the decision-maker is truly in the best interests of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, it is my case that POFMA can easily become a proverbial Damocles sword that would hang over members of the public who do not support the Government’s narrative or toe the Government line.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Here, the Committee's Report deliberated on which entity should become the decision-maker in determining what is a falsehood.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the SC outlined three other alternatives.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At paragraph 364 of the SC Report, the Committee acknowledged the views of some representors, including those who were sceptical of the Executive as the decision-maker.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ironically, much of the concern that has been expressed in the public realm since the First Reading of the Bill was actually foreseen by the SC Report.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At para 364(b)(iii) it read, and I quote, "Representors raised concerns about whether Executive action would be credible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There was concern that Executive action could feed fears over the abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was also pointed out that Executive directions would not be able to deal with falsehoods spread by the Executive." In contrast, the proposal to have the Courts as the decision-maker did not illicit any significant apprehensions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To reinforce this point, it is apparent that the Bill gives remarkable leeway to the Executive to define what a falsehood is, especially since the Government has said that it will not act on all falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the public understanding, this clause gives broad latitude to the Executive to clamp down on what it deems to be even misleading statements, which may not be false per se.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, it is fathomable that some statements the Executive may interpret as offending are likely to exist along the misinformation and disinformation spectrum eloquently laid out by Claire Wardle in her submission to the SC.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some statements would exist in the middle of the spectrum where reasonable people would disagree about whether such an offending statement is, indeed, prima facie false or misleading and against the public interest.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Clause 4 lists six broad considerations of what would be in the public interest.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Reference is also made to a diminution of public confidence in the Government, again a term that I would argue can turn on how thin-skinned or thick-skinned the Government of the day is – be it today or in the future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, some weeks ago, some critics of what many reasonable people would consider, correctly or incorrectly, to be a pro-Government influencer Nas Daily, were accused of seeking to undermine confidence in public institutions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These critics alleged double standards on the part of the Executive in allowing the applicant, a foreigner, to mark his presence in Singapore because of a different interpretation of what the Executive would deem to be a cause-based event.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This led the Singapore Police Force to release a statement which framed the allegations of the critics as, I quote "a malicious attempt to undermine confidence in public institutions." Sir, if this example, rooted in a different perspective of how the Public Order Act is applied, outlines the contours of what the threshold of undermining public confidence as defined in the Bill is, then the irresistible conclusion must be that the public interest limb detailed in clause 10 can potentially be very easily invoked by the Executive.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Operation Spectrum or the Marxist conspiracy of 1988 is a good example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is public knowledge that a senior Cabinet member left the Executive after expressing doubts about the Executive’s exercise of powers under the Internal Security Act.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Senior Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam was also quoted by the media as being doubtful about whether the individuals arrested in 1988 were communists.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are not the opinions of lay members of the public who have access to all the relevant information and individuals involved to make a decision or clarify their understanding of events.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would appear that reasonable people even within the Executive would opine very differently on some matters, but yet, each Minister can invoke the powers under this Bill, even if a fellow Minister may not be in agreement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To avoid such inconsistency, would the Courts not represent a more neutral, transparent, accountable and uncontroversial platform to rule on such matters?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government has argued that under the proposed Bill, the Courts are the final arbiter of truth and that an uncomplicated appeals process to the Courts would address the concerns of aggrieved parties.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even so, Sir, the judicial culture in Singapore is highly non-interventionist.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Courts cannot overrule Executive directions lawfully undertaken, pursuant to legislative powers passed by this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: False statements, which can include misleading ones, nonetheless, require the independence and neutrality of the reasonable man who, in this case, will not be a Judge in the first instance, but a People's Action Party Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is open to question whether a traditionally non-interventionist judiciary will challenge what the Executive deems to be reasonable under the Bill, particularly in the face of broad definitions like "misleading statements" and the "public interest".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, an appeal to the High Court for a Part 3 direction under clause 17 does not give leeway to the Court to order what is just and equitable in the circumstances, powers which a genuinely neutral appellant authority must ordinarily host.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More fundamentally, the Executive will have to carefully assess and determine what constitutes a statement of fact, something which is not necessarily a straightforward exercise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What is not stated in unequivocal terms by the Government is that the line between satire, opinion or comment, and what the Executive may deem to be a false or misleading statement of fact in the public interpretation, can be highly subjective.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This point was raised in the Court of Appeal judgement in Review Publishing vs Lee Hsien Loong quoting Evans on Defamation, albeit in the context of the defence of fair comment, where it was said, and I quote:  "It will often be very difficult to decide whether a given statement expresses a comment or   opinion, or by contrast constitutes an allegation of fact.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The same words published in one context may be statement  of fact, yet in another may be comment .

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, whether this element of the defence is established is one of fact, is dependent upon the nature of the imputation conveyed, and the context and circumstances in which it is published.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The test in deciding whether the words are fact or comment is an objective one – namely, whether an ordinary, reasonable reader on reading the whole article would understand the words as comment  or   statements of fact." However, in acknowledging that deciding between an opinion or a comment and a fact can be a difficult exercise, to say nothing of misleading statements, it would follow that the application of a nonetheless objective test in some cases may likewise not be a straightforward exercise, especially in cases of misleading statements where politically-charged decisions need to be made.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If so, it would be important to put this factor into perspective and consider alternatives that seek to balance the urgency of moving against an online falsehood and having a decision-maker that is more acceptable than an unchecked Executive.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And to this end, the ex-parte process is not an unusual judicial remedy to deal with certain time-sensitive applications.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But one need not reinvent the wheel here.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The prospect of interim orders made in favour of the Government in the face of a prima facie falsehood, just like how an individual or company would apply under POHA, can possibly also operate to deal with online falsehoods and manipulation quickly and effectively.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, Parts 3 and 4 of the Bill have close similarities with the remedies for online falsehoods this House passed earlier, under Part 3 of POHA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In cases of sensitive matters involving national security, in-camera applications can be made by the Executive to the Harassment Courts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I believe there is scope to introduce processes involving duty judges to deal with an urgent application from the Government speedily or at very short notice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Likewise, there can be times where there is a heightened risk of false or misleading postings online.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In such a scenario, urgent interim orders can be ordered by duty judges available at short notices to quickly deal with false content that threatens to subvert the election process.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The difference in the time taken between an Executive direction and an Expedited Order through the judicial process in such cases may not be significant.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Now, that suggests that there is some room for the Courts to deal with issues speedily.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, an aggrieved party is also free to apply to the Courts to challenge, vary, suspend or cancel a Court's decision.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The fake news domain is already a very controversial one.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Others will fake innocence when rightly called out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And there would conceivably be a whole litany of other scenarios and circumstances to consider.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On its part, the Executive will act in some cases of falsehoods and, in other cases, it will not.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In both scenarios, questions will be asked why the Executive acted as such.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Yes, Mr Speaker, I have a clarification for Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He quoted me earlier in my speech in the POHA debate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I went on to explain all of that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the terms that I have just set out?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But philosophically, I have a different view as to who the appropriate decision-maker is.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And it is my belief that we should try and see how the Courts can deal with these falsehoods as quickly as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That may be Mr Pritam Singh's philosophical position.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But the Member was trying to quote my speech to make that point.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Fake news is extremely detrimental to society, and the severity of its effects cannot be understated.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Its negative impacts range from the weakening of national security and public institutions to influencing election outcomes.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It also influences the actions of people and affects trust, which, in turn, may lead to violence and loss of lives, warping social and public discourse.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: We also cannot rely solely on non-legislative measures, such as self-regulation of online platforms or only focusing on promoting media literacy.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Countries that rely on such approaches have not found much success in tackling fake news.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Battling fake news is similar to combating terrorism or fighting a war on drugs.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: However, neither should a blanket policy be applied.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Formulating a solution will require vigorous debate and consideration before executing a final calibrated response, much like a surgeon using a scalpel to remove necrotised tissue and not harming healthy cells.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Shanmugam shared that the current existing laws give the Government more powers and are broader.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In view of the recent public concerns, should we not then seriously review this, rather than using existing laws as gold standards, because those are big hammers and I believe they are intended for a different purpose?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, I am aware of the following countries that have enacted laws against falsehood.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: For example, Germany's Network Enforcement Act or the French anti-fake news law against the manipulation of information.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In both instances, a "notice and takedown" order is issued against purveyors of fake news.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister has suggested that the Bill put forth offers a more calibrated approach wherein correction orders are possible.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Large tele-media companies have the ability to counterbalance and respond to challenges from the Ministry.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It is quite different for individuals or smaller organisations and, hence, the concerns about the impact on general freedom of speech.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to highlight some concerns regarding the definitions listed in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This will help agencies effectively implement the Act and give the general public a general grasp of what it means.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The law cannot be set up just to be understood by the Court, and citizens do not understand at all.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The consequences of these overly broad definitions can lead to chilling effects on freedom of speech and expression for our country.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Our citizens will need to think twice if a view is a fact or an opinion before expressing it and be able to correctly interpret a view even if information is not readily available.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This issue is compounded by the fact that Singapore does not have a Freedom of Information Act, where citizens can request for data from the Government instead of having to do their own fact-checking and analysis.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Can we remedy this by providing information that the public seeks?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Minister consider implementing both Bills together as a counterbalancing approach?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Citizens would also need to consider if the content they share or upload is targeting a person or the Government and take precautions to avoid legal consequences with laws, such as the Defamation Act or the Internal Security Act, amongst others.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: How would these Acts cooperate or conflict with one another, given their overlapping functions and how will they be handled?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Depending on how this law is implemented, there will be heightened concerns with legal ramifications.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Apprehension and over-cautiousness will arise from expressing views and uploading content for fear of swift legal reprisal.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Citizens will feel inhibited to raise or discuss sensitive topics related to the issues close to their hearts.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: There is also concern of the legislation being used against citizens who criticise the Government or have views contrary to the ruling party.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Law Minister Shanmugam has clarified in The Straits Times that opinions, criticisms, parody and satire will not be covered.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: However, these reassurances are not explicitly addressed in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Proactively including this language will go far to allay these concerns.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: How do we ensure consistency in approach across Ministries to determine between fact and opinion?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: How do we see to it that there is no "cherry picking" when it comes to acting against specific information not in favour of the Government?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: If fake news originates from the Ministry itself, who then decides to have that Ministry take it down?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: That said, there is no mention in clause 17 of the Bill for an expeditious recourse.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I would, therefore, like to propose a stipulation in the primary legislation for the Government to respond in a timely fashion for information clarification and facilitation of the appeal process.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This signals a stronger reassurance that prompt access to remedy is readily available and any future Government will have to go back to Parliament to have this amended.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Though the final arbiter will be the High Court, what about cases that do not appear before the High Court?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This is pertinent if actions will be taken against individuals or small groups of people compared to large tele-media companies, whose access to resources provides greater efficiency for recourse in Court.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This oversight council is in line with the SC's Recommendation 10c: "Existing efforts should be reviewed, to consider whether they are adequate to achieve transparency, participation and communication and accountability".

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Having an independent oversight council to evaluate the effects of fake news will allow directives to be issued in an effective manner and ensure credibility in our governance.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed council is not meant to be at odds with Ministries or the Courts in any way, but to allow for transparency, accountability and synergy.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It will clearly add much-needed integrity to our entire political system.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, the case studies compiled from the council's annual report can be used for public media literacy education, and to establish consistency across Ministries in refining future Bills.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister has said that Parliament should be the final check and balance, and in this place, should we then not dissolve all the existing councils.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I believe they are set up for a reason.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: As the first country in the world to enact a Bill with such broad strokes to curb the volatility of fake news, a steep learning curve is to be expected.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that we will get it right, striking a balance between curbing fake news and ensuring freedom of speech.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Central to the discussion is the element of trust in pursuit of truth.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The majority of Singaporeans support the vision and bravery of this Bill and trust the sitting Government to be honest and just in its implementation.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: As implicit in the asking of trust from the people, trust should also be paid forward to the people, that we are able to discern fake news as a highly educated populace.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill will have a huge impact on the average Singaporean's freedom of expression and possibly our nation's progress.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I think it is our moral obligation to give constructive criticism and proposals to finetune this Bill in the best interests of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: If left unrevised, this Bill may have long-term repercussions on freedom of expression and speech, impede the development of an engaged and intellectual public, and erode the trust in our Government.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: At the end of the day, it is our solemn duty to uphold the mandate by the people and justify their trust through uncompromising policymaking and rigorous debate.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Undoubtedly, I certainly have strong reservations for the Bill in its current form.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: While I do see positive elements within the Bill, Mr Deputy Speaker, this Bill, in its current state, will need further clarifications before it is ready to be passed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore must be bold in making legal moves in light of global trends which have disadvantaged the citizenry, public institutions and governments via a deluge of falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is easy to wave a banner, whip up emotion and say freedom of speech at all cost, but much harder to sit down, study the subject and put in place measures to ensure that freedom of speech does flourish without the destructive nature of falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In essence, the proliferation of online falsehoods undermines freedom of speech.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because no discerning Member here could disagree with the following contention, that falsehoods, cyberbullying, trolling and hate speech corrode, rather than promote, public debate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They damage society's shared public space and reality.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If non-reality is allowed to become reality, this harms society as decision-making is prejudiced by falsity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Falsehoods can unfairly inflame passions, to prevent rational debate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Falsehoods, especially when amplified by bots and trolls, can intimidate other voices, thereby preventing people from being exposed to a diversity of views.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It devalues and delegitimises the voices of experts and authoritative institutions, thus undermining society's ability to engage in rational discourse based on shared facts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Brexit referendum is a classic example of how falsehoods can penetrate and prejudice even mature democracies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must learn from that and prevent falsehoods from penetrating the precious crucible of public debate in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, some of the things that had been said in Brexit could have led to Michael Gove's exasperated comment during the height of the Brexit referendum campaigning in which he said, "People in this country have had enough of experts." Falsehoods can undermine the concept of an objective truth.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This may have the negative effect of causing citizens to disengage from public discourse altogether.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My next point is that legislation cannot be viewed as the antithesis to freedom of speech.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To the contrary, legislation is needed to protect freedom of speech.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because leaving corrections to somehow organically or innately work themselves out is simply ineffective.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The point I am making is that to rely on existing legal remedies would be far too insufficient to deal with the threat at hand.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As Dean of Singapore Management University, School of Law, Prof Goh Yihan stated, existing laws are limited in terms of speed, scope and adaptability.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Simply put, while criminal penalties may apply to punish perpetrators, there are no legislative levers to ensure the timely correction or removal of fake news.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many people have expressed concern that the Bill will create a chilling effect on public discussions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The corrections regime encourages free speech, by ensuring that people are exposed to more viewpoints and more facts, not less.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is in line with the "marketplace of ideas" theory.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In line with this, we need good public debate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, I would like to ask: what are the Government's plans to assure well-meaning members of society that they should continue to contribute to meaningful civic discussions?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Pritam Singh questions why the Executive needs to be part of the solution.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He says that the Courts should be part of the solution in the first instance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the type of decision-making model is key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
