text: And for the record, I disagree with Mr Pritam Singh, and I do not think that the Courts are the best placed to hear this in the first instance and decide whether a takedown notice needs to be made or a Correction Direction needs to be made.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Why do I say that the type of decision-making model is key?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because we should be completely aware of the nature of the threat which lies before us.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They need to be curbed and responded to robustly before they can cause harm.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Falsehoods can threaten public safety and create riots.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, against the nature of the beast, what factors ought to shape the model of the decision-making in the first instance?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In these situations, there is no luxury of time to make decisions, going through the Court process, and so on.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A riot can break after the Courts close.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The decision-maker also needs to be equipped with the information to make the decisions speedily.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The decision-maker must also be the right person to weigh in on issues of public interest.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Let us say that there is a riot.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And during the course of the riot, there is a statement that the Police killed the person because of the person's race.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Now that needs an immediate intervention by the Executive in the form of a Minister to say, "That is incorrect." He has to decide whether or not it should be taken down or put up a Correction Direction in the form of what is the truth.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: You want to refer to the Courts for that?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Half an hour later into the riot, it says that the Police are opening fire on innocent people.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Minister again, having to deal with the consequences, must look and say, "What correction must go out?", "Does it need to be taken down?", "Does another piece of information need to go up to put that in perspective, to balance it?" Refer to the Courts again?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Half an hour later, oh, another allegation, out of the blue, "The Police are trying to disarm the closed-circuit television (CCTV) to get rid of the evidence." That is false.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Again, the Minister, at the time well after court hours, maybe, will have to make a decision, "What do I do?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Issue a Correction Direction?" Surely, the Minister, being the Executive, has the play of all the facts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He has got the officers reporting to him.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He has to make decisions very quickly, life and death.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, this may not only just be about falsehoods per se, but the consequence of what those falsehoods would lead to.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Pritam Singh says philosophically, he has a disagreement; philosophically, it should not be the Courts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I ask Mr Pritam Singh to look through and decide practically what Singaporeans need in times of crises.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And after all, in the first instance when the Executive makes the decision, that is reviewable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is reviewable through two mechanisms, and not one.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What happens if there is an endemic that is breaking out in the hospital when every minute matters?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have great respect for the Courts, and I think as a tier above the Minister, a tier of review – I should rephrase it – a tier of review, they are best-placed to decide whether that order was correct or not to begin with, but not to put the Courts in a mix where it is such a dynamic situation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ms Irene Quay has also discussed this issue of another body, I read the Order Paper Supplement, and I think it is called an "independent council" that looks into the issue of falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I do not agree that there is a need for that council.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If one looks at the Order Paper Supplement, one of the functions of the council seems to want to replace the Ministerial decision-making and also determine what is fact.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, it seems to want to do two things: both the Executive role as well as the judicial role, when actually, there is, every time we sit, an ability to hold the Minister to account in this decision-making process.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, we have to be very clear about the nature of the beast that we are dealing with.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am quoting from the Executive Summary of the report of the SC on Deliberate Online Falsehoods and I want to deal with the point he made about riots and having to wait for a Court order.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I want to suggest to him that sometimes Executive action in itself can be problematic and I am going to quote from this example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: For example, when German police debunked a false claim that immigrants have raped a girl, they were falsely accused of covering up crimes committed by immigrants.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This contributed to street protests." I can understand the Member's view that urgent action is important.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But Executive action, in itself, may not always be the solution that will solve the problem.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think it is important to understand that there could be other solutions that may inevitably work, that members of the public could be persuaded by other forms of action like a Court order.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Principally, I will quote four sections of the report where it states specifically that swift action is key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In all of these instances, I would humbly suggest to the House that our Executive, our Ministers, the officebearers who are fed with information on what is happening on the ground can make the best decisions within the limited time that they have.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And if there is any delay, goodness knows what the consequences could be and that would harm Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Irene Quay, you want to make your clarification?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching
text: Yes, I would like to make a correction that when I meant "independent council", I am not referring to a council that will make Executive decision.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching
text: So, what we are proposing is a post review council for learning purposes.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching
text: So, our stand of independent oversight Council is for review of the past cases to finetune future Bills.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Indeed, I thank Ms Irene Quay for that clarification.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Hitherto, I do not think the wording in the Order Paper Supplement suggested that explanation, but if it is a clarification, then it does put some perspective.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, the Minister for Law just now said that the powers of the Government under this Bill is narrower than the existing legislation.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The fact is, however, after this Bill is passed, the Government will continue to have the same powers as before; powers given to the Government under other legislation will not be rescinded by this Bill.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The important thing is that in the other legislation, the powers of the Government are directed at websites or companies, but this Bill is targeted at remarks made by individuals on the social media.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The Minister also said that the Bill is to deal with online falsehoods with calibrated legislation.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: However, the Bill presented to Parliament is very disappointing and surprising.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In our view, the purpose of the Government in introducing this Bill is not simply to deal with the challenges mentioned above.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: As soon as the Bill was presented to Parliament, the mainstream media has started reporting and one of their key points is the harsh penalties prescribed in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In the future, the Government can selectively punish a few offenders to achieve a chilling effect.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is the so-called "to scare the monkey by slaughtering the chicken." People will try to protect themselves by self-censorship.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The true aim of the Government is to protect the ruling party and achieve political monopoly through this Bill.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Today, there are various types of online falsehoods, and they, indeed, have brought challenges to the political system and social management.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: No doubt, we need strategies to deal with them.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: But do not forget, the Internet and social media have also empowered common citizens to discuss politics and hold the Government accountable.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is a positive development brought about by technology.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Nowadays, people do not just discuss politics at coffee shops or only start to open up after a few drinks.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: When people have doubts about the Government or certain political figures, the talk is not limited to quiet whispering only.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This shows that Singaporeans have stepped out the shadow of the white terror of the Internal Security Act (ISA) which allows the Minister to detain people for a long period of time without a trial.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is a great step towards openness and democracy for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In fact, modern technology and the prevalence of the Internet have provided opportunities for modern democracy to improve and develop.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Online opinions have provided the Government with a feedback and response platform which is effective, timely and can change flexibly as scenarios change.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The Government can communicate with the people directly, know their needs and the issues they face, hence make better policies to improve people’s lives.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Public opinions are no longer reflected only during elections.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: A Government that can make good use of this platform will be able to accurately introduce policies that are pro-people, therefore, making sure it stays in power.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, people can also express views on Government policies through the Internet, or become an organised force through the Internet to exert pressure on the Government.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: If a common citizen can express his opinions online and criticise Government policies or a certain politician, the whole world can see.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Even if the mainstream media controlled by the Government is ambiguous or try to trivialise the matter, it is becoming more difficult to do so.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The Government believes that any rational person will agree that we need to legislate to deal with online falsehoods, and takes this opportunity to empower the Minister to judge public comments and have absolute power to take actions.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is a Bill with a hidden agenda.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It is like during a match, the Minister is both player and referee.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Prime Minister Lee pointed out recently that the prevalence of technology and the social media has made it very easy for hate speech and falsehoods to spread.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: People with malicious intent can easily manipulate opinions and even influence elections.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is seemingly convincing, but how can we be sure that the Ministers from the ruling party will not manipulate opinions and spread falsehoods in order to win elections?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Although this Bill allows people to appeal to the Court against the Minister’s actions, for a common citizen, after being dealt with by the Minister then having to go to the Court to complain, it is both time-consuming and energy-sapping.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: No common person can have the kind of resources like the Government which has the whole Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) behind it.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: To engage in a legal tussle with the Government, it is easier said than done.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It should be up to the judges to decide.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the Government has no interest in studying this further; it just wants the people to hand the power to it and decisions are up to the Government to make.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: After the Bill was tabled in Parliament, the Government has faced many opposing voices.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: To win support, the Government has to clarify on what constitutes falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The Government has been trying to convince people that they are only targeting fake news, not personal opinions.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: However, in this regard, I have no faith in the Government.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: After the implementation of the Bill, will the Government show its true colours?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I think because of the wide definition of falsehoods in the Bill, the Minister can make a decision on whether it is information or opinion according to need.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, the same words coming from different people may be interpreted differently by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: For example, "the older generation can’t accept a non-Chinese Prime Minister", if these words come from the Minister himself or his supporter, the Minister may say that this is a personal opinion.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: However, if these words come from the Minister’s political opponent on the social media, the Minister may say that spreading such falsehoods will create racial conflicts, even riots, endangering national security.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: He can demand this person to publish what is acceptable to the Government, otherwise he will be punished.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is a modern version of "literary inquisition".

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The Government had previously misinterpreted laws to deal with those it disliked.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: For example, when the Protection from Harassment Bill was passed in Parliament, the purpose was to protect individuals.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: But a few years ago, the Government tried to use this Act to include Government agencies as objects to be protected although the High Court ruled that the Government had no right to cite this Act because the Government is not an individual.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The case dragged on for a few years which would be a huge burden for any individual who has limited resources.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I think that the correct way for a society to develop immunity to falsehoods is to enhance civic education and to instil in citizens a habit of finding facts from online news, so that they will not believe in online news easily, nor react to "big news" or Internet instigations.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The Internet is an open platform, netizens can rebut irrational, extreme and unfair online remarks.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Relevant Government agencies and Ministers can also come out to clarify and state the stance.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: By doing so, the true nature of online rumours, fake news and misleading remarks will be known, netizens can also be educated and enhance their ability to judge.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In the situation where possession of resources is totally unequal, to be engaged in a legal tussle with the Government is like hitting stone with an egg.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: To introduce such a Bill is not what a Government which claims to defend democracy and public interests should do.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It is more like the actions of a dictatorial Government that will resort to any means to hold onto absolute power.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Given our society today, I wonder if we ask too much of the law and too little of ourselves.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, let me say that I agree with the premise of the Bill, that the impediments to full, transparent discourse is less a matter of lack of information than one of too much, too complex and partly false information.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The word "partly" is important because online falsehoods are seldom completely false.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Most misleading messages hold a grain of truth, but their sum total is a lie.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Minister has given a few examples, and I will give one more later on.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Second, I also agree with the instrumental value of the Bill, namely, to reduce the instances of such falsehoods and to empower the Government to correct and, as last resort, remove such falsehoods that are deemed to cause public harm.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The hon Member Mr Pritam Singh expressed deep concerns about how the Bill supposedly confers the Executive excessively broad and unprecedented power.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But I think Mr Pritam Singh does not address Minister Shanmugam's explanation that the Bill, in fact, narrows power under existing laws which themselves have been around for more than 30 years.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Mr Pritam Singh also raised the example of Nas Daily.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But Minister Shanmugam had also addressed the example in his speech and explained when and why statements in respect of that would be covered.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Last year, I had spoken in Parliament about this, arguing that any proposed legislation on Deliberate Online Falsehoods stands against two common misconceptions about freedom in discourses – that truth will emerge naturally from a contestation of ideas.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Political scientists know that ideas are a function of power as well as merit.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is the very concern of academics and advocates.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I say it straight, that the hegemony of the People’s Action Party will lead to their ideas travelling further and hitting harder than others.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Minister for Education had last week said that this Bill does none of that.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is less a matter of giving power to some ideas, than correcting falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the majority of cases, merely putting out the right facts against the wrong ones, rather than taking down the latter altogether.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The assumptions are less to do with political power than the behavioural bias embedded in all of us.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I had previously spoken about two false assumptions that unfettered freedoms rely on: first, that people have infinite time and capacity to make decisions; and second, that people change their minds when presented with new facts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As a member of the SC, we examined and noted the extent and serious consequences that Deliberate Online Falsehoods can cause.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This duty to reduce Deliberate Online Falsehoods is one whose specific form is being debated in democratic countries across the world.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Last year, when I had spoken on the Motion on Deliberate Online Falsehoods, I had said that current provisions were manifestly inadequate and requires further action on two fronts: the private sector and society itself.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Social media platforms must recognise the primacy of public interest over private profit.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, the Minister had stressed this in his speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I had also argued for the moral duty of members of the public to think before sharing falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At the time, I had in mind political information and content of the sort that related to political events in Britain, and the elections of other countries that the Minister had also spoken about.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In light of events in recent weeks, I would say this moral duty of the public requires a lot more attention.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There are too many falsehoods, promoted and fanned by too many parties, with harm caused by a million paper cuts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The law does not touch these, and I repeat, rightly so.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I do not ask for the law to be widened.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Chief among these must be the development of online norms against guerrilla justice and vigilantes.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The recent case of Ms Monica Baey in the National University of Singapore (NUS) is instructive.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The truth is that Nicholas Lim committed a terrible act and Monica Baey suffered greatly.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Monica Baey deserves to feel safe in her own hall of residence.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Nicholas Lim deserves to be punished for what he did.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But he certainly does not deserve the online hate, flames and persecution.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is something Ms Monica Baey herself has disavowed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But the punishment of Nicholas Lim cannot depend on the grace and magnanimity of Monica Baey.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Justice is not a lynch mob to be swayed and directed like a throw flame of moral panic.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It answers neither to Facebook nor Instagram posts, no matter who writes them, nor to the distress or trauma of victims alone.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But in today’s context, lynch mobs are easily and cheaply formed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Minister shared how much the market rates are for some of them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Digital technology, such as social media platforms and digital advertising tools, can be a force for good.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Yet, increasingly, we have seen how they have been abused by bad actors to weaken society, to affect democratic processes and to inflict harm.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They provide convenient, accessible and cheap platforms for bad actors to exploit.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: On Facebook, we saw a livestream of Christchurch shootings, which reached a wide audience through re-sharing.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is the glamorising of terrorism, which many may participate in inadvertently.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Twitter has allowed hate speech to proliferate on its platform.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For example, in the name of freedom of expression, it has refused to ban Alex Jones’ Infowar account even after there was clear evidence of him spreading hate speech and disinformation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Closer to home, in Indonesia, after four Chinese nationals were arrested for allegedly planting imported chili seeds contaminated with "bacteria", these false claims were spread on Twitter, with the contagion spreading to Indonesian newspapers which accused China of using a "biological weapon" against Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This made its way back to social media, with many posts carrying anti-Chinese sentiments.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: On Google, in October 2017, during the Las Vegas shooting, divisive hoaxes continue to appear in top search results – anti-Semitic material topped search results.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the meantime, there were Youtube sites which were monetising this harmful content.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As a member of the Committee, I must say that we decided to give a large role to ignorance and agnosticism.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In line with our earlier laws on information, we do not stop the flow of information, but we do want to stop bad actors from profiting from falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: These will only apply to individuals who deliberately spread falsehoods which harm the public interest.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The current form of legislation sticks closely to many of the SC’s recommendations.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The SC comprised Members of Parliament from both sides of the House.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The SC’s recommendations were detailed and signed off collectively.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As expected, some opponents now criticise the legislation, but they have little to offer in response, except mere generalities.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They did not contest the SC’s findings that online falsehoods are a serious problem, that they cause serious consequences in a very, very short time, that "drip feed" falsehoods have enduring harm.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But when we offer a practical and calibrated solution, when this is proposed, they cry foul.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If we all agree that this is a serious problem, what are the solutions?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Since the SC’s recommendations, the Government has moved on many of the recommendations: first on the non-legislative front, and now on the legislation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What more can the public expect in the near term?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For example, can there be an establishment of a fact-checking entity, something which has been done in some countries?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Instead, there will be additional facts for people to consider, perhaps to accept if they are convinced, perhaps to reject if they are not.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We cannot grow strong unless we are first made weak.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We cannot develop unless we have freedoms, including the freedom to make mistakes and identify falsehoods for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the process, we must develop an online culture of what it means to be a Singaporean, to be fair-minded, seeking recompense and justice; to be compassionate; dispensing mercy and second chances.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As a young nation, we must grow into the best version of ourselves as Singaporeans, not just in our real and daily lives, but in our online norms and dialogues.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We should not ask this of the law only.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: (In Mandarin):   Deputy Speaker, the Minister and a few Members of this House have talked about the problem of online falsehoods.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The extent of destruction that online falsehoods can cause is evident.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is like a new form of "virus" that can spread widely within a very short period of time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Societies afflicted by online falsehoods are like people who have been infected by viruses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If we cannot find a new treatment for these new viruses, we will continue to be plagued by them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If we are sick, we should see a doctor.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Singapore is not the only country that is battling against this virus.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Last year, together with Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong and Mr Pritam Singh, leader of the WP, I attended the Committee Hearing on International Fake News and Falsehoods organised by the British Parliament.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We discussed the issue of falsehood with representatives from eight countries.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Many other countries, such as France and Germany, are also drafting new laws to counter fake news online and setting up regulatory regimes specifically for digital platforms.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Countering online falsehoods is also a common practice in other countries.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Singapore and other countries are working together to fight against this new virus in order to safeguard the well-being of our nation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Well then, is this proposed new treatment a good treatment?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I think we need to look into two aspects when we are considering the merits of this treatment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: First of all, is this treatment better than the existing treatment?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Let us now look into these two aspects.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: First of all, is the new Bill better than our existing legislation?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Internet platforms that have been issued Correction Orders will only need to put up corrections alongside the falsehood to avoid punishment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In many other countries, the primary measure taken is to request the Internet company to take down the falsehood entirely.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Comparatively, the new Bill proposed by Singapore is more tolerant and more in line with the needs of the new environment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Furthermore, the new Bill is targeted at false statement of facts, while personal opinion is not considered falsehood.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Therefore, we will not face criminal punishment if we express our opinions in our daily lives, or if we accidentally share online fake news.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Here, I would like to share my personal experience.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I have quite a few elderly relatives who are very health conscious and often share information with one another, especially with regard to food safety.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Some time ago, they received information from friends, claiming that consumption of broccoli together with prawns will trigger a chemical reaction in our bodies that will cause originally harmless substances to turn arsenic.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: By consuming prawns with broccoli, one may start to bleed and eventually die.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: After listening to this horrific piece of information, I assured them that fried broccoli with prawns is a common dish and there is no need to worry.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Then they started to worry if they would face criminal punishment under the new Bill if they had unwittingly shared the information with family and friends.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I told them firmly that the new Bill is not targeted at kind-hearted common folk who are unaware that certain information is false.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Instead, it is meant to deal with purveyors of falsehoods, people who deliberately spread falsehoods with malicious intent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Then, will this new Bill affect freedom of speech?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is also what Mr Low Thia Khiang is concerned about.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I believe that by requesting for the correct information to be put up alongside the false information, we are turning on a spotlight for everyone, so that they can refer to more information and judge for themselves.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Therefore, the new Bill will not affect freedom of speech.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Instead, there will be more information channels and greater freedom to obtain information.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: A further question is, will this new Bill lead to the abuse of Ministerial powers?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I have a personal view, which I believe can help allay some of the concerns raised by Mr Low Thia Khiang.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I think that the Chinese character "众" (zhong) used in "公众利益" (gong zhong li yi), the Chinese phrase that refers to public interest, is made up of three "人" (ren), the Chinese character that refers to people.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Just like the three "人" or "people" that make up the character "众" (zhong) or "public", the Minister will be monitored on three fronts under this new Bill.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Individuals or organisations that have been issued the correction order can lodge an appeal at the Courts and challenge the Minister's decision.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong also explained that although the Courts can try to expedite the trial for cases concerning falsehoods, this is plagued with challenges as a lot of details are involved, and if we do not stop the spread of falsehood quickly, it can do a lot of harm.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Earlier, the Minister also mentioned that this Bill merely provides a framework.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Within this framework, we must all do our part to combat falsehoods.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Therefore, I would like to come back to the Chinese character "众" (zhong) or "public", which is made up of three Chinese characters "人" (ren), or "people".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is symbolic of the need for society to work together to tackle this problem.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Dealing with falsehoods is not only the Minister's responsibility, but also the Court's responsibility, Parliament's responsibility, and every Singaporean's responsibility.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The new Bill encourages everyone to cooperate in countering the problem of fake news.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At the same time, mechanisms are put in place to ensure that there are checks and balances, so as to avoid side effects.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang also mentioned earlier that he does not feel confident about delegating a senior Government official to take over the decision-making role of the Minister during elections.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I felt upset to hear this and I am sure any civil servant who hears this would be upset, too.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As I explained earlier, dealing with falsehoods requires everyone to work together, not just the Minister.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang also mentioned a few examples earlier.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: He was worried that there is a hidden agenda behind this framework by using very broad definitions, it will allow the Government and Ministers to decide for themselves what are public interest and falsehoods to satisfy their personal motives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Minister has also explained earlier that these circumstances have not surfaced yet.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, he did give a few examples to illustrate the difference between falsehoods and personal opinion.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: By giving examples, the broad principles and basis are laid out to provide some kind of guideline that is applicable for different situations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To say in Parliament that the Pioneer Generation Package or the Merdeka Generation Package is a vote-buying tactic by the Minister, is being suspicious of others' good intentions without having proper justifications.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: So, I do not think that we should engage in such extreme behaviour in a solemn setting like this.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We should discuss this very meaningful Bill positively.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is also more tolerant, more refined and more targeted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Singapore is not the only country that is combating online falsehoods.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Other countries are also drafting new laws to suppress online falsehoods.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Today, our focus is on online falsehood, which should not be confused with conversations by common folk in coffee shops.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Online falsehood is a new form of "virus" that requires new, more targeted and more advanced innovative treatment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Let us all work together to counter the harm inflicted on our society by online falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: (In Mandarin):   Senior Parliamentary Secretary Sun talked about a very interesting Chinese character "众" (zhong).

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Of course, there is nothing wrong in saying that there are three "人" (ren) or "people" in the character "众" (zhong), but ultimately, there is a "人" (ren) on top in this character.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: This means he wields all the powers, and I do not wish to see Singapore's Ministers having so much power.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: The problem with this is that they may make the wrong decision.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: However, under this Bill, for the three characters that represent "people" in the character "众" (zhong), the one on top, which is the Minister, makes the decision, while the other two "people" just sits below him.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: You can decide whether this is in the public interest or not based on the above interpretation of the character "众" (zhong).

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: (In Mandarin):   I thank the Member for his clarification.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I do not agree with what the Member has said.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Furthermore, when the Minister executes his power under this law, he must satisfy two conditions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Second, he must prove that public interest is affected.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If one really insists on interpreting the character "众" (zhong) as being made up of a "person" on top, with two "people" below, then I think the one on top should represent the Court.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I was the one who used the Chinese character "众" (zhong) for illustration.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Since I used this as an example and have clearly stated that the Court is the ultimate adjudicator, I can say that in the character "众" (zhong), the "人" (ren) on top represents the Court.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I mentioned in my speech, that when you explain these principles clearly using examples, it serves as a more meaningful guidance.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are there any clarifications from yesterday evening that anyone would like to pose?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Last year, I had the privilege to sit on the Select Committee (SC) on Deliberate Online Falsehoods together with several other Members of this House, including Mr Pritam Singh and Ms Chia Yong Yong.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We went through all the submissions and invited 79 of those who made submissions to elaborate on their submission at a public hearing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Over the course of eight days, we heard oral representations from 65 individuals and representatives of organisations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Committee had observed that falsehoods can appear in a broad spectrum of circumstances, from deliberately fabricated content to satire and parodies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They can also have varying degrees of impact, causing minor confusion to threatening national security and dividing societies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Committee emphasised that Government intervention should be calibrated in a manner that takes these factors into consideration.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am heartened that the Bill today has taken into account one of the SC's recommendations on the creation of new legislation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In my view, the Bill has captured the essence of the Committee's recommendations and has done well in calibrating the responses to deliberate online falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note that some may not share my view.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In the wake of the First Reading of the Bill, I received feedback, heard and read about concerns of some people of the impact the new legislation may have on our ideals of freedom of speech and how some felt that this Bill may have been rushed through without proper consultation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I disagree with these views but appreciate that my perspective was very much shaped by my experience and what I had learnt whilst I was on the SC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It would be impossible to set out my whole experience in this speech, but I would like to touch on several learning points that left a deep impact on me.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Falsehoods have a great potential to deepen fault lines and polarise society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Singapore is one of the most diverse countries in the world.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We are small, multiracial, multi-religious, with great digital connectedness.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Racial and religious tensions may be inflamed quickly.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A Nielsen survey indicated that more Singaporeans access their news over the Internet and social media, compared to hardcopy newspapers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The same report found that over three-quarters of Singaporeans used social media.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In addition, several security experts who presented at the SC pointed out that foreign disinformation can be expected to occur in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Targeting friction points in Singapore society, and weakening Singapore’s will to defend itself, are a more attractive strategy than conventional military warfare.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Further, the tools for disinformation campaigns are readily available in our region.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Several experts gave evidence on this issue, including Dr Ben Nimmo of the Atlantic Council's Digital Forensic Research Lab and Dr Elmie Nekmat, Asst Prof of Communications and New Media from the National University of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Falsehoods may play on existing "slow burn" issues, such as simmering communal tensions, to create more serious crises in the long run.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In particular, Dr Mathew Mathews from the Institute of Policy Studies warned of “low-level” misinformation about particular ethnic, religious or immigrant groups on various matters, such as their loyalty to Singapore, potential to commit anti-social acts and others.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: And these could lead to friction within the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One notorious example is an article by The Real Singapore, which falsely reported that a complaint by a Filipino family resulted in commotion between Hindu participants and the Police during a Thaipusam procession in 2015.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Viral, drip-feed falsehoods may play on slow-burn issues.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Such lies may not trigger immediate violence, but they can poison debate and irreversibly damage the fabric of our society like race relations and confidence in public institutions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: All these can culminate in violence in the long run.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They should not be considered "less dangerous", and Singapore cannot afford to be complacent about them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The breakdown of society due to a spread of what may seem like innocuous falsehoods can and will happen if we do not take action to correct and curb them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Thirdly, falsehoods are very, very difficult to combat.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, there is a need to act swiftly and decisively in certain situations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The evidence before the SC pointed to three difficulties: (a) human cognitive tendencies, (b) weakness of truth compared with falsehoods, and (c) the further and faster reach of falsehoods than the truth.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Basically, in short, we believe what we want to believe, the truth is not as salacious as falsehood, so it is harder to believe the truth, and falsehoods can go viral much faster that the correction.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some of them explained why longer-term or indirect measures, such as fact-checking and public education, were not enough to deal with online falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In light of the things that I have learnt, I am, therefore, pleased with the calibrated approach taken in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Government needs to be empowered to quickly react to falsehoods if there is an adverse impact to the public.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In certain circumstances, there cannot be any delay, and the truth has to be brought to light immediately.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   Singapore is highly vulnerable to the threat of online falsehoods that can potentially destroy inter-racial and inter-religious relations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The adverse impact of falsehoods which have become widespread is hard to repair.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, under certain circumstances, the Government has to be given the power to curb the spread of such falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many have voiced their concerns about how this legislation can affect people's freedom of speech.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Let us take a step back and think about what we want for our society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We want a society that knows how to think and is able to conduct healthy discussions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This can only take place when there is a space that is free from slander and falsehoods because otherwise any debate will not be beneficial.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some also questioned the power granted to the Government in this Bill which is seen as too broad.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Government must ensure that the information is false and affects public interest.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Any view and opinion that are based on true facts will not be categorised as falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Government does not have the final say in determining whether the matter is true or false.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In my opinion, there is a calibration in this Bill's approach and I think this is a good approach.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): I am happy to note that corrections will be the primary response and there is no punishment for the majority of cases if there is no malicious conduct.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am satisfied that there are sufficient safeguards in the form of a recourse to the Court, in the event there is an objection to the allegation of falsehood.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On this note though, I appreciate the lay persons’ concerns about the cost and complexities involved in seeking recourse from the High Court.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have intended to seek clarification on this, but I note that, in his opening speech, the Minister for Law had explained the simplified processes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe this should address the peoples' concerns.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At the end of the day, it is clear from the various explanations that the Ministry has given through news articles and videos, that the Bill does not affect ordinary Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Such persons must not only know that the statement they are sending is wrong; they must also know that such statement will undermine public interest.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, it is not a criminal offence to forward or share messages without checking for accuracy first – although I think you should.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I feel that ordinary Singaporeans should be happy to be warned about falsehoods and to receive corrections.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This will help to build a community of more discerning Internet users.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It may be useful to continue to guide and educate the public about this new legislation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Perhaps the Minister can consider efforts to educate Singaporeans on what type of falsehoods will be covered under the Bill so that they can better identify and avoid spreading these falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On this note, I would highlight that the SC has recommended a multi-pronged approach to help deal with the issues of deliberate online falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is very important to educate the public to help equip them with skills to tell false from fact and to build healthy online habits.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Over the longer term, I believe that the new legislation, along with the suite of non-legislative measures put in place by the Government, will have the effect of cultivating an informed, discerning population.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Hon Members of the House, if "fake news" was the word of the year for 2017, "POFMA" could go down in Singapore’s history as the word of the year for 2019.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, this acronym for the "Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act", nifty by accident or design, has entered into our colourful Singlish lexicon.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: People have since been heard saying such things as "you better watch out, they POFMA you then you know!" or "wait you kena POFMA!" Indeed, so versatile is POFMA that it can serve as both a verb and a noun.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Jokes aside, the sheer liveliness with which this new Bill has been discussed, both online and off, has brought to light several issues.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans acknowledge the scourge of online falsehoods and recognise the need to do something about it.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: But Singaporeans also care deeply about our online space, and our freedom to discuss and debate within it.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, there have been several aspects of the Bill that have stoked the greatest debate.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These have been given considerable airing over both online and mainstream media and addressed by the Minister yesterday.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As currently proposed, POFMA requires Internet intermediary companies to reactively respond to the directives of the state rather than proactively develop other strategies to douse the spread of falsehoods.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This may not be the best use of their resources.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, we should consider a more cooperative relationship that can facilitate mutual cooperation, education and engagement, where the state can be apprised of the latest technological trends and solutions, and technology companies can be schooled and reminded in the societal values that they must uphold.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Since being tabled, POFMA has drawn criticism for vesting individual Ministers with the power to determine falsehoods and take action.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Such views reflect the visceral resistance that people have to granting exclusive authority to a small number of individuals in our pluralistic media landscape.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, the proposed key measures of targeted and general corrections are based on evidence that when consumers are presented with both the original falsehood and the correction, they can consider the information in its totality and form their own conclusions.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Although POFMA is meant to be platform-agnostic, the evidence we currently have on the effects of corrections is platform-, context- and even demographic group-specific.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Will targeted and general corrections counter-productively amplify the original falsehood to a wider audience, without a guarantee of the original or new audience reading the accompanying correction?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Will we perversely and inadvertently create a cognitive shortcut where people seeing an official correction presume that the original falsehood must be true precisely because it is being vehemently debunked?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Will falsehoods that do not come with corrections be summarily assumed to be true?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Such unintended outcomes of a correction strategy cannot be ruled out, despite our best efforts and intentions.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: With the relentless proliferation of new communication platforms, many of which increasingly offer encryption to safeguard privacy, consumer habits, skills and even biases will evolve constantly.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, a correction or takedown order in some situations might be either inefficacious or serve to further entrench the falsehood in question.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Further, the type of targeted action could differ, depending on the type of media platform – what works for Facebook may not be as effective for Telegram or YouTube.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The role of the technology companies in this panel is thus not to promote vested interests, but to identify industry best practices on what is most efficacious and practicable in the circumstances.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The workings of such a panel need not slow down the process.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Members can be pre-appointed and deployed at short notice to advise the Minister.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: There is no issue of accountability because the Minister retains the final authority to take action.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: But with this panel, the Minister can act with the benefit of a wider range of views extending beyond those of civil servants.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These can be pegged to a graduated scale commensurate with, for example, their annual returns from advertising.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: It should also play a capacity-building role to professionalise newsmakers in the production of quality information and raise ethical standards within the media and technology industries.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: It can also set the research agenda by offering grants to investigate the effects of online falsehoods and potential solutions to the problem.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Consumers, too, can also be involved in helping to flag suspect news.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: With robust fact-checking accessible to all consumers, we can nurture greater individual discernment and reduce our reliance on state-issued corrections.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Communication platforms are evolving rapidly and, along with them, the media usage patterns of consumers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   	Sir, the Government stated that POFMA is a regulatory effort through legislation to deal with the problem of falsehoods that is becoming increasingly prevalent online, especially through social media.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is also stated that this piece of legislation is necessary to protect social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We are of the view and we are confident that this suggestion is more appropriate in achieving the primary purpose of protecting and preserving social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We disagree with the basic principles of POFMA because it contains elements that can lead to abuse of power and, if this happens, it will undermine social cohesion, something that runs counter to the primary objective of having a law to prevent and control online falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We must acknowledge that in this context, social cohesion can also happen if the decisions and actions that are taken by the Minister contain elements of power abuse.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The concern over abuse of power has been mentioned by many groups – the public, politicians, journalists, civil society organisations, academics and so on ‒ ever since the First Reading of POFMA took place on 1 April 2019.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In my speech, I will first speak on two provisions contained in POFMA that have raised concerns about potential abuse of power on the part of the Government and, secondly, I will also touch on several arguments by the Government in its response to the negative aspects of POFMA.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Minister is a political member of the ruling party.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many have said that, if there are situations where criticisms are directed towards Government policies, or if there are negative opinions on the ruling party, can the Ministers make fair assessment and decision?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because in this situation, the Ministers become a conflicted party.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This can happen when, in order to defend Government policies as well as to defend the dignity of the ruling party, the word “misleading” under clause 2 can be exploited by the Ministers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Based on this interpretation, it is not wrong if there are concerns about the possibility of abuse of power in order to defend the interest of a political party.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Mr Lee was in the position of a conflicted party.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In this matter, allegations that impacted the integrity of the Prime Minister and the Government were brought forward.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This was acknowledged by the Prime Minister himself, and I quote several statements from his speech.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In English): "I am making this statement today because my siblings Dr Lee Wei Ling and Mr Lee Hsien Yang have made serious allegation of abuse of power against me and my Government." (In Malay): Second quote.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In English): "These allegations are entirely baseless but they have already damaged Singapore's reputation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Unrebutted, they can affect Singaporeans' confidence in the Government." (In Malay): Third quote.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In English) "In normal circumstances, in fact, in any other imaginable circumstance than this, I would have sued immediately, because the accusation of the abuse of power is a very grave one, however baseless it may be.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: And it is, in fact, an attack not just on me, but on the integrity of the whole Government.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But suing my own brother and sister in Court would further besmirch our parents' names.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: At the end of the day, we are brothers and sister, and we are all our parents' children." (In Malay): Prime Minister Lee's statements show that it is not easy to make decisions in a situation where he is a conflicted party.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many have questioned whether the decision taken by Prime Minister Lee regarding this matter is correct or not.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This clause further reinforces the view on the possibility of abuse of power by the Ministers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This clause provides powers to the Ministers to take appropriate action if there are false or misleading statements intended to negatively impact public confidence in the Government.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In such a situation, the Ministers, once again, become the conflicted party, if we take into account the interpretation of the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew’s statement that the PAP is the Government and the Government is the PAP.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: First, when the Government was asked why Ministers were chosen instead of the Judiciary as first arbiter, the answer given was that the judicial process would take time and this is not acceptable because immediate action is needed to curb the spread of falsehoods and limit the potential damage on social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This point was already mentioned and elaborated on by my colleague Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The second argument is about the reply on the possibility of an irresponsible future government exploiting POFMA.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I am of the view that the Minister's reply is problematic and baffling.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: One example is the Government's policy of creating a second key for the national Reserves where this function is given to the Elected President.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: First, please let me thank Minister Shanmugam for his comprehensive reminder of the legislative intent of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I wish to state plainly that I support the legislative intent of the Bill because I agree that online falsehoods can distort and demean public debate in our secular democracy by inciting polarisation and populism for all the reasons that the Minister has outlined yesterday.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I also agree and appreciate that the Government has a responsibility to protect harmony, social cohesion and the integrity of public institutions and political processes against online falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Singapore joins robust democracies like Australia, France, Germany, New Zealand and the United Kingdom (UK) seeking to use legislative measures to curb online falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: This Bill has added first-in-the-world features, such has Correction Directions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: However, the Bill currently grants far-reaching powers to the Government on online communications which raises significant concerns across different segments of our society that these tools may be used, intentionally or otherwise, to suppress or chill debate for political purposes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: For any avoidance of doubt, I want to state plainly that my debate here is once again not about "why" we have this Bill – I reiterate that I agree online falsehoods should be legislated – but about how the Bill can realise its full function with these amendments.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: A major area of contention that the House has heard is the definition of "fact" and "falsehood" under the Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: A statement of fact is defined as "a statement which a reasonable person seeing, hearing or otherwise perceiving it would consider to be a representation of fact" while a statement is false "if it is false and misleading, whether wholly or in part, and whether on its own or in the context in which it appears".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I understand that the use of the phrase "a reasonable person" is common in legalese and is used as shorthand for a hypothetical individual who exercises average care, skill and judgement in conduct, and who serves as a comparative standard for determining liability.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: In the eyes of the Court, this "reasonable person test" is one that is objective.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: However, it appears broad, imprecise and highly subjective to the ordinary citizen who would rightly be concerned with the chilling fear that giving an opinion could be wrongly construed as a false statement of fact.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Many non-governmental organisations (NGOs) are also understandably concerned with such an unclear definition because it is common for NGOs to rely on firsthand accounts of the individuals they represent.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: They often craft reports, public awareness campaigns and make recommendations on issues with these accounts as the primary source material.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: However, these accounts may conflict with official interpretations of data by policymakers or are challenged as inaccurate, especially with the information asymmetry.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Many of these may technically be considered as opinions to most rather than facts, yet MOM presents these instances as a "fact check", and formats these refutations with author's "claim" which is then countered by MOM's "fact".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: A sexual assault victim might feel uncomfortable sharing the full details of his/her assault experience with the Police but might later disclose important details to case workers, counsellors and researchers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: If the NGO grounds its recommendations to legislation on evidence from such accounts, would the Government reject the basis for such recommendations because the accounts do not align with their official records of those cases?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Would the findings of the NGO be invalidated if they conflict with what the Government has on record as the “facts” of the case?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Besides the ordinary citizen and civil society, Mr Speaker, the concern with the definition of "fact" and "false" as drafted is also shared by the arts and media practitioners, academics and researchers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: To mitigate this definitional concern and without meddling with matters of jurisprudence, we propose that a new section called the Principles of the Act be included in the body of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: One of the proposed clauses in this section states explicitly that the Bill targets materially false statements and does not apply to "opinions, comments, critiques, satire, parody, generalisations or statements of experiences".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: We have similar legislative precedents for guiding principles on implementation and administration in the Mental Capacity and Vulnerable Adults Act.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira will elaborate further on this proposed amendment in his speech.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The Government has explicitly assured the public that this Bill is not intended to stifle or chill free speech, debate and criticism, and, in fact, aims to ensure such debate can occur without the corrosive presence of online falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: However, the Bill, as written, when tabled, does not contain such assurances that limit how the Bill's powers can be used.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: This definition is reminiscent of but broader than existing laws, such as section 11(4) of the Computer Misuse Act, where words like "serious harm" and "disruption" prefaces and qualifies the basis of a diminution of public confidence.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: When does a statement cross the threshold from inconsequential personal expression to a threat to public confidence?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Would someone opining that the Government is incompetent on Facebook be subject to a Correction Direction if their post gains enough shares or likes to be considered capable of influencing public confidence?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: In the case of the death of Full-time National Serviceman Dominique Lee, Facebook's recent posts by his mother critical of the Government received viral status and revived attention to the three-year-old case in 2016.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I am heartened that the Minister agrees with the need for Ministers to provide more specific reasons on falsity and on public interest since this is currently not in the Bill when it was tabled.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: He assured this House that this will now be set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Subsidiary legislation, however, can be amended without coming before Parliament.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
