text: So, our intent with the amendments clauses 13 and 25 remains unchanged – that this amendment will ensure that any future Minister and/or Government would have to first change the primary legislation – that is, tabling it in Parliament, therefore, a higher barrier to clear.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The appeals process in clauses 17, 29 and 35 could potentially limit the ability of appellants to seek judicial oversight because all appeals must be made first to the respective domain Minister.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Currently, no timeframe is provided in the Bill for a decision on the appeal to be made when the Bill was tabled.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: We seek to amend the clauses to state that the Minister shall do everything reasonable to ensure the appeals process is expeditious and low-cost.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Again, I am grateful that Minister Shanmugam has agreed that this provision that we have proposed is needed and clarified in his speech that this shall be addressed in subsidiary legislation with details.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Again, Mr Speaker, our intent with clauses 17, 29 and 35 remains unchanged – that this amendment will ensure that any future Minister and/or Government that attempts to use subsidiary legislation or internal practice to unnecessarily delay the appeals process would have to first change the primary legislation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: They highlighted, and I quote, that "there is no one silver bullet to combat this complex problem, and a multi-pronged approach is necessary".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Indeed, we must refrain from viewing legislation alone as a "silver bullet" that will sufficiently address this complex issue of online falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I will refer to this henceforth as "The Council".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The Council's primary objective is to assure the public that the Government is accountable for the routine exercise of powers under the Act.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: It ensures that regardless of whether Parliament takes an active interest in the exercise of powers under this Act, there will still be routine independent oversight.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The Council is empowered to evaluate the actions of the Government under the Act, evaluate other measures taken by the Government to address online falsehoods, and make recommendations to the Government on the exercise of powers under the Act.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: In our amendment in clause B(5)(i), the Council will publish annual reports of its activities, findings and recommendations.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I do hope I have clarified for Mr Christopher de Souza on his misunderstanding yesterday of the Council as taking over the Ministerial function.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: We had shared this in the Explanatory Notes which were sent out with the Notice of Amendment on 30 April 2019.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I am glad that the Minister also shared in his speech yesterday that he agrees with the intent of the Independent Council.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I believe that councils for such a purpose do not lead to unnecessary bureaucracy because we have numerous precedents to cite in support of this, such as the National Council on Problem Gambling set up in 2005 in conjunction with the Casino Control Act to address the social issue of problem gambling.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Casinos were introduced to Singapore for the first time then, and we may have been able to clearly justify the economic benefits of the new legislation then at that time, yet we could not have known with certainty the collateral issues and damage, social or otherwise, that may result.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: We believe that this ensures that the Council stands as a separate and independent body from the Government.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: So, yes, we agree with the Minister that the Executive is accountable to Parliament and all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: But the Council serves more than the role of oversight.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: If there is one thing this House agrees unanimously on through this debate so far, it would be the importance of public education in our war on online falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The expertise and knowledge provided by the Council will help enrich these cross-agency and whole-of-nation efforts.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The best antidote against the potential harms brought about by fake news is an educated and discerning citizenry.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: An informed citizenry can only be created and sustained if the Government remains open to debate and criticism in an increasingly complex world.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Mistrust in public institutions also facilitates the uptake of falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat recently stated that the biggest "unknown" challenge that Singapore will face is the "nature of politics".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I understand that to be a question of whether Singapore – that is, the people and its Government – will be able to collectively wield sufficient political consensus for the best interests of the country in the long run.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I agree with Deputy Prime Minister Heng and believe that, for that to happen, we need the basis of trust between the Government and the people to be grounded in a climate of psychological security, one which allows all citizens to participate actively in the future of Singapore from a place of safety and responsibility, not fear of punitive consequences.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I acknowledge that it is in the interest of the Government to maintain and further public trust.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: This would mean using executive powers to protect society and limiting the use of these same powers when they may discourage or chill robust criticism.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Parliament must meaningfully exercise that authority to further public confidence in our robust Parliamentary processes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Minister Shanmugam has said that Ministers exercising their powers under this Bill will be accountable to Parliament and the public, and I believe that process starts with the consideration of these proposed amendments that we have put forth to the Bill, for an inclusive and thriving society that we will and can be.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I urge Members of this House to review the amendments set out in the Order Paper Supplement.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Your vote for the specific amendments does not mean you are standing against the legislative intent of the Bill to curb online harms from falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: It means you believe in this Parliamentary process to register your, and your constituents’, concerns with the Bill and to ensure that this and future governments are bound to the intent of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The threat of online falsehoods is a real and insidious threat that subverts the idealistic notions of free speech.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a teenager, I grew up believing in the concept of the marketplace of ideas where if everyone is free to speak, eventually, lies would be exposed and the truth would prevail.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On this basis, there is very little need for the Government to legislate in relation to free speech.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Subsequently though, the experiences of life and certainly the study of law have made it clear to me that this idealistic notion is not supported by real-world problems.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The laws of almost all countries prevent inciting violence or inducing people to commit crimes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Defamation also results in liability in many countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In Singapore, there have always been laws that prevent people inciting hatred against others.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Generally, the law steps in when freedom of speech is abused to cause harm.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The latest abuse of free speech is the threat of fake news.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Minister Shanmugam has set out in vivid colour the nature of this threat in his speech.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In parallel, there are many who profit from fake news and these include those who originate as well as those who help circulate it, such as social media platforms which make money from advertising revenues.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Fake news is often sensational, interesting and plausible, so it goes viral.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The cost to produce it is not so high as no real research work is needed and it is easy to circulate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In contrast, serious news providers are suffering because the cost of producing real news is high.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: You have to pay journalists, opinion writers, the cost of publication and even airtime.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Ironically, after incurring all these costs to produce real news or considered opinions, which are often not sensational because they are presented fairly, they are increasingly losing market share to those that peddle fake news.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: News providers all over the world are suffering from falling revenues and profitability.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, this is the complete inverse of the marketplace of ideas – the fake news prevails over the truth.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Essentially, the truth gets drowned out by falsehoods because it is more expensive to produce, less interesting and, ultimately, there are fewer people producing it as news providers go out of business.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This, in turn, also subverts the democratic process which works best when people are well-informed and able to make decisions based on the facts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is clear that everyone in this House agrees fake news is a threat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The differences in relation to this Bill are, in fact, relatively minor, and it has to do with how to address this threat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My friends from the WP are with us on the nature of the threat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Fake news is easy to generate, it is going to be voluminous, and you will need people who will be able to deal with this as and when it comes up.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, you need people who can make a large number of decisions relatively quickly.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this sense, it makes perfect sense to leave it to the Executive or a competent authority.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If someone disagrees with the competent authority's decision, they can take it up to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The allegations that Ministers will abuse power and insinuations that because they are all from the party, it will be used for political purposes; if a Minister were to do that, it can be taken up to the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Judge will decide one way or the other, the Government does not always win, so it is a fair process, and it will be open to public scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, if there is any abuse of power, there will be public scrutiny on this as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my view, it is a fairly sensible mechanism because it allows things to function efficiently while creating avenues for checks and balances.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Fake news moves fast and moves quickly, and you need an authority to deal with it in a quick way.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I was also interested in the variety of tools.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A lot of attention has been given to the Directions, which include statements of correction.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on how these powers would be used?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is also an interesting question about what happens to fake news that is already there, already in the public domain, that means news that is not generated in future.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Will these laws apply and give the authority powers to deal with that as well?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My own view is that it should, because the fake news is out there.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The WP made a lot of allegations about how the Judiciary would be impartial and, therefore, should make the decision and the Judiciary can make the decision quickly.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a practising lawyer, I have to say the Judiciary has a very huge caseload.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If the Executive has to go before a Judge for every single decision, which we would have to wait several days, depending, because fake news is so easy to generate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In a volatile period, you may have hundreds of fake news articles circulating in a day.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Are you supposed to have hundreds of applications in Court, with the Executive going up against the defendant each time, and the Judges to decide under the gun?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, the Minister is, in fact, taking more political risk by doing that, as opposed to leaving it to the judges, in which case, the political risk can be abdicated.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, in this sense, it puts the responsibility in the right place for an efficient operation of the mechanism.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Because what you want is a process that operates well and efficiently.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It seems to me the work of the council really is to scrutinise how the authorities are exercising their powers and to publish reports on that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think many of the objectives for scrutiny and all that can be done through much simpler mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is a much needed piece of legislation to deal with the present threat.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just to follow up on his point that the volume of applications may upset the process, and efficiency could be at risk.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When we passed the Protection from Harassment (Amendment) (POHA) Bill yesterday, this House envisaged the setting up of the Protection from Harassment Courts (PHCs).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The remedies that are provided for under POFMA are also available to ordinary Singaporeans, companies in Singapore, thousands of companies under POHA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would have imagined that the Court actually would be prepared for this volume of applications that could be made to it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even more so, as we found out yesterday the application process is quite simple.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My point is, would it not be foreseeable that actually the Courts could take on that additional task of looking through applications whether it comes from an individual, a company or the Government?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: And then, if there is a challenge later, that can come up through the judicial process, which is I think a more prudent use of judicial resources.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I believe that the threat of online harassment will not be as prevalent as fake news, because fake news tends to coalesce around certain periods of time and that is when you need to move fast.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just an additional point of clarification to the hon Member Mr Vikram Nair.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He mentioned that the process of a judicial review of directives under POFMA would be unworkable because there would be hundreds of cases of fake news every day.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is the hon Member suggesting that the powers in POFMA are likely to be exercised?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: But certainly, in the elections in Europe and the US, during those periods, there were very large amounts of fake news.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Much as I believe that there is a need for some form of legislation to deal with online falsehoods, the remedy must be appropriate.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, the Bill has generated much concern and objection from many Singaporeans since its First Reading in April.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will share some of the concerns I have about the POFMA Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As part of the conditions for the granting of the various directions under this Bill, under clause 4, the Minister must be of the opinion that it is in the public interest to issue such a Direction, and clause 4 provides a list of definitions or a set of different scenarios of what constituted "in the public interest".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am concerned with some of the definitions provided in clause 4.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I find them to be too general, and the precise scope is not clearly spelt out.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, in the context of falsehoods, what does it mean by "to protect public health or public finances" or "to secure public safety or public tranquility" under clause 4?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What acts or words will definitively trigger each of these definitions?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This brings me to the second point of concern about what is in the public interest.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this connection, the Minister mentioned the availability of judicial review yesterday.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As things stand, the procedure and cost regimes for judicial review will be quite different from the procedure and cost regimes for the appeal procedure under clause 17(5) and 29(5).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Minister intend to apply the same cost, procedure and timeline requirements for all Court applications or appeal under POFMA, including judicial review?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would it not be better for the Bill to expressly provide for the Court's ultimate jurisdiction over all areas of the Bill, including the issue of public interest, and for the same procedure and cost mechanism to apply?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am concerned about what else may be read by a Minister as a further definition or example of "in the public interest" in the future.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe that the diminution of confidence in the Government as a factor warranting legislative action is not found in fake news legislation elsewhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am concerned that the extension of the definition of public interest to include not diminishing public confidence in the Government may deter or prevent bona fide criticism and well-meaning intentions to expose genuine Government failings.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Above all, no government will always be correct, perfect or beyond reproach.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is for the Government, by its own efforts, to earn and maintain public confidence in itself and any use of the law to deter the diminution of public confidence will run counter to that.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, the Bill provides, at clause 2(2), the definition of a statement of fact and a definition of when a statement is false.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Already, many commentators have said that the distinction between a statement of fact and an opinion may not always be easy to draw, not to mention the difference between a statement of fact and an opinion of a statement of fact.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Different surveys using different parameters produce different outcomes; they may all not be wrong, they may even constitute statement of facts in different ways, but they prove that there can be divergence on what can constitute statement of facts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The definition of "if it is false or misleading, whether wholly or in part, whether on its own or in the context in which it appears" under clause 2(2) is too wide, especially the requirement of "misleading" alone.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would be misleading according to whose standards or opinion?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, if I were to say something in good faith according to my own views, but what if the Minister and even the Court decide that it meant something else and is different from what I have explained?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I did not even think of the Minister's view when I uttered those words.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would that not be very unfair to me as I did not intend that meaning?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why should I be subject to his Correction or stop Direction?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why should I have to appeal to the Courts?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Should he not apply to the Court if he feels aggrieved in the first place and the Courts can decide at first instance whether a Correction or stop Direction is necessary?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, according to clause 2(2), an article can be deemed to be a false statement even if only a part of it or a small part of it is false or misleading.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is there a risk that as a result of a small or even irrelevant or inconsequential factual error in an otherwise cogent article with serious issues, the article can be taken down, preventing the bulk of the meritorious arguments and issues raised in the article from being read and disseminated?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am also troubled by the definitions of "statement of facts" which have been defined as not false or misleading, rather than just "false" or "false and misleading".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such definitions can be open to different interpretations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, if I were to tell some people that I made a Police report against someone, in my opinion, that is a simple statement of fact, period.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is nothing much to disagree or to dispute.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I made the Police report, surely, I know that as a fact.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But when one applies the definition "misleading", what I have said may be interpreted by another to be something beyond what I ever intended to say or mean.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And history has shown that such statements could be subject to different interpretations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And how would it affect articles or reports of an opinion nature which premised its theories or findings on anonymous contributors?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This could be by a journalist or even an academic.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those who contributed their opinion or feedback or even to a survey may have good personal reasons for their anonymity and not necessarily because they are, as a matter of integrity, afraid to stand up for what they have said.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How will the journalist or newspaper be able to challenge an order on appeal given the circumstances?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I fear that this new law will discourage journalists in their writings, particularly where the source of information cannot, for whatever reasons, be fully disclosed or cited in Court.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To me, the most uncomfortable aspect of the Bill is the Minister being the first and even final arbiter under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many in Singapore have voiced this concern about the Government or the Minister being the final arbiter.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has been saying that the Courts are the final arbiter.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For Parts 3 and 4 Directions, that is only true insofar as any appeal comes within the three narrow grounds in clauses 17(5) and 29(5).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Courts are the final arbiter, why circumscribe and limit their powers in these ways?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why not let the Courts be the sole arbiter under this Bill?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As I have said earlier, even the Minister's opinion of whether the Minister was correct or not in arriving at his opinion that it is in the public interest to issue the Direction cannot be decided by the Court when it hears an appeal under clause 17 or 29.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And even for appeal under the three grounds in clauses 17(5) and 29(5), it may only be true if the party being subjected to a Minister's order under this Bill does, in fact, actually appeal to the Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if the party affected does not appeal to the Court for whatever reason, the Minister's order would have gone unscrutinised by the High Court – rightly or wrongly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even when the appeal is pending, the Bill expressly provides for the Minister's Direction to continue.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would this not create injustice if the appeal was later allowed, proving that the Minister was wrong in the first place?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In such cases, if the aggrieved person has suffered damages, he may not even be able to claim against the Minister.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Further, in certain circumstances, a Minister may potentially find himself in a position of conflict of interest when he invokes POFMA in respect of criticisms or complaints of wrongdoing either on his part or in respect of his own Ministry.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is there any provision to handle such conflict of interest?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, we do not have a Freedom of Information regime and well-meaning citizens may not have the same access to information, unlike the Government, and complaints may have arisen from well-meaning people where it may not be convenient to disclose the source of their information.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the situation where the Government has access to certain information and for whatever reason refuses to disclose full facts in the first place, even on request, it would be unfair to penalise anyone arising from a media report or something discussed in social media.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Any aggrieved person wishing to make an application under POHA applies to the Court.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If that works for everyone else, should the same procedure not apply to the Government in the case of POFMA?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not currently the case as under the POFMA Bill, the High Court hears any appeal against the Minister's Direction or order.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, applications under POHA are heard in the State Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Without derogating from my earlier position that the Courts should be the only arbiter for POFMA, let me now deal with some procedural aspects of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For Parts 3 and 4 of the Bill, if the affected person wishes to appeal to the Court against the Minister's stop or Correction Direction, he first needs to apply to the Minister in question to vary or cancel the order.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This seems odd to me as I am rather circumspect that a Minister will change his mind within a matter of days after his order.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The additional step of notifying the Minister is akin to being part of the appeal process itself and will merely add time to the affected person's wait for the Court hearing his appeal, but time may be of the essence to the affected person, especially when the Minister's Direction is wrongful and is bringing wrongful harm to the individual.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In any case, I find the idea of, in effect, appealing to the accuser to be a little odd.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, in POHA, an aggrieved party applying for an order has essentially the burden of proving his case to the judge deciding on whether an order should be given.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even when a defendant who is subject to a Part 3 Direction feels that the Minister is wrong in issuing such a Direction and wishes to appeal to the Courts, the Minister does not seem to have the primary burden of persuading the Court de novo that it is entitled to issue the order in question.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In any case, this is not clearly or expressly set out in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In both civil and communal actions, it would be fair to say that the plaintiff and the prosecutor, respectively, bear the primary burden to prove the case in Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In closing, the Minister cannot be an arbiter for any order or Direction under POFMA.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Courts should be given that role exclusively.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It may encourage journalists or academics to err on the side of caution for falling foul of the law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If a Minister or the Government is not forthcoming in providing clarificatory facts, it may encourage journalists or even common citizens to practise self-censorship at the expense of truth.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will discourage bona fide criticism and stifle public debate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Promoting the heliocentric theory that the Earth travels around the Sun.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the geocentric model, which incorrectly puts Earth at the centre of the Universe, was accepted fact for thousands of years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Galileo’s contribution was to use the first astronomical telescope which he invented to precisely observe the stars.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Galileo argued these observations meant the heliocentric model was a provable fact, and not a theory.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Inquisition did not reject Galileo's scientific evidence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, they found his evidence fundamentally incompatible with The Bible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Bible has passages stating the Earth is immovable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Inquisition interpreted this as a matter of fact.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Galileo was forced to recant, on pain of being condemned as a heretic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Legend has it that Galileo said, after recanting, “And yet it moves”.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: First, when we speak of the problem of online falsehoods, the real concern is our shared reality as a society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I agree with the Minister that this is the central concern: what is the infrastructure of facts that we depend on as a society?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Galileo was part of a wider battle to define shared reality at the end of the Renaissance in Europe.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Would reality be defined by science and reason, or by tradition and religion?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Second, governments are concerned about shared reality, because our beliefs have practical consequences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Galileo's findings supported a reality that threatened the temporal power of the Church.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Populists today and in history have spread lies to promote the alternative reality where society is under threat, justifying the use of extraordinary powers to save democracy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Points one and two, taken together, mean that judgements about shared reality by governments are inherently political acts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I do not mean they are always partisan acts, carried out for narrow political gain.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A good government would not act that way.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But they are political acts because they serve the definition of public interest that the government of the day believes in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Third, governments can get assessments of fact wrong.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Church of Galileo’s time was not opposed to science.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The earliest degrees granted by universities were in the fields of law, medicine and theology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Galileo’s supporters included princes and priests of the Church.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They were among the few people in Europe who had the education at the time to appreciate his findings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But even a government of experts can have blind spots.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A good government must act to defend the shared reality that best serves the public interest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But even a good government may face the temptation to gradually conflate the public interest with their own political gain.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It may be through sins of omission, by neglecting to fix blind spots in judgement, rather than by promoting falsehoods outright.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It may be true to believe that the public interest demands the suppression of all competing ideologies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But as with Galileo, these good intentions may eventually lead a good government to ignore reality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That is why the best government of all will shackle itself where necessary rather than grant itself more power.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I believe this Government understands this dilemma more than most.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That is why this Government sincerely believes it has crafted a Bill that shackles itself while granting the necessary powers to defend our infrastructure of truth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our disagreement is about whether this Bill has got this balance right.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: You will find in their statements broad agreement with the Bill’s legislative intent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Even if there is no malevolent intent, they may distort our shared reality and lead to harmful decisions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They are not readily corrected through self-regulation or education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I do not agree with all of the concerns expressed by the parties I have cited.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister has been kind to correct some of the misconceptions out there.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: My concern rather is that some of the debate around this Bill has conflated criticism of the Bill with support for irresponsible freedom of speech or with sinister intent towards Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Academics do not challenge the right of governments or the public to dispute scientific facts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But such disputes must honour the essential character of scientific research, which is evidence-based, driven by scientific methods, and held up to the highest standards of scrutiny.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Academics are concerned that when a government adjudicates scientific disputes there is a fundamental conflict of interest, as in my earlier example of Galileo and the Catholic Church.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: All governments have a political objective to defend a shared reality that suits their interest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the US Environmental Protection Agency changes its views on the climate change science depending on who is President.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Is it in the public interest for science to be unnecessarily determined by politics?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: An academic whose scientific findings are the subject of a Direction would not be able to communicate them online without risk of contravening the Direction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: She might have to write to scientific journals to ask for a retraction or correction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If our Government is not able to answer to the satisfaction of international experts, it would bring scientific condemnation on our country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Is it in the public interest to discourage, even inadvertently, research that uses Singapore for field studies or to further our knowledge of social science and ourselves?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We are concerned the Bill does not sufficiently limit, guide and oversee the exercise of Executive powers against online falsehoods.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While we have concerns that these give the Executive very broad powers, we could not develop constructive amendments that would be feasible for the Courts in trying facts, while also granting the Executive the discretion to act urgently to protect the public interest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We also accept the Executive must have the power to act urgently.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Developing an amendment to create a role for ex-ante judicial or independent oversight proved challenging and risks considerable harm in the event of an immediate threat.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, accepting the Bill as it is in these areas means we accept the Executive should have considerable latitude.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: My colleague Ms Anthea Ong has spoken on the Council.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I will discuss the Principles which provide a guide to the exercise of powers under the Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It codifies that the Act is targeted at statements which are materially false and not opinions, comments, critiques, satire, parody, generalisations or statements of experiences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I believe the Minister’s view is that the Government accepts many of these Principles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, the Minister also believes the Principles create legislative confusion because they may already duplicate elements present in the Bill or in law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, I believe the Minister's view – and that of a Senior Counsel – is that proportionality in the exercise of powers is already incorporated in the "necessary or expedient" term used in the public interest clause of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But given proportionality is so important to avoid unnecessarily restricting speech and to build trust with the public, we believe the Bill must state clearly the principles behind what proportionality means in practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We can accept that there may be better ways of phrasing the Principles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, we disagree that it would be sufficient to have the Bill without the Principles of Act at all, or other amendments in plain language that have similar effect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has previously defined plain language Principles of the Act in the Mental Capacity Act and the Vulnerable Adults Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is important because these Acts give Government officials significant power over the autonomy and rights of persons.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill will also give Government officials significant powers over speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is crucial that every Government official involved in the exercise of powers abide by a common set of principles in administering the Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What is the difference between doing so in the Bill, versus leaving it to subsidiary legislation or internal regulation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Subsidiary legislation can be changed without a Parliamentary vote.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The real value, Sir, of these Principles comes in using them as a basis for building an institution that the public trusts, an institution that is not dependent on the political interests in charge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I believe the opposing benches are agreed that one such institution is the Judiciary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I will now discuss what this Act will mean in practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: How would the Executive use the powers under this Act?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Is there a specific subject statement that is potentially false?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I assumed that the public interest test would be satisfied since these cases were serious enough for a Government response.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Of the remaining 60 cases, while facts were disputed, seven did not identify a subject statement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: There is either no specific disputed fact or no identifiable subject statement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The remaining 53 cases are for specific subject statements with an identifiable source.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: These are cases where the Act may have potentially applied retrospectively, for example.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Forty-three of these 53 cases are disputes involving the facts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The other 10 involve disputes over the conclusions drawn from facts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Overall, the Government is quite clear about how it labels disputes involving the facts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Most are considered falsehoods, although some are considered clarifications or misrepresentations instead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: In 2017, MSF reported data showing a sharp rise in ComCare assistance recipients between 2012 and 2015.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: A subject statement made the claim that this was, and I quote, "the worst poverty result ever officially reported in Singapore", end quote.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: MSF called this and I quote, "not true", end quote, and MSF explained that a growth in ComCare recipients reflects more generous social welfare policies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: My view is that this is a difference of opinion based on the same facts and not a falsehood.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I will stand corrected, but I do not think there was an attempt by the subject statement to make up or distort the ComCare numbers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: It was simply an interpretation of the facts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I think a Ministry should be free to make value judgements about criticism, including labelling criticisms as false.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But more caution is required to avoid the incorrect exercise of powers under the Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But these differences in opinion may arise because the public may only have partial information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: In this case, they may know about ComCare receipts but they may not know about changes in social welfare policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: We should not label such differences in interpretation as falsehoods, especially if the Ministry has not released all the relevant information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: We must ensure the public continues to have trust in the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: This is why we have proposed the Principles of Act, which will help to build an institution that appropriately limits the exercise of these important powers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I understand why Members of the Government may not share my reservations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I accept they have great confidence that their present good governance will continue.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Before I speak on this Bill, Mr Speaker, I would like to comment on what Assoc Prof Walter Theseira talked about.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I think as a Member of the House, I, too, appreciate and support free speech.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I, too, support the investigation and exploration of new ideas and so forth.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I believe that if there is indeed a "Galileo" today in Singapore, we will all be cheering rather than stopping what he is doing.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: This Bill, which met with quite a lot of discussion, is actually not that complex.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: While there are many discussions about what truth is, is it epistemological truth?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: But fundamentally, we have a real practical problem, and we have to deal with it.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Rather than tinkering with the separation of powers at the state, be it elected Members and the party having the largest number of Members forms the Government and separating this Executive power with Legislative power and Judicial power – and we have modified that with Presidential powers – to tinker with this, just for the purpose of this Bill, is quite dangerous.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I think all parties should give deep thought to whether or not we should introduce another layer of power structure, which the Nominated Members of Parliament called the Independent Council to oversee the Government when Ministers supported by civil servants are already elected, already have a mandate, to ensure peace and order in the society and is always accountable for their actions in this Bill through a judicial review or statutory appeal, but more importantly, every five years at the ballot box.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Would an Independent Council be subject to that?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I think we need to think carefully before we decide which direction to take.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: It is very heartening that most Members of Parliament who have spoken agree that fake news is a real problem and we need to deal with it, especially when public interest is at stake.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: So, the parts of the public critique and comments and criticism that do not impinge on these two conditions, would be free to flow, as they have been.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: But the disagreement seems to be, "Who should be the decision-maker?" Should it be the Executive branch, which I interpret as the Minister supported by the Civil Service; or the Courts; or a separate council?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Now, I understand from the Nominated Members of the Parliament that the separate council is not the party who would make the decision whether an issue is true or false, but to be a review committee, over and above, for Executive branch decisions.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I do not see where they get the mandate to do that.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: There can be three possible bodies which can be the decision-maker.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Let us see which makes the most sense.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: To answer this question, it is important to know that fake news that have gone viral and yet undermine public interest have to be dealt with very, very quickly.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: So, "speed" is the first criterion to judge whether the Executive branch is best-placed, Judiciary is best-placed or an independent council to oversee is best-placed.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: We have heard many examples that have been discussed here.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The accusations were made, falsely of course, against the French Roma community or the Gypsies.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The Gypsies were attacked by unprovoked vigilante mobs, even though this rumour is totally false and baseless.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Two men from the Roma community were hospitalised and their van burnt.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Another example, in Medan, Indonesia, in July 2016, a woman complained about the use of loudspeakers at a mosque near her home.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: So, a lack of speed, and these are the consequences.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The second criterion, I believe is, the issue on "accountability".

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: If the Government is elected and the party with the most seats in Parliament forms the government, they have not only the mandate and responsibility, they are accountable to make sure that public peace and social stability are at all times preserved.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: It also has the resources, being backed by the Civil Service and the expertise in many, many domains, whether it is medical, security, health, water and so on.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Falsehoods can be quite insidious in any one of these areas.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I really do not see another institution in Singapore which has this deep expertise in many, many domains, as I described.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: In management science, it is logical that the party who is held accountable and with the resources and the expertise, must be the party who should act.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Just yesterday, I heard Mr Pritam Singh debating on the POHA Bill.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: He was basically asking that, if the aggrieved party wants to have an Expedited Protection Order (EPO) and so on, would the Court be fast enough?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: So, I see a contradiction of why the WP is supporting the Judiciary as the party to make such orders in the case of POFMA.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Also, there was a paragraph in the SC report, paragraph 364(B), where Assoc Prof Goh Yi Han, Dean of the Singapore Management Univeersity School of Law, was a proponent of the Executive option.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Court processes require an application for Court Order to be made, together with a supporting affidavit.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The application must then be served on the person against whom the order is sought and that person can then file an affidavit in reply.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Actually, to think about it, at the end of the day, the ultimate arbiter are the voters at the ballot box.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just to be sure so that I do not misquote him, I understand his two main issues were that I was part of the SC and the SC's recommendation was that quick action was important – response time being within a matter of hours.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second was that yesterday, during the POHA debate, I asked whether Courts will be fast enough.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And let us remember, virality is not an issue that only affects the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Of course, it would mean raising the Courts to be able to deal with those problems.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That means that the case the Government brings to the Court, the PHC, is this a prima facie falsehood?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Fake news can bring real harm.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Although the authorities had clarified, many seniors still went to the CCs with their walking stick in hand and waited there.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The seniors do not know how to verify online news and can be easily fooled by fake news.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This has caused much anxiety amongst the elderly.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As for those who create such fake news, do they not have elderly parents and grandparents, too?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that after POFMA is passed, if such incidents happen again, we can prevent more seniors from being fooled and bring the perpetrators to justice.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Our racial and religious harmony can easily be harmed by fake news.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We all know that many Asian countries also have "fake news factories" trying to do damage to our racial and religious relations.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To protect the elderly and minorities, we must quickly correct falsehoods and limit their spread.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If we only rely on the Court or an independent committee, they still have to verify with the Government agencies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The speed of correction may not be that fast.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Ministers will also have to stand in elections.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If they abuse the law, Singaporeans will definitely make wise choices.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, many residents asked me: if someone inadvertently forwards a fake story, what will happen to him?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): Sir, I support this move to criminalise the creation and dissemination of falsehoods that would harm the public interest.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many elderly people have gradually become accustomed to using Facebook and WhatsApp.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But they are a lot less savvy when it comes to identifying and clarifying fake news and understanding how photographs and videos can be altered.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They are inclined to take things they see on the Internet at face value, especially information circulated by their friends.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry of Transport clarified that seniors have 10 months to apply for subsidies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But we still saw long lines at many CCs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Although we deployed staff to explain, many frail seniors still waited in line for a long time.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When staff sent me pictures of the elderly lining up, some with canes or wheelchairs, it really pained me.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are also other hoaxes that make the elderly worried about their CPF savings, saying the savings would not be given in cash to their heirs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Even when they are clarified, the clarification does not reach everyone, and many elderly are still unnecessarily distressed.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And when the elderly are victims of fake news, for example, when elderly stallholders are accused of selling contaminated food, they might not be notified promptly or might not know how to clarify online.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I do not know why people would create fake news that targets old people.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Do they not have elderly parents and grandparents, too?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that with these new laws, we can stop the news from spreading and punish such despicable people.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The other group that can be badly affected are the minorities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In many countries, fake news about minorities has led to attacks against them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Often, this fake news comes from fake news factories abroad, including in mature democracies like France, where the Roma people were attacked after rumours of them kidnapping children, which my colleague, Mr Cedric Foo mentioned just now.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We know there are fake news factories in many Asian countries, so this could happen to us, too.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How will we enforce the law when falsehoods originate from overseas?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Do we have agreements with other countries and tech companies to help us investigate and prosecute these criminals?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When fake news circulates, especially if it targets the elderly and our minorities, we need to make sure the clarifications reach everyone.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We will save these vulnerable groups plenty of heartache and even prevent violence against them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, I agree with the idea of the Government making a quick decision to ask the tech companies to clarify or take down fake news.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If we leave it to the Courts, or a committee, they will be comprised of generalists and, to determine whether something is true or false, they will have to get information from the Ministries anyway.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: By the time the decision is made, maybe riots will have already broken out.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Certainly, the fake news would have spread far and wide.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministers' decisions could be challenged in Court, and they can be voted out if they make a decision that is obviously just to suppress critical opinions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Compare that to a committee that is appointed and paid by the Government, and gets most of its facts from the Government, but cannot be voted out, which one is more accountable?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: My next question is, many residents have asked me, if they do not know a story is false and forwarded it, what will happen to them?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They do not seem to have read the Bill and have made a variety of misleading statements to fearmonger on the Bill.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What is the Member's basis for saying that the Government is trying to increase its powers?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If the Government was really as power hungry as the Member describes, why put forth a Bill that is narrower in scope?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why would a Minister expose himself to a challenge he will lose?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang also gives misleading examples to claim that the Bill has an expansive scope which will affect Singaporeans' daily lives.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He says that if a Minister says that the older generation cannot accept a non-Chinese Prime Minister, this will be an opinion, but if a political opponent says the same thing, a Minister may use the Bill against that opponent.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And if the Government were to use the Bill as the WP alleges, do you think Singaporeans will take it lying down?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He is trying to mislead people and create fear.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: I just want to ask him if being a Member of the SC and having had the chance to read the SC report and agreeing to it, specifically Recommendation 12 where in the first instance, the first principle, in order to deal with it, we must deal with it with speed, in a matter of hours.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: So, the first part of my question to him is: does he deny that now?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Does he now say that countering fake news can take much longer?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Or does he still subscribe to the fact that it has to be dealt with in a matter of hours?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I thought I have made that clear, but I will repeat myself.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But the question is whether the SC report commits itself to the Executive being the decision-maker.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: He also said just now that he agrees that the Judiciary needs to be "bulked up" or whatever exact words were used, in order to respond in a matter of hours.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: And coming back to the earlier point, I am not saying that the SC report made a decision or conclusion on who the decision-maker must be.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: But if the Judiciary has to be bulked up to be able to handle issues in a matter of hours as opposed to the Executive branch which is supported by 16 Ministries, about 135,000 officers with years of experience in different domains like security, economics, health, education, and fake news can occur anywhere, how long does it take to bulk up the Judiciary before it can respond in a matter of hours?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And it is in that context that I believe that a speedy response is possible through the Courts because those Courts are going to be set up by virtue of the amendments we passed under POHA.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Cedric Foo, are there any new points?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Yes, probably the last engagement to give others a chance to speak.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: POHA is for private matters, and if somebody felt that they had been harassed, as a private individual, they will go to the Courts.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: I think the Minister and the Senior Minister of State have spoken about how to make the Courts a little more efficient and lower costs for such purposes.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: These are huge, these are public interest matters that have to be dealt with much faster than individual interest under POHA which, whilst important, are not as urgent as in cases under POFMA which are both important and urgent, and have to be dealt with right away.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: So, if it is to equip the Courts to have the same capacity, response time, experience and domain knowledge as the Executive branch, then I think it is a very far-fetched idea.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: I do not see how the Courts can reach that state.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If not, there would be no provisions for interim orders.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I disagree with this idea – unless I have gotten POHA completely wrong – that individuals and companies cannot expect a fast, expeditious solution to falsehoods that have been carried against them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, again, the WP will stick to the point and we believe that the Courts actually can respond to online falsehoods speedily.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Government should have the powers and the objectives should be achieved as follows: provide access, limit or block exposure, disrupt the digital amplification, discredit the sources.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The opening words cannot be any clearer: "The Government should have the powers...".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, equally importantly, let us not argue with qualitative words – "Courts can move fast, no reason why they cannot move fast" and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Let us stick to the clear recommendation – "matter of hours".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Does the Member think that in every case that is necessary, the Court can decide in a matter of hours?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Member knows the process: it would have to be filed, it would have to be served.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The defendant may wish to come to Court and say, "I want to argue this" which means due process.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: How long do you think it will take to get a duty judge?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I do not know whether the Member has tried.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But over 22 years, I have tried several times.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the duty judge is in a hearing, it can take up to end of the day.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This SC would have been mindful of all of that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is not possible for the Member or for me or for anyone else in this House honestly to say that the Courts can do this in a matter of hours.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, let us stick to the SC's recommendation – "in a matter of hours".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You know how long it takes to get a duty judge?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When are you going to get a duty judge?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Sometimes, you can go to his house and see him.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What if he is engaged in something else?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He can only give you the time that he can and it is possible that the defendant will turn up.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You cannot say all the time that it should be ex-parte.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Even in ex-parte, there is such a thing as contested ex-parte.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If it is a responsible or respectable party, like a platform, you could say, the platform turns up and says, "No, we want to argue this case".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Due process means you must allow them to argue.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That means you have to set a hearing date.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: How long do you think that will take?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But there will be other times when the judges are not available.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is why this Recommendation 12, which is a critical recommendation, says, "The Government should have the powers to swiftly disrupt the spread and influence of online falsehoods".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And it says, "It should be done in a way to achieve the objective of breaking virality by being effective in a matter of hours".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I will say so by looking you in the eye.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Courts will tell you that is not possible.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, let us not use words like "Courts can decide quickly".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But, as I said to the Nominated Members of Parliament yesterday, what does that mean?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have given concrete examples where things happened within a matter of hours.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For private interest, you cannot have any other way other than going to Court.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We set up a dedicated set of Courts for the State Courts.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We asked them to set up a separate tribunal but that does not mean that an order can be obtained within a matter of hours.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We can do the same thing in the High Court.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But that does not mean that a Court order can be obtained within a matter of hours.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There might be times when there is no defendant and you can try and get an ex-parte, sometimes over the phone but, often, there is a platform where these things are carried, and the platform might want to be heard, Facebook, Google or somebody else.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, I think the WP should try and clarify without using subjective terms and bringing in POHA which is quite different from POFMA, that is, this Bill, together with the SC's recommendations.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Is he saying he no longer stands by it?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And if you stand by it, how does your current position make any sense because you accept that is a serious problem?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You accept that something has to be done.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It must be broken within a matter of hours.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The only difference that I see between you and us now is who makes that initial call.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And your method does not gel with what the recommendation says.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, maybe, I can hear from the Member.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think a number of points have been made by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: First, it has to do with my position on the Committee and the recommendations per se.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not think it is an attempt to try and wriggle around the words, "The Government should act swiftly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: POFMA is the legislation that the Government has put forward.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the issue is really response time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think that is the key pivot that the Government and the WP have —

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that it says "The Government have the powers to swiftly disrupt" and says "This is the way it should be done."

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The SC report, we went through several revisions of it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I was part of the team that looked at Recommendation 12 closely.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not want to share what the deliberations of that small group were because those are confidential and I do not intend to abuse my Parliamentary privilege for that purpose, but I have those emails.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The point is, I believe the SC had to put forth an approach on how we are going to deal with the problem, but as to the specific modality, that was something for Parliament to decide.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, that is dealing with the SC's phraseology and how the issue was put out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Certainly, there appears to be two regimes when the Government needs to apply for an interim order to move quickly against either an individual or a company; in this case, let us say, a tech company like Facebook.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The prima facie case is something that the judge can rule upon as a matter of course.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That means, the order is given but as to the arguments that have to be dealt with later, these can be dealt with accordingly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Targeted Correction order, this is clause 21, Part 4 of the Bill, is issued to the Internet intermediary that provided the Internet intermediary service by means of which the subject material has been or is being communicated in Singapore requiring it to communicate by means of that service to all end users in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Once that standard is met, let us say, by a duty judge, the question of hearing the arguments can be dealt with later.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I think this is the point which suggests to me that there is some scope for the Courts to deal with the urgent issue that the Government wants to resolve, at least in the interim, and then when it comes to the proper hearing, the Government can make its case in full and the aggrieved party will have the time to respond.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Singh, that does not quite answer the question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On Recommendation 12 and whether the Executive is mentioned or not, I think we stick to the wordings here because I am also aware of those emails.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it is quite clear what Recommendation 12 says, but I do not want to put you in any sort of embarrassment on that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us just deal with the point on hours.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
