text: I think it is unarguable, prima facie or whatever, the starting point is for you to file and get an attendance before a duty judge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You will accept that that is not always possible in a matter of hours.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you serve it, and sometimes you will have to, particularly, say you decide to make the platform the defendant, and they turn up, and they say, "No.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Before you make a prima facie order, we want to make an argument.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court, are you sure, will each time make a decision within a matter of hours, assuming you can even get the judge?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the judge is in a hearing for the whole day, you get to see him at the end of the day, if he wants to see you, if he is able to see you.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is unarguable, is it not, that there will be times you cannot guarantee that if you go down this route, you will always get it within a matter of hours, prima facie or otherwise?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I mean you are good enough to accept that, I think we can move on.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: On the first point, Minister, it is no question of an embarrassment for me.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think I am quite clear as to what I think is the appropriate position taken by the SC report.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Decision-making – it was not explicitly stated which would be the entity and I think I want to leave it at that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second point I think is an important one.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The first question was in a matter of hours.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I think the Minister makes a fair point in the case of the duty judge.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If, indeed, there is only one person, then it really comes down to a question of whether that should be increased.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Minister may say look it is going to be quite difficult to execute in practice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I happen to think that, again, depending on how urgent the problem is, how bad the situation is, that can be dealt with.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is an important point because it deals with issues of natural justice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Again, we look at POHA and interim orders, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Serious falsehood put out there; and the Court may decide, "Look, I think service is of a second order importance right now, we need to deal with this problem but parties have to come back before me".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Singh, I think let us try and get clarity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The first point is not just a question of resources.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I told you, there can be weekends, there can be public holidays, there can be other issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The simple point is that neither you nor I nor anyone else can guarantee that it can be gotten in a matter of hours.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I assume you have practised in this area.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if you have not, I will make that point to you.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If it is a known platform and there is an identifiable defendant who is not a rogue party, when you go to the Court and the Court says, "Why have you not served on this party, why are they not before the Court?" What do you say?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, what really happens is, each time you just go and get an ex parte order, all that the judge has is what you are giving him.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And he confirms that you should get the order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think you have an insuperable problem there because of the availability of the judges.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if your point is, each time the Government wishes, it goes ex parte because it is urgent, then how is the Court to substantially check other than the fact that the Government puts up an affidavit, explains it and says, "I think it is urgent" and the Court gives it?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But my fundamental point is, are you sure it is done in a matter of hours?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Are you standing here as a party and guaranteeing that, every time it happens, it will be done within a matter of hours?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you say that, we will just leave it as that; if that is your position.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think it requires a caveat, of course.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: A caveat is important and that caveat is that there has to be capacity for a duty judge to be available at that time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I had intended originally to pose a clarification to Mr Cedric Foo.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But I think in light of the Law Minister's comments at this point, I will just pose some clarification to him.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: By definition, is that impossible in the future if we take all these steps to put in the resources to put in the process, if necessary create a special of class of judges and so on, so forth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I would add that in other jurisdictions, to the best of my knowledge, and I may stand corrected, in other jurisdictions, for example, in some states in the US, it is my understanding that an arrest warrant has to be approved by a judge under certain circumstances.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: These arrest warrants are very time-sensitive and the judge has to make a decision on the balance of probabilities whether to arrest the person.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That is a serious matter, whether to arrest a person in extremely time-sensitive circumstances.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Sometimes, late at night, the law enforcers will go and see the judge.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Because that system has been created and structured and resourced in such a way that it is possible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us take the sequence, the process of these things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, you got to draft something and file in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are now talking about the SC's recommendation to do something within a matter of hours.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You got to put aside some time for that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us say in the Member's scenario, we have a High Court Judge who does nothing but sits there 24/7 because it can break out anytime, and will be available as soon as the Government calls.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, you can have a judge who does nothing but this, and no other cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because if he is hearing a case, he cannot break the case and come and listen to you.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, there are further factors which have further levels of uncertainty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You file, you go before a judge and you say, "Look, Judge, it is so urgent that I am not going to serve this on Google, Facebook or whoever, wherever it is spreading.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I just need an urgent order, ex parte, and then later on I will serve".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sometimes, the judge may agree but the judge may also disagree.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Supposing he disagrees, then it takes a further length of time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The decision-maker, the person who has the facts, might take one view and the responsibility for dealing with that situation also rests with the Executive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Have you not known of instances where within 24 hours, there have been riots and people have been killed?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Supposing the judge says, "I think I would like to hear the other side, urgent as it is".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Urgent ex parte applications have been heard on a contested basis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But he could also ask for contested ex parte.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He could ask the other side to turn up quickly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And I think that there are a number of points that the Minister made which relate to judicial capacity, for want of a better term, and process.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I would imagine that, based on what the Law Minister has said, he can envisage that the necessary capacity can be created to deal with such a caseload, based on what Law Minister said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Possible, if the judge does nothing else but waits for the applications.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, I would take it that necessary capacity can be created.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We can create a special class of Courts, duty judges.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, with sufficient resources applied, necessary capacity can be created.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And I think the Law Minister alluded to the fact that while the Government will have to word the submission, even an ex parte submission to the Court, and that is time-consuming, and while this is going on, the clock is ticking away and the falsehood is viralising and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But within the Ministry, or the Statutory Board or agency, the civil servants also have to word the submission to the Minister or communicate with the Minister.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Can we not create a process whereby the communication, the form and the format of communication between the civil servant and the Minister is very similar to the form and format of communication between the Government and the Court in those very time-sensitive cases, to obtain an initial prima facie decision?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, my point there is that I think, at the level of process, a process can be created to minimise the time lag from Ministry to Court.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I would put it to the Minister that a process can be created in that way.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And I think we have addressed the issue of capacity and we have addressed the issue of process.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The Minister has been talking about the current situation, right now, with the capacity we have and the process we have.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If we can add more resources and capacity, and we change the process to make it expedited to arrive at that prima facie decision to stop the viralisation, I would put it to the Law Minister that that is perfectly conceivable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And I also want to address the other point that the Minister made, that in some cases, the judge will not agree.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In some cases, the judge will not agree.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If the judge feels that he is being asked to make a prima facie decision, but he is looking at it on a balance of probabilities and he feels that the Executive is over-reaching or the Executive is abusing its power, so he may not agree in that case.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And that is precisely the value of the check.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would ask Mr Perera not to put words in my mouth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will be very good to clarify that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you believe that that can be done by simply putting some submission to the Court?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is that it, whatever the civil servant submits to the Minister can simply be submitted to the Court?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have got the clarifications I needed, Sir.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We have seen what happens elsewhere when falsehood fans sectarian hatred, swing elections and harmed national security.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We need tools to limit the reach of truly dangerous falsehoods spread by malicious actors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But while we agree on the goal, the WP and the PAP disagree about the means to achieve that goal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We disagree because we look ahead to the future of this country after this Bill is passed and we see a country where too much power is vested in the hands of any and every Minister.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We see a country where free speech debate and thinking could become stifled, especially on the very important matters of public policy and politics on which so much health in national life turns.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We disagree because the cure that the PAP Government has placed in front of us could lead to outcomes worse than the disease.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Yet, section 2 suggests that a particular collection of facts may be construed as misleading if the "opposite facts", as it were, are not given what the Minister thinks its sufficient weight.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The same Minister may not correct statements made by the Government or its supporters that present mainly their facts as it were.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: How do we deal with statements like, for example, "Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats are more like rental flats than owned assets since lessees lack strata titles.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The HDB controls many aspects of what you can do with your flat and the value declines over the long-term towards zero dollars at the end of 99 years".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Would such a view be deemed subject to a Correction Order under POFMA?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If this wide definition of misleading facts is maintained, the Courts should at least be the first arbiter of truth in respect of formulations, such as this one, rather than Ministers who have and will be seen to have their own political interest, a point I will come back to.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In section 4, it would seem that anything that impinges on national security, public health, public finances and so on, in however microscopic or indirect manner, would be upheld as vulnerable to corrections or penalties.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The language of section 4 states "expedient" and "necessary".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: To what degree of harm to those things?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Should section 4 not be worded to define "public interest" with reference to a real risk posed to the things described?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In lieu of this, any statement having however minor an impact on the things described would qualify as correctable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And this is setting aside section 17, Part 5's circumscription of the scope of what has been said will be fast and cheap POFMA High Court appeals to exclude consideration of the degree to which public interest is impacted, a point which my colleague Mr Dennis Tan and which my Party Chairman Ms Sylvia Lim will expand on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: This lack of a threshold of significance stretches the risk of abuse of POFMA powers to correct matters which have a very minor impact on the public interest.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Next, my colleagues have spoken about the chilling effect POFMA may have on free speech.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It is by virtue of this Bill's peculiar cocktail of three things, of section 2, defining what the Minister deems a misleading presentation of facts, not only false claims of facts, as correctable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And thirdly, section 6, which establishes Ministers as the decision-makers of truth and falsehoods in the first instance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It is through the combination of these three aspects of POFMA that this Bill is likely to chill free speech and debate about the Government, policies and politics, particularly, expressions of views that run counter to the Government narrative.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Correction and takedown orders could damage, if not destroy reputations and careers, for journalists, activists, academics, public intellectuals, politicians, professionals of various kinds.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If your post becomes subject to such orders, what would your employers think, your lecturers and tutors, your professional colleagues, friends, spouse, business associates, partners and customers?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: When we bring in the risk of massive fines and lengthy jail time under section 7 for a single offence of "having reason to believe" that one statement is false or harmful as POFMA defines it, which includes undermining confidence in the Government, and with no threshold of significant impact on public interest specified in the law, the risk, Mr Speaker, Sir, is not just chilling free speech, but of hurling it into an industrial freezer.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: By free speech here, I refer particularly to public speech regarding policies and politics that may contain criticisms of the government of the day or the ruling party.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I note in passing that for offshore sponsors of deliberate online falsehoods like state actors or offshore extremists or sectarian groups, it would be difficult, if not impossible, to subject them to these criminal penalties.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The burden of these penalties and the fear they generate will fall primarily on domestic actors, on Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Of course, penalties for harmful falsehoods are necessary.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But when the penalties are severe and attached to language like that in sections 2 and 4 and with Ministers as the first arbiters of truth, the prospect of chilling public political debate is very real.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What would Singapore look like if most Singaporeans avoid commenting publicly in ways that may be seen as critical of the Government and its narrative?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What may take hold is self-censorship and the restriction of online comments in favour of verbal conversations amongst friends or talks held amongst small groups.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And the reason for this is clear to see.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Many citizens will not have the stomach to risk a Correction order or a criminal charge even if they are confident about their facts, as many will not want to take on the effort, time, cost and risk entailed by a legal appeal, let alone a full-blown judicial review action.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Many will choose not to take up that burden and simply not speak up.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Next, Sir, section 11 raises a related issue.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: A Correction statement must be worded "in the specified form and manner" specified by the Government.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Is there any requirement that Correction statements be as concise, factual, reasonable and non-pejorative as possible?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Where is the requirement of proportionality in wording Correction statements?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: A price we pay for this Bill may be to live in a country where alternative media activists and journalists are afraid to bring certain information to light, possibly information about lapses, abuses, scandals or corruption, because they need to protect people who have shared information confidentially but are too afraid to be named.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In this case, under section 7, potentially, even the expression of public suspicion on the publishing of information from confidential sources by reputable journalists and writers using accepted, investigative and journalistic methodologies, may attract criminal penalties.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Will practitioners in the media industry and academia err on the side of caution?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Does that help Singapore's reputation as the global business, research and development and knowledge hub?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Will scientists and public health professionals with a different view from the Government on the public health impact of e-cigarettes, for example, hesitate to publish clinical research showing harm reduction to confirmed smokers for e-cigarettes out of fear that they may be subject to Correction order because they did not also publish in the same statement facts about how many young first-time smokers are taking up e-cigarettes in the US and, hence, that research will be deemed a misleading collection of true statements?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: As a result, will they refrain from publishing such facts due to the personal consequences they will have to face?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: How does the impoverishment of policy debate that may ensue from that help the formation of good policies?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: How do we mitigate the risks that the academics and the media may come to see a need to soft launch their ideas before publication with Government officers to minimise the risk of POFMA action or, worse yet, simply self-censor or water down outputs that disagree with the Government's narrative and hence may be deemed to undermine confidence in the Government under section 4?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Next, let us look ahead to the future post-POFMA in respect of politics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Singapore will be a country where any Minister can determine in the first instance what is truth and falsehood – in the first instance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Post-POFMA, ours will be a country where Ministers with the political interest they are seen to have, can correct statements they deem misleading, but the very same Ministers will not be subject to the stringent, immediate and broad strictures of the POFMA law.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Ministers and Government spokespersons can say what they want, including misleading statements with a partisan political character.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What is the restraint on the Government here?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Can victims of possible Government falsehoods go to the POHA Courts?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: They can sue for defamation, but again, how many would do that?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Would defamation apply to statements made by Ministries and agencies as opposed to Ministers?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What if a falsehood perpetrated by a government affects the outcome of an election?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Would a positive defamation verdict for a victim of government fake news after the election help?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What if a rouge government uses these powers to stifle criticism, block the circulation of embarrassing information about lapses, abuses or corruption, perpetuate fear and entrench itself in power?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What if such a rouge government exploited the reluctance of many Singaporeans to sue the Singapore Government in Court to its advantage?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What if such a government exploited the lack of a public interest defence to suppress genuine and responsible investigative journalism?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Do we serve future generations of Singaporeans by passing such a law and passing into the hands of the government of the day such a powerful weapon not knowing how it might be used?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: When asked about the possibility of a future rogue government abusing POFMA, the Law Minister said, and I quote, "I cannot vouch for how a future government will act." Some would say, and the Law Minister also said in the same interview, I am not taking it out of context, that a rogue government or a Minister who abuses their POFMA powers will be held to account in elections.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: To say Parliament is a check against abuse is neither here nor there.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The abuse may affect the composition of the Parliament itself.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Some might say that chilling free speech a little is the right price to pay for preventing foreign powers, extremists and opportunists from destroying our communal harmony or even our independence as a country.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Resources can be provided to ensure that duty judges provide fast, prima facie decisions in time-sensitive cases.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The Court should be the first arbiter and not the final arbiter.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: (In Malay):   	This Bill may reduce the reporting of information seen to be critical of the Government.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It can also be misused by an irresponsible government, if Ministers, who may be seen to have their own political agenda, issue correction directions that are written in a way that will embarrass their critics, or they may even commence actions to take down the news that was published as well as stop the circulation of information that can embarrass the Government.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But we oppose when we see something that does not support elements of the national interest like this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: When we look ahead post-POFMA, we see a country where only the rich and brave may dare to speak up.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In time, the chill on free political speech may also affect our young people in our schools and higher education institutes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Will they come to self-censor their thoughts and their expressions to align with the Government's narrative?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Will they internalise the fear of not diminishing confidence in the Government as section 4F of POFMA details?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What will this mean for Singaporeans becoming independent thinkers who can navigate a world of disruption?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Bear in mind what the hon Member Prof Lim Sun Sun said about how, among the general public, people are now using POFMA as a verb, "I will POFMA you".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But this Bill is not a carefully crafted tool, it is a blunt weapon, handed to a conflicted surgeon, able to cause a great deal of collateral damage to the democratic body politik in this country.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The Bill, as it stands, needs a radical overhaul, not just minor tweaks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We do not oppose for the sake of opposing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But we do oppose when it is right for Singapore and this is one such time.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On one hand, the free flow of information is a form of knowledge democracy; on the other hand, due to the low or non-existent barrier to online participation, falsehoods and misinformation are pervasive.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The online space has remained unregulated for a long time.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Cases of how the Internet has been manipulated to gain profit, cause racial and religious disputes, incite harm and cast doubts on public institutions abound.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The consequences for us as a nation would be dire if we leave such a situation unchecked.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We will have difficulty telling the truth from online falsehoods, affecting our ability to make informed choices and decisions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have already seen how online abuse and misinformation had led to injuries and deaths in other countries, spurring them to take action.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Global sentiment is shifting as governments around the world now realise that regulation of the Internet space is needed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We, too, need urgent and comprehensive measures to address the menace of online falsehoods and manipulation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even tech companies now acknowledge that there is room for greater government intervention as they cannot be dealing with these problems themselves.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am very concerned about the impact of online falsehoods and fake analyses on our young.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must teach them how to discern truth from lies, how to analyse information they read online and how to think critically.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Values are ingrained in people from a very young age.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, from young, we must teach them fundamental values which transcend religious and racial differences, such as mutual respect and tolerance, integrity, justice and fairness, kindness and empathy.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If they are taught well, they will be inoculated against anything which violates basic human rights and values.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For parents, they will have to develop media literacy themselves and be able to discern facts from online falsehoods, so that they can have meaningful conversations with their children.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These conversations have to be consistent and ongoing.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Dialogues must remain open between children and parents, so that our younger generation can be groomed into a people who can think critically and independently.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our education system must be constantly updated in methods to teach the younger generation media literacy in a fast-evolving sector and equip them with the necessary skills.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am pleased to note that research-based assignments are very common in schools now.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Teachers can engage students through these projects to examine various sources of information.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Students learn how to determine which sources are credible and which are not.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They are exposed to questions and frameworks where they can apply themselves and determine, in each case, if information is true or false.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this sense, our education system is forward-looking in preparing our young for the future.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is also a need to enhance digital literacy for the elderly as they may be a vulnerable group that is susceptible to fake news.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: IMDA has developed a set of customised curriculum to increase infocomm literacy among seniors aged 50 and above.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Silver Infocomm Junctions are senior-friendly learning hubs that offer affordable infocomm training and customised courses.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These are encouraging steps forward to enhance digital literacy among senior citizens.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Bill provides measures to mitigate the impact and harm caused by online falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It would be better if the abuse of these platforms can be prevented in the first place.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I, therefore, welcome the upstream regulation of technology companies through the inclusion of codes of practice, which will go a long way to ensure a clean online space.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I sincerely hope that tech companies will cooperate and work closely with our Government so that Singaporeans will feel safe and have greater confidence when using their services.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   	The Bill provides measures to mitigate the impact and harm caused by online falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It would be better if the abuse of these platforms can be prevented in the first place.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I, therefore, welcome the upstream regulation of technology companies through the inclusion of codes of practice, which will go a long way to ensure a clean online space.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I sincerely hope that tech companies will cooperate and work closely with our Government so that Singaporeans will feel safe and have greater confidence when using their services.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will stakeholders be consulted on how the obligations should be framed?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): In conclusion, we need continuous efforts to keep our Internet space safe for all Singaporeans and I am confident that the Government will continue to do more to educate our young and the elderly on the dangers of fake news and what they can do to protect themselves and their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   	Yesterday, I listened to the speech of the hon Mr Low Thia Khiang.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He accepts that online fake news brings harm to the society and must be curbed.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He also accepts that the Court can act as an arbiter of fake news, although he is of the opinion that it should be decided by the Court instead of the Minister.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The focus of today's Bill is on information falsifiers who disseminate false information online with the intention of causing harm, rather than the responsible and constructive network users.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It has been said that good people will gravitate towards doing good and the bad towards evil.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most people have a natural understanding of fairness and justice.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although Mr Low Thia Khiang’s worries can be understood, he does not need to worry too much unnecessarily.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Each of us has received interesting information forwarded by friends.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also often remind myself that for the information which is questionable and cannot be verified, when forwarding, I also alert the other party that the information may be false and cannot be substantiated.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Everyone can develop this habit, so that they can have better peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although the Ministers have the power to make a clarification or take down a post, they are not likely to abuse this power and make decisions that violate their credibility and abandon the public’s trust.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, we will allow freedom of speech to flourish, and it can also enhance the credibility of the network platforms and maintain users' confidence in the platforms.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I want to remind everyone that everyone could be a victim of fake news.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do not forget that users on some popular online platforms do not need real-name registration.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In other words, some people can open up thousands or even tens of thousands of fake accounts, men pretending to be women, women pretending to be men, elderly pretending to be young and young pretending to be elderly.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is also why online fraud cases are constantly emerging.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I had encountered a resident asking for help.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: His relatives’ child, impersonating the mother, set up an account to vilify the religious beliefs of others and provoke hatred.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Recently, the US also has to legislate to control fake news, especially deepfake technology that allows people to combine images.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By attaching former US President Obama's face to another person and then making a false statement, it is possible to mislead the audience to think that Obama is speaking.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If those with bad intentions can send out false information using such technology to impersonate the US president or the presidents of other countries about launching a nuclear bomb to a certain country, the consequences would be unimaginable.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think these platforms should use real-name registration systems to allow netizens to register accounts for effective control.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the saying goes, upright people with nothing to hide do not do things secretly, so we should encourage a constructive and responsible platform for free speech, instead of using these platforms to put other people down and create social unrest under the banner of freedom of expression.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are all familiar with the traditional game "pass the message".

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the process, it is not difficult to find out that when the message reaches the last person, the original text from the first person has been distorted.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is not hard to find that some people, in order to add emphasis and persuade others, add bits and pieces to the message, and a real message could become a false message.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If you cannot determine the authenticity of the information, you can attach a disclaimer clause to remind the other party that you cannot research or verify the information, so that the other party can also be vigilant.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, the introduction of the POFMA Bill is another crucial step to fortify our financial and economic stability.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we all know, financial systems are particularly sensitive to market rumours and online falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This vulnerability can have devastating consequences for individuals, companies and our entire economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is a need to act quickly and decisively to protect our financial system.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Allow me to share a couple of examples.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In June 2017, a false post on 4Chan claimed that the founder of cryptocurrency had died in a car crash.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To prove that it was all fake news, Buterin had to copy some data linked to the latest block mined on the Ethereum blockchain on a piece of paper, took a selfie with it and post this photo on Twitter.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore’s financial markets are certainly not immune to such incidents.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thus, any measures to counter falsehoods must be fast and decisive.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Otherwise, opportunistic actors will be able to use falsehoods to cause panic, create instability and erode confidence in our financial infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some have argued that applications to remove articles or news should be first made to a Court or independent party.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Of course, there is another angle which we should consider.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I heard Member Mr Gan Thiam Poh saying something in Mandarin about what I said is similar to what is provided in the Bill – 异曲同工，我听不清楚，你可以再说一遍吗？I am not clear what he said about different views but the same objective.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Because, ultimately, the Court will still be the one that can decide, even though it is a matter of sequence, as what the Member pointed out.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: (In Mandarin):   	So, Member Mr Gan Thiam Poh meant to say that although the Minister has the decision-making power under this Bill, you can still go to Court to challenge the decision.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: But the WP believes that if there are any complaints, the Minister should lodge a complaint with the Courts and let the Courts decide.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Do you believe that the two approaches achieve the same objective?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: No, it is not achieving the same objective.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: But this is like executing someone first and then allowing him to appeal later.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: The person would have been executed already, what is the point of making an appeal when he is already dead?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: (In Mandarin):   	Let us not forget that this is falsehood.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: When the Minister issues a takedown order, he will explain his action.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: If you disagree, you can go to the Courts and let the Court decide.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: (In Mandarin):   First and foremost, you must follow the Minister's decision to take down the message, you cannot go to Court.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: It is different from the situation where the Minister goes to Court first and requests for the information to be taken down, and you are given a chance to state your reasons and defend yourself in Court.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Under this Bill, there is no room for you to defend your case.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: So, it is like executing first and appealing later.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are there any new points to be made, if not, we move on.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: (In Mandarin):   	I think it is not possible for the Minister to go against public opinion and risk his credibility by doing this.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: If you think that you are right, you can still lodge an appeal.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: (In Mandarin):   	You assume that the Minister will not do this, but is your assumption correct?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: It may be correct now, but will it be correct in the future?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Even the Minister cannot guarantee that, he said he cannot be sure that future governments will not abuse their power.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Please allow me to first speak in Malay on the Bill.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   	Mr Speaker, the need for proper public education on the impact of fake news and falsehoods from online sources cannot be understated.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With easy access to online information sources, we may not always be able to distinguish between information that is true and accurate and that which is not.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although some may argue that this Bill will limit freedom of expression and access to information, not having this Bill will also curtail certain liberties, such as personal freedom or the right to a fair trial, such as when one has been wrongly accused and judged unfairly in the court of public opinion, and having many people who often exaggerate the actual situation.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, comprehensive and continual public education is necessary, including the education of our young, starting at home and in schools.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I did my doctorate research in information and media literacy, and I completed my work more than a decade ago.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I look forward to contributing my experience in this area as a Member of MCI’s Digital Readiness Council Steering Committee.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, while I will not speak on specific clauses of this Bill, I wish to speak on the Bill in general in my capacity as an academic and faculty member in one of our local autonomous universities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Substantial discussions have been made in the academic circle on the impact of this Bill, once enacted, on academic freedom.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is, essentially, the lifeblood of academia and research work.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, I fully understand the concerns among my fellow academics on the impact of POFMA on academic freedom.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There have been, and will continue to be, instances where the work or paper we publish may contain some "statements of facts" which may be deemed to be false, and which may contradict data available or shared by Government Ministries or agencies.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Current data by Government Ministries, such as MOE or MOM, may show that there is little to no incidents of discrimination in schools or workplaces.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even if there are, swift and decisive actions are taken to quell such instances of discrimination and allow current laws to deal with the perpetrators.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The numbers may be small and the incidents may appear well under control.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, we must recognise that these numbers are only based on those reported.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are incidents and instances that go unreported.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, the data available may not always reflect what is real and what is experienced.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Research studies conducted by academics that deep dive into the psyches and experiences of individuals, not just through quantitative data or quantifiable information, but through rich qualitative data, such as engaged interviews and discussions, observations, ethnography, phenomenological approaches or through the use of grounded theories, have usually revealed much more than what quantitative data collection methods are able to show.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are times where these much richer qualitative data may counter or even dispute quantitative data that is much more easily and quickly reported or captured, but which only scratch the surface of most people’s psyches or experiences when it comes to complex issues, such as discrimination, for example.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a result, these academics or researchers who then publish their work and qualitative data which may counter or dispute the data owned and shared by Government Ministries or agencies, do we then conclude these academics or researchers as having published "false statements of facts" because they do not support the data or facts owned and shared by the Government Ministries or agencies?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Illustrating yet another example: we may have an academic or researcher who publish their work where because of the research methods employed or because of the statistical modelling tools applied, the data generated may not be the same as that owned or shared by the Government Ministries or agencies, do we then also conclude these academics or researchers have published "false statements of facts"?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is essentially the moral code or ethical policy of academia, a term coined by Don McCabe.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Academic integrity includes the avoidance of cheating or plagiarism, ensuring honesty and rigour in academic research and publishing.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This means that the work we publish must be based on data that has been honestly and rigorously collected without tampering for any specific agendas or purposes.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And in upholding academic integrity, we academics and researchers need to ensure that we do not propagate false information.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To elaborate, there is a need to ensure we do not propagate disinformation or misinformation, both referring to false information.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Disinformation is known false information that is deliberately spread or propagated so as to deceive others.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Misinformation, on the other hand, is a little bit more difficult to determine.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While misinformation also propagates false news or information, often times, people who propagate misinformation may not always realise the news or information is false, hence the propagation of false information may not always be deliberate – just misinformed.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, there may be instances where false information is propagated without the deliberate intent to stir controversy or prejudice public opinion.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Here, if I may address the point raised by the hon Member Leon Perera.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe this Bill is not a life sentence for academics.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This may be similar to the Singapore Medical Council that reviews medical practices and practitioners.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, long-drawn Court appeals that may result in high costs or extended appeal durations, can be avoided.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I understand that academic and research work and publications can traverse a wide array of disciplines, the Academic and Research Advisory Panel is meant to provide general oversight and counsel on matters related to academia or research work and publications.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Specific Subject Matter Expert Committees can be convened to preside over academic or research work or publications in specific areas or disciplines.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also do understand that having the proposed Academic and Research Advisory Panel which provides general oversight and counsel on matters related to academic or research work or publications or even these Specific Subject Matter Expert Committees to preside over academic or research work or publications in specific disciplines may both require much time for deliberation and review and which may be an expense to speed and efficiency, compared to a directive decided by the Minister.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, efficiency and speed alone should not be our only goal.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The concerns ranged from the creation of bots to spread disinformation, profiting from knowingly spreading falsehoods and possible interference in elections by external state's sponsored actors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, the Bill before the House to tackle online falsehoods has generated alarm and strong concern.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My Party colleagues before me argued some of the key objections of the WP that compelled us to reject the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During a constituency event over the weekend, some residents expressed to me that when POFMA is passed, they would likely be very, very careful about what they post online and about private messages they send through their phones.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, when I saw The Straits Times opinion piece of Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong on 6 May, I was struck by the headline which read "that only a small group was crying wolf".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I know that his intention in writing that piece was specifically to respond to the Asia Internet Coalition.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But as he himself explained yesterday, the Bill before the House is platform-neutral and will apply to communications on closed platforms, such as messaging groups.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some Nominated Members have proposed amendments to the Bill in Committee.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The amendments seem to accept the powers being given to Ministers to be the arbiters of truth and public interest but attempt to scope them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The amendments also asked for more transparency and for an independent advisory council.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While I appreciate their intention and efforts to try to mitigate the dangers of the Bill, the WP's objections are more fundamental and require us to reject the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For my part, I will focus my speech on the following concerns: one, the limited role of the Courts under POFMA; and two, why POFMA may endanger the national interest.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The WP Secretary-General, Member of Parliament Pritam Singh, had earlier set out why the Party believes that the POFMA powers to issue directions should be vested in the Courts rather than Ministers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government, on its part, has been stressing that Ministers are circumscribed by an appeals process and judicial oversight.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is important to examine the details of this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Appeals are basically requests to relook at the original decision on the merits to decide if the decision was right or wrong.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under what circumstances can appeals be made to the High Court?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Bill has restricted the grounds of appeals against Minister's directions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These are the only three grounds on which the High Court can set aside the Minister's Directions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is potentially very onerous due to information asymmetry between the Government and individuals, a point that I shall return to later.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The appeal to the Courts is thus very tightly scoped.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The High Court cannot inquire into the merits of the decision whether in the Court's view the decision should have been made in that way.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On an appeal, the Court, for example, cannot ask important questions, such as: (a) Is the Minister over-reacting?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: (b) Did the Direction impose obligations on the communicator which are excessively onerous or harsh?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: (c) Does the public interest require the Direction to be issued?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The argument, as I understand it, is that these matters can be looked into under the usual judicial review route.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I agree that POFMA does not carry a clause ousting judicial review of Ministers' decisions, so judicial review exists.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, judicial review is a public law remedy which requires the individual to take up a separate legal action against the Government, usually by suing the Attorney-General as the Government representative.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In order to do this, the person must first apply for leave of permission from the Court to commence a judicial review.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If leave is obtained, the judicial review application can then be filed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Two sets of legal costs will thus be incurred.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The litigant will also be facing the formidable Attorney-General's Chambers with limitless resources to defend the Government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There was no mention by the Minister yesterday that the judicial review process will be made simpler or cheaper.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The purpose of judicial review is to determine if the Minister's decision is legal and rational.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, if a Minister asserts that a Correction Direction is needed in the public interest, the Court cannot delve into the evidence to weigh up whether the Direction should be issued or not.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So long as the Minister's reasons are in line with the purpose of the Act, the Court will generally not interfere.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Judicial review is thus a difficult proceeding to mount and to win.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Criticisms and queries may well arise out of genuine concern and provide opportunities for detailed and measured responses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If we wish to imbue citizens with a real sense of ownership, we should focus on empowering minds and hearts with knowledge.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This knowledge should not just come when falsehoods emerge, but on an ongoing basis.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government has confirmed that it agrees that arming citizens with knowledge is a powerful weapon against falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, the Government should do some introspection as to how it may itself have contributed to the spread of falsehoods by its control of information.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One past episode on how incomplete information may lead to erroneous conclusions happened 15 years ago.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The two economists were labelled as irresponsible and unprofessional.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In their defence, they said that they had taken the initial figures from MOM's website while the newly released figures were information they had no access to.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If the same had occurred after POFMA was enacted, would the professors be required to tag corrections to their reports online?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How would the professionals' standing thereby be diminished in the eyes of their colleagues, students and the world at large?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Worst of all, would they and other economists choose to steer clear of researching or writing about Singapore to avoid such backlashes?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If so, Singapore would be the poorer for it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Minister or the alternate may even require the Correction notice to be published in print form in a specified newspaper, which cost will have to be borne by the person concerned.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As it would be up to the Minister or the alternate to specify the size of the correction notice, the person will have to buy the required space from the newspapers which could easily run into thousands of dollars.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government says that it is giving assurances in Parliament that that would be recorded in the Hansard and other controls will be enacted in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As POFMA is a law that potentially catches all Singaporeans who use digital communication, the Government should make the law as clear and as accessible as possible.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is it reasonable to expect an ordinary citizen who wants to understand POFMA to have to cross refer from the Act to subsidiary legislation, and then to the Parliamentary debates as well?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, there was discussion about whether the Court could respond quickly enough in certain situations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As debated by my party colleagues earlier, we believe that this is a matter of how the Courts are resourced and how the processes are streamlined.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, we believe that it is possible if there is political will to do so.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If the Government wishes to correct any statement that is floating online, it does not have to wait for POFMA.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It has many channels of communication at its disposal through the mass media, through its own Internet channels – I think more than sufficient to get its information out to combat the effects of any falsehood as it deems fit, even if it has to wait for POFMA adjudication.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, Sir, in totality, I do not believe that the Government would be helpless if POFMA requires the Courts to be the first arbiter in this respect.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: (In Mandarin):   	Speaker, Sir, I have listened to the debate between Members Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Low Thia Khiang, and Mr Low used an analogy that seemed a little violent, so I would like to clarify.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe that under this Bill, the Minister is actually "merely reporting" and not "beheading".

speaker: Ms Sim Ann (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, there is no cause for claiming that "beheading" has occurred.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The WP suggests that the Minister should lodge an application with the Court and let the Court decide.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the Minister has explained that online falsehoods can spread very quickly.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is precisely what today’s debate is about; we do not want slow remedies.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: (In Mandarin):   	With regard to the issue of "using water far away to put out a fire nearby", during the Second Reading of the Bill, the Minister has said that there are already many existing laws and powers that the Government can utilise and this Bill is only a small part.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Therefore, using "water" near or far away is not an issue.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: The Government already has measures on hand and is able to take action immediately when a falsehood surfaces.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Because the Minister can decide which action to take.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: The WP Chairman spoke on this just a while ago.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: For example, for the two economists involved in a previous case, they were badly affected.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: This is why we believe that one should not be punished first.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Instead, the case should be brought to Court first and be decided by the judge.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: (In Mandarin):   	I think we have now come to a very important theme of the debate.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I believe there is some confusion over the scale of the issue.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I think Members from the WP have tried their best to conflate the impact of falsehoods with the impact of personal opinion when they are entirely different.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The SC Report has pointed out that the effects of online falsehood can come thick and fast and are far-reaching.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This is why I used the analogy of "using water far away to put out a fire nearby".

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In the event where society and security are seriously affected by the proliferation of falsehoods, how can it be that we should still seek "water from far away" to put out this "fire" raging nearby?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: (In Mandarin):   	I have stated clearly that the Government already has a lot of power under existing legislation.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: The Minister also provided a list in his opening speech that stated clearly the legislation the Government has at its disposal to stop the propagation of online falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: He said that POFMA is a relatively small weapon and there are other stronger weapons on hand.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Even if there is an urgent problem, the Government has other powers.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: So, the scale of the problem does not matter, as the Government already has weapons on hand to stop the propagation of online falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: (In Mandarin):   	Speaker, Sir, I think this debate has become more bizarre.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The WP seems to believe that the Government has some kind of weapon to tackle the problem of falsehoods, weapons that even the most advanced governments and countries of the world do not have.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I believe that Mr Low Thia Khiang may not have looked at the SC Report in detail.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The problem of online falsehoods is a global one which has left many countries at a loss about what to do.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: If you say the current Government already possesses tools to stop the proliferation of fake news immediately, does it not mean that this debate has been totally meaningless?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: (In Mandarin):   	Our Secretary-General is in the Committee.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: He told us about the contents of the Committee's discussion, so we know what was discussed in the Committee.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: This means that you can take measures if the situation is very urgent, even without POFMA.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Unless there are any fresh perspectives, I would suggest you move on.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: (In Mandarin):   	I believe that Mr Low Thia Khiang has just undermined his own argument.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Member claimed to have understood the Report very well, but whether you have understood it or distorted it will become clear.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We still have plenty of opportunity and I believe the issue will become obvious as the debate continues.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Much has already been said about this Bill in the public domain and in this House by my colleagues.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thus, allow me to frame my speech into three parts: (a) what is the most important aspect of this Bill; (b) why it is important for Singapore; and (c) can the new regulations create a more informed and discerning society?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This reflects the Singapore Government's trust in the electorate to decide, and it is also a recognition of how our society has matured.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Most agreed that policy intervention is necessary to correct this failure and reduce the cost of this externality.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For Singapore, this is very important because of how open we are as a society and country and also because the very levers of attack that these online falsehoods tend to target are the pillars of our society.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the crux of the problem are the nature and intent of fake news.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is designed to cause divisions and distrust in society.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And the best ways to divide societies are to deepen the natural fault lines of race, religion, political ideologies and xenophobia by feeding into people's fears or insecurities, thereby fuelling panic and hysteria.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To that extent, it is not dissimilar from terrorism.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Terrorism is also meant to strike terror into the heart of society and, therefore, creating divisions and distrust along societal fault lines.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I do not believe I am exaggerating, therefore, when I say that fake news is not far from terrorism in its intent and malice to divide.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That fake news has that ability to strike divisions in society is something that we cannot take lightly in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is no secret that our social stability hinges on our racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It has always been a pillar of our nation-building, which is something we cannot compromise on.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have seen in the recent example of the Sri Lankan bomb blasts on Easter Day that a society where fault lines have existed can be a fertile ground for terror groups even when there was little or no apparent threat there in the first place.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our diversity makes us a vulnerable target for bad actors who wish to divide us along racial and religious lines.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The reality of our world today is that there are people who will weaponise religion to achieve their aims – to win an election or to radicalise others with their views.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The truth is, today, social media and digital technology have become convenient, cheap and fast tools to amplify their views and to drown out other legitimate voices.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The confluence of these two factors can lead to dangerous results.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is sufficient evidence around us to show that these observations are very real.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Take our neighbour, Indonesia, for example, which ranks as the third largest market for Facebook, and the top five market for WhatsApp, Instagram and Twitter.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During its recent Presidential Election, Mafindo – the country's fact-checking agency – documented a surge in political fake news that used ethnicity and religion to target both candidates.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some of these false claims include that Jokowi was Chinese, Christian and a communist.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Other false news included that Jokowi wanted to ban religious teachings in schools and abolish the call to prayer, among other things.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The falsehoods will follow different fault lines in each country.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: All of this has happened in our very neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Why would Singapore be any different if such false news were left unchecked here?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, the impact could be far worse and could create a severe and irreparable dent in the social harmony that we have worked so hard to build and uphold.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we take all other aspects of national security very seriously, as we should, then fake news should be treated no differently, given its potential harm.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The legislation and powers in place will easily separate what is fake and untrue from what is true, fact-based and analytical.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That will then allow readers the choice to decide for themselves what is right or what is wrong.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such efforts will thus create a more informed citizenry with accurate information rather than disinformation, thereby increasing the quality of policy analysis or political discourse and help us create a more informed and discerning society.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Most importantly, the public has to recognise that the Government is acting for the betterment of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This law will ensure that our children will not grow up in the future in a society where they will be the subjects, victims or consumers of fake news.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Government has attempted to provide stability, peace and safety to generations of Singaporeans and has always acted in the long term.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: No reason why it should not continue to do so with POFMA, whether it is against the perils of fake news, terror or social instability.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would want to provide that peace of mind to my children.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My response to the WP's continued insistence that the Court be the first arbiter of fact, but based on what has been discussed so far, it seems that the only arbiter is the Court and that you portray the Government as an untrustworthy bogeyman.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Well, my response is probably summed up in the following quote.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Former US President Franklin Roosevelt said, "Let us never forget that Government is ourselves and not an alien power over us.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The ultimate rulers of our democracy are not a President and senators and congressmen and Government officials, but the voters of this country." Mr Speaker, Sir, and my respected colleagues in this House, given all the problems with falsehoods, and the issues it has already created the world over, as well as our current inability to address such externalities created by the advent of new media, the Bill is timely and pertinent.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   	Mr Speaker, the rapid development of technology, including information and communication platforms, has brought many benefits to the world and greatly helped to make our lives easier.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, alongside these great benefits, potentially harmful effects also exist.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As we harness technology, we must also be aware of any negative impact that comes with it and consider the best ways to overcome them without hindering the convenience and advantages that we can use.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Online platforms brought many benefits to the world but, like many other things, any misuse, whether intentional or not, needs to be dealt with.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is especially so for Singapore, a small multiracial and multi-religious country where there are minorities and the majority.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our different races and religions have been able to live harmoniously, whether in schools, in living spaces, at work and in businesses.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have worked hard to develop policies and initiatives that instil trust amongst the different races and religions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, we should not take things for granted and be complacent about the peace and harmony that we enjoy today.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our diversity makes us vulnerable targets for bad actors who wish to divide our society along racial and religious lines.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have seen this happening in other countries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, we need to build a proper defence against it.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore is a country with a multiracial and multi-religious society.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our different races and religions have been able to live harmoniously, be it in schools, living spaces and at work.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The reality of our world today is that there are people who will weaponise religion against followers of other religions to achieve their aims; to win an election or to radicalise others with their views.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Social media and digital technology have become a convenient, cheap and fast tool to amplify their views and to drown out other legitimate voices.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have seen this happen in nearby countries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Indonesia, for example, is the third largest market for Facebook users and the top five market globally for WhatsApp, Instagram and Twitter.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The propagation of fake news that utilises religious elements can be fatal to the country, where the majority are Muslims while minorities comprise Christians, Hindus and Buddhists.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This fake news appeared in Facebook, followed by Twitter and WhatsApp, by percentages.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Around 30% of this fake news was shared in digital media, rearranged neatly and bolstered by other details and accounts.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The fake news was created according to the fault lines of a particular country.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We cannot take the position that these cases occur far away from our country and we are not vulnerable to the dangers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One of the detainees was said to believe that the war in Syria was a result of Sunni-Shia conflict.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He wanted to join the Free Syrian Army and fight against the Shia followers in Syria.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Imagine the impact of such tensions in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this country, Sunni followers form the majority of Muslims, while Shia followers comprise around just 1%.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The fact is that Singapore is not immune to hatred targeted at the Shia, which is gaining traction around the world.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are also comments on YouTube and social media that refer to the Shia followers as having gone astray, becoming apostates, and, in fact, called them "monkeys" and "the Devil".

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These videos aim to create trouble between Shia and Sunni followers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He agreed that the tension between Sunni and Shia followers worsened in Singapore after the videos were exchanged and posted.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The fact remains that if falsehoods are allowed to propagate, it will be a threat to our country.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The strategy to deal with it has been widely discussed.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The proposed measures have been considered carefully without any intent to hinder the flow of information or to curb opinions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This includes asking which authority can take action, and if there should be a fact-checking body.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, based on the examples I have mentioned earlier, the speed at which falsehoods spread, especially those that pit religion against one another, can result in an undesirable situation if it is not dealt with immediately.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
