text: The proposal to delegate the responsibility to either a body or a committee is a good suggestion, but, in terms of implementation, it will create another layer, and its process may take up more time.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And such a body will also need to be appointed by the Government.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, we will be going around in circles.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, the proposal for the Minister to take the step of issuing a factual correction on any falsehood is the best method, because it can be done more quickly, but at the same time, it does not mean that the Minister can act without any strong justification.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Readers can then decide the truth for themselves.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There may be concerns that, through the Act, are the Ministers or the Government being given too much curbing power and who can override the Government's power?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this matter, I welcome the availability of open processes and channels for those who wish to challenge the decision and to bring the matter to the Courts, and the process will also be made quick and convenient.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Earlier, Mr Faisal Manap and Mr Leon Perera highlighted a few things that question the Government's integrity and the intent of POFMA.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although clarifications were made by Minister Shanmugam about protection with the Court as a final arbiter, they continue to ignore that fact.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Minister Shanmugam had just explained earlier that the Courts are part of the process, like our citizens.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government must be at the frontline because the Ministries should be in a position to respond quickly.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If riots or violence occur as a result of falsehoods, the Government needs to act quickly.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Court is not necessarily open at all times and the judge will need to be briefed.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is a practical matter for the sake of national security.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The ability to act quickly will determine whether damage is irreparable or not, and whether people will suffer or not in the end.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But this does not mean that the Court is not involved.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The WP continues to ignore the fact that the Minister can be challenged.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Do not forget that if the Court finds that the challenge is successful, this would also impact the Minister's political performance because people will be questioning his judgement.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, I do not think that the Minister or the Government takes things lightly.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: More importantly, POFMA's approach is quite different from other countries which have dealt with it through a takedown order.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The people can decide for themselves whether what they see is the truth or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The approach is to make the correction alongside the original post.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that they do not underestimate the people of Singapore as not being smart enough to make a decision.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew stated that PAP is the Government and the Government is the PAP, I believe that it was based on the standard of democracy in the Westminster Parliament.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He meant that the Government is formed by the party that wins the most number of seats in Parliament and the party that forms the Parliament is elected by the people to exercise wisdom for the country.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If the WP wins the election one day, it will be a WP Parliament.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The same term is used commonly around the world for any similar system.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, let us not twist the quotes of our Founder just to support unsound arguments.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the end of the day, Singapore is not free from challenges and threats, such as online falsehoods, and we must agree that a careful and effective strategy must be taken and we should not delay this.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have been facing the dangers of online falsehoods for a long time and seen that its adverse impact includes dividing society.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is the duty of any government to protect every member of society and safeguard national interests.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The people have all along given this trust to the PAP Government and this Bill is just another step to extend that protection to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Usually, in previous pieces of legislation passed by this House, when it comes to exercise of the Minister's discretion dealing with public order issues, there is no providing of an appeal as a matter of right to the Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is a limited recourse in the form of judicial review of the Minister's decision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In some statutes, the Court's power of review has been ousted, for example, the Maintenance of the Religious Harmony Act and ISA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This regime deals with the point that the hon Member Assoc Prof Walter Theseira made about what happens if the Government gets it wrong, by reference to Galileo's case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In Galileo's case, the Church took more than three centuries to correct itself.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Originally, I was concerned with the structure of the Bill leading to the appeal process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because when I looked at it, I saw that the appeal is made "after the fact", meaning after the Minister's decision is made.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And it will only be initiated by the respondent to the Direction made under POFMA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The concern I had was that, ordinarily, it would be for the Executive to make out the case first, as opposed to requiring the respondent at the outset to state why the Executive got it wrong without knowing the Executive's case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In relation to this point, the hon Members Ms Anthea Ong as well as Assoc Prof Walter Theseira said, "But that is in subsidiary legislation".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When the Minister made his statement at the Second Reading of the Bill, that goes into the corpus of the Hansard on how the legislation is to be reviewed and that creates a legitimate expectation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When the Court reviews the exercise of power against the legitimate expectations created, it can strike down the power which is used outside the legitimate expectations it has been created.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, the Executive's case would be crystalised at the outset.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The respondent would know what case he or she has to meet.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, the hon Member Mr Leon Perera said but, in the process, the legal burden would be on the respondent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With great respect, that is not how I understand POFMA to be.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hon Members of Parliament have engaged in a lively debate on which is the proper entity or person who should make a decision to issue Directions under POFMA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When it comes to deciding what is in the public interest, what kind of decision-maker do we need?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is the point that hon Member Mr Cedric Foo made very cogently a few hours ago.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We would need a decision-maker who is in touch with the ground situation, not just in Singapore but even overseas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He or she would have to have access to intelligence reports, gauge what would be the likely reaction of Singapore residents, what steps are needed to address the problems on the ground.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With due respect, it is not easy for the Courts to make such a decision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Courts are best suited to apply the law, including the law promulgated by this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am not saying that the Court cannot review a decision made in the public interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I recalled when the Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) (Amendment) Bill was moved in this House, my Parliamentary colleagues from the WP spoke about the development of judicial review in Singapore, by reference to the speech delivered extra-judicially by the hon Chief Justice in America.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His Honour said that "judicial review is the sharp edge that keeps government action within the form and substance of the law." His Honour also spoke about the doctrine of substantive legitimate expectation within the context of judicial review.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, there is a robust system in place.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is the system that will guard against actions of a rogue government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This would ensure that powers are only used in the manner that the Government has promised at the Second Reading of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Decisions of what is in the public interest are, therefore, best to be left with Ministers who head the Ministries, have access to Civil Service apparatus, are elected and are accountable to the people through the ballot box.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Prof Lim Sun Sun said that Ministers would benefit from inputs from advisory panel and I agree.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It may well be that the Ministers, after the passing of this Bill, may want to set up advisory panels to get the necessary inputs and make appropriate decisions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Mr Pritam Singh made a comparison between POHA and POFMA, and pointed out that there is regime for expedited protection orders issued by the Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He, I believe, wondered why this same route cannot be used for POFMA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Looking at just the legal ingredients, there is a singular difference.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The issues under POFMA, unlike POHA, affect public interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This means a lot more is at stake.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am not trivialising the effect of harassment of a POHA victim.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But what I am trying to say is that, when it comes to POFMA, we are talking about public interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is a potential for disaffection amongst groups of people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It can change the complexion of society if something happens.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Mr Leon Perera spoke about the American experience where, in America, a judicial officer would make himself or herself available to issue a warrant of arrest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In Singapore, I believe, by the 1970s, we have moved ahead.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In Singapore, Police Officers are vested with powers of arrest without warrant.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These are serious powers, but they are accountable and they do it in the right circumstance and we see the effect of it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: From the 1970s to date, actually, our crime rates have come down so much and, really, we need not compare ourselves with America in this situation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Leon Perera also talked about the impact on the individual who is visited with a Direction under POFMA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We need to compare because we are talking about public interest as a potential for large groups of people to be affected.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Yes, there is an impact on the individual.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But what is the kind of impact we are talking about?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, we need to strike a proper balancing act between the impact on an individual and the potential for disaffection amongst lots of people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And I think this Bill strikes the right balance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to the issue of assessment of the representation of fact.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Several hon Members in the Opposition, including the hon Member Mr Low Thia Khiang, expressed the view that POFMA is meant to chill criticisms against the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He then went on to state, "I have no faith in this Government" or words to that effect, and that the Pioneer Generation Package and the Merdeka Generation Package were meant to buy votes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As stated by the hon Member Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, both statements are clearly statements of opinion and not caught by POFMA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Just like if I were to say that some hon Members in this House are fearmongering.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How can there be a chilling effect introduced by POFMA in these circumstances?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What we need to be mindful about is that as the hon Minister mentioned yesterday, what the Government is trying to do through POFMA is to narrow the powers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He mentioned about two pieces of legislation where there are broad powers and, if used, may be like using a sledgehammer to break a nut.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Here, you have fairly forensic powers, including that of issuing a Correction order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If the Government were to commit to use a narrow set of powers, is that the sign of a government which is not acting in good faith?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Members Ms Irene Quay and Ms Anthea Ong mentioned that there is nothing in the Bill that states that the focus of POFMA is only on statements of facts and not opinion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But that has been stated by a number of frontbenchers on a few occasions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And if one were to look at the interpretation of statute, read it with the Interpretation Act, the Courts will know what to do.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They will know what is the intention of the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They know that POFMA Directions are not meant to be applied for opinions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Members Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Dennis Tan highlighted that, under POFMA, statements which are misleading are also caught, in addition to statements which are false.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They seem to suggest that there is a significant enlargement of the scope of the Bill in these circumstances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Now, I looked at the definition under the proposed section 2(2) of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is clear is that the main criterion is that there must be a statement of fact, and this is a point that the hon Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong made.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, the usage of "misleading" does not enlarge the scope of the representations to include opinion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, in relation to the hon Member Mr Dennis Tan's example of a person who states, "I lodged a Police report".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That assessment is either true or false, and if you were to put in the definition of misleading, it does not change.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The ultimate outcome is whether or not the statement is a statement of fact which is true or false.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, with respect, I do not see this as significantly enlarging the issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, the wording is essential to deal with the mischief this Bill is aimed at addressing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is also a point made by the hon Member Mr Low Thia Khiang about the Government being a player and a referee.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I believe, with respect, he may have conflated a number of scenarios together.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I think that no one in this House would raise an objection if a POFMA Direction is issued to deal with a public interest, race issue, language issue, religious issue or issues dealing with relations with foreign powers or national security.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In these kinds of situations, both sides of the House must unite.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is sometimes good in debates to highlight what is the common ground that is achieved between both sides of the House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We are left with areas where, potentially, powers can be used for political purposes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Mr Faisal Manap talked about conflict of interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He gave an example of the Prime Minister stating in this House that he does not wish to sue his siblings because they are his siblings and he is in a conflicted position in relation to the allegations made by his siblings against him about abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But that is in relation to him, in his personal standing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But when it comes to the Government, that is a completely different thing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Somebody else would have to make a decision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, the issue of conflict would not arise in these circumstances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Ultimately, we must all remember our fellow Singaporeans are looking at us, and they would be holding the Government to account through the ballot box.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do think, however, it would be useful for the hon Minister to provide an outline of how he intends that the powers under POFMA be exercised, in terms of the variety of tools, to effect a Correction, for example, or effect a takedown, because we hear from the hon Minister that, in most circumstances, it would usually be a Correction order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This outline can help even the Court later to assess whether the exercise of power under POFMA is within the legitimate expectations arising from the Minister's statements when it reviews the Minister's decision later.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It sharpens the ability of the Court to review Executive action that ensures that this is legal and proper.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I made mention at the outset that is not usual for statutes to have these two levels of judicial oversight, and I have some sympathies for the draftsman.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In a situation where a respondent both prosecutes an appeal to a Supreme Court Judge and also intends to take up judicial review, the Supreme Court Judge listening to the appeal in relation to whether a statement of fact is true or false, would only deal with half the issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His decision on the appeal is not dispositive of the matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hon Members of this House may recall an incident involving a market operator issuing a flyer in four languages, namely, English, Mandarin, Malay and Hindi.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Let us consider a situation where a person noting this incident publishes a representation online referring to the above matter and announcing "Hindi has become a recognised language in Singapore".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Let us assume that the Government takes action against the person under POFMA and the person appeals to the High Court on the issue of whether the statement is false and also seeks a judicial review.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under our current rules, the High Court appeal has to be disposed of first before the separate judicial review application.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because, under our rules, judicial review applications are measures of last resort.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The High Court would then have to decide first whether the statement is true or false.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This may seem like a binary choice – true or false.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But the reasons underpinning the decision may be relevant on a consequent issue of public interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Let us assume the High Court decides that the representation is false and provides an explanation for its decision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Looking at the representation, it could be false in a number of ways, but I will highlight just two.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One, it could be false as it suggests Tamil is being replaced by Hindi.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This obviously would create feelings of enmity and ill-will between groups of people, particularly involving Tamil-speaking people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It may be in the public interest to correct that representation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Or it could be false as it suggests that Hindi is being added, not replaced, as a recognised language.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Here, whether or not there is a public interest involved, it is more arguable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some in this House may ask whether there is a need for the High Court to articulate its reasons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Supreme Court is an independent branch of our Government that is vested with judicial power under Article 93 of the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It has a responsibility to build jurisprudence, explain its decisions through grounds that are released, unless the issues are really plain and obvious, especially if there is an appeal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Let us assume that the person loses the appeal and then commences the High Court action to review their decision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The High Court, listening to the judicial review application, is not bound by the decision of the other Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The focus of the review will be on public interest, but it overlaps with what is assessed to be a representation of fact because that is what the lawyers call a jurisdictional fact.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It can overcome the procedural hurdle that the appeal has been disposed of before the judicial review process begins.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My suggestion is a bit different from what the hon Member Mr Dennis Tan has suggested because he said the High Court should have oversight over all issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That is a decision that has been made by the Minister for the reasons I mentioned earlier but, of course, can be subject to a review.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Even if the same High Court Judge is designated by the Chief Justice to hear the judicial review matter, so long as the matters are separate, he is not bound by his prior decision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, by twinning the process, there is no risk of inconsistent decisions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a point that my learned friend Ms Sylvia Lim made, for the same reasons as to why the appeal procedure has to be cost-effective as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would welcome the hon Minister's thoughts on this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am not saying that this is a likely outcome.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But I think there could be some risks and I would be grateful for his elaboration on this matter.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Murali Pillai, you need to wrap up.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: If I have used up my time, then I will stop here, Sir.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I would respectfully just ask for a few points of clarification.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Would the hon Member acknowledge that it would only become a legal burden, as in a pleading before the Court, if the respondent actually went to Court?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And would the hon Member acknowledge that there are, I think, many respondents who would not take up the burden, would not want to take on the Government in Court for the reasons that my colleagues have shared?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My second point is that the hon Member referred to POHA Courts dealing with matters that are perhaps less important in the bigger scheme of things than POFMA.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I actually understand where the hon Member is coming from.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think there is a grain of truth there.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I would not sort of wave that off.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Would there not be a further argument for the Government, the state, the society to actually invest in developing judicial capacity, structures and processes even more for the administration of POFMA than what has already been done for the administration of POHA?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We recognise that POFMA is dealing with actually more important societal or political issues as opposed to POHA, which is dealing with individual cases, that affect individuals only.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And the last point really is, I think, the hon Member mentioned that I talked about the effect on individuals of receiving a Correction directive and it could affect their reputation and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: There are individual issues at stake, but we could balance that against the societal issue.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Would the hon Member acknowledge that actually the point I was making was not so much that it is bad for the individuals but that it actually chills free speech, it may lead to self-censorship, it may lead to self-censorship affecting political discourse and, therefore, by implication, political outcomes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, there are very large societal and political issues at stake.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It is not just a matter of balancing individual against social.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, having said that, I thank the hon Member and I, respectfully put forward these requests for clarification.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He raises three issues and I am grateful to Mr Perera for the opportunity to clarify the points that I have made in relation to these three points.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: But that is not the end of the matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As I mentioned in my speech, at the outset, the Minister would have to nail his or her colours on the mast, because he would have to issue the reasons why a Direction is issued and that is gazetted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And that is available to members of the public as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, we are looking increasing at judicial resources at the Supreme Court level.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: At the Supreme Court level, you are talking about Supreme Court Judges who are at the top of the game.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: They have security of tenure, you have to make sure they do not just deal with POFMA matters but they deal with the whole gamut of issues and make sure they superintend justice in the way that reflects public interest, that ensures and safeguards the interest of our country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is not easy to build resources that way.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: That is why, having regard to the limitations we have as a small country, I thought the configuration that POFMA envisages in relation to Ministerial action with accountability to the Courts always is a good balance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We need to be honest about the resources that we have or do not have.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The point about individuals and the chilling effect on them, I hear my learned friend.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: But I think the point I was focused on is this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Like, for example, when a person says, you know, that "the Merdeka Generation Package is meant to buy votes", if the person says that "I have no faith in the Government." If they were to say all these things and the assurance from the frontbenchers is that, "No, it is not caught in POFMA", that I am trying to see how then POFMA introduces a chilling effect.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Like what I also said in my speech was that there is nothing stopping the individual who is the subject of a POFMA Direction to comment on the POFMA Direction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, he has that right in relation to what has happened to him.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I do see where my learned friend Mr Leon Perera is coming from.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Sometimes, we do not know exactly how things are going to pan out.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We make the best judgement on the facts that we have and what we think would be the reasonable assessment or reasonable way people behave and then we see how it goes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I believe I have covered all three points.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I completely agree with the hon Member that this Government will definitely move faster than the Church did with Galileo.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But that is because the Church or the Inquisition did not have a robust fast appeal process in the primary legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: So, I hope he would agree that that might be a good idea to have so that random changing of Popes and all that would not result in the appeal process being drawn out too long.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: It cannot be said that this new Bill does not contain harsh terms.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Is a statement of fact false or genuine?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The Bill has given every Minister ample discretion to decide.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Under the Bill, "falsehoods" is defined as information that is “false or misleading, whether wholly or in part or whether on its own or in the context in which it appears". "Information" is defined as “any word (including abbreviation and initial), number, image (moving or otherwise), sound, symbol or other representation, or a combination of any of these". "Public interest" is defined to include public confidence in our Government.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: That is to say, if any Minister believes that a particular falsehood has affected public confidence in the Government, including confidence in the Ministry he is in charge of, he has the authority to require that the false information be corrected or removed.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: If the party involved disagrees, he can lodge an appeal with the Court after he has made the corrections or removed the information.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Even then, the Court will not be able to review the Minister’s determination of whether a false statement of fact has affected public confidence in the Government.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: This is simply the Government carrying out its work.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: If the people are not happy, they can change the Government at the next elections.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: What is more, the Minister is a dependable public servant.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Even if the text of the Bill grants him great powers, he, in fact, will not abuse them." This is a big topic which I touch on briefly here.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: I believe that the success of a political system in delivering results for its people, whether in the West or the East, depends to a large extent on effective checks on the exercise of power.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: These checks take many forms: democratic elections are one; so is the rule of law, also the moral and ethical codes that guide and constrain the behaviour of government officials and the people; the public disclosure of information, including online information; the freedom of speech, including online speech and so on.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: They are all mechanisms that provide checks on the exercise of power.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The more of them we can integrate and accommodate, the better.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Let us talk about the checks on power provided by laws.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The rule of law has had great success in the West historically.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: To promote the rule of law in opposition to the rule of man is also a growing aspiration in the East, making the rule of law increasingly a universal human value.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: But the rule of law is not achieved merely by a high volume of legislation.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The existence of a large number of laws does not, in itself, effectively constrain the exercise of power.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: If the laws we make grant the Minister great powers, to be used at his discretion, if we do not clearly calibrate in the text of a law its constraints on power, then we will not be able to say that we have successfully met our challenge: that we successfully married the rule of law with our hopes for a rule of virtue.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is a fact that we have sat for nearly six hours.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is my opinion that we should take a break now.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting until 5.05 pm  Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.43 pm until 5.05 pm.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Online falsehoods can lead to very serious law and order concerns in a very short time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is because purveyors of falsehoods prey on our societal fault lines, such as race and religion, in order to exploit social media algorithms, draw eyeballs and go viral.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Around the world, we have seen a pattern of falsehoods proliferating in the wake of serious public order incidents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And various examples have been cited in this House by various speakers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The ban was only lifted one week later.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I support the Bill, I would like to highlight some ground concerns and also to seek some clarifications from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Bill has put in place clauses requiring online platforms to spread the corrections.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While this is a good move, the key to making this work lies in its implementation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If the correction is put up too late, we risk having the correction just as a token measure as the misinformation has already spread and few, if any, will read the correction if it is put up too late.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When it comes to increasing the reach of the corrections, social media sites must play their part.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While the Bill requires online platforms to help alert users to the correction, sites will need to review the way they manage the original post to raise awareness about the correction.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One example is the "share" function on Facebook.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I propose that following a correction, all shared posts be applied with a filter, similar to the violent content filter that we already have, to alert users that there is an attached correction to this particular news.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This way, new readers can be made aware that the content contains certain falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Stories that are peppered with blatant false facts can be easily identified.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But stories with just the right mix of facts and false statements can be hard to distinguish, and individuals do share these stories with their friends.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But there is still much confusion on the ground, especially among our more elderly residents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They are worried because some people are telling them that they will get into trouble with the new law.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, they are worried, what if I forward something on WhatsApp to my friends?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What if I shared something on Facebook or Instagram?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is, therefore, important for the Government and Members of this House to continue reassuring the public on what happens if they are unwitting pawns of a purveyor of fake news.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I think the short answer is, nothing happens.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, the definition of public interest under the Bill is rather wide.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I acknowledge the need for the most workable version of defining public interest, such a wide definition could still be constantly challenged.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Courts be the final arbiter of whether an issue is of public interest?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Does the Minister foresee many legal challenges on this front and what will be done to educate Singaporeans on what constitutes public interest?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government will also need to work together with the Courts to put in place a simple and expeditious appeal process.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How fast will it take for an appeal to reach the Court?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can a person seek a review of a Correction Direction without needing to engage a lawyer?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These are all important operational concerns that need to be articulated to the public, to assure Singaporeans that the exercise of powers under the proposed legislation is subjected to proper oversight by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government's approach to countering fake news is different from other countries and, in my view, different in a positive way.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Rather than requiring all originators of fake news to immediately take down the questionable content, which is what Germany has done, this Bill focuses on ensuring that facts are stated accurately and that readers are aware of the inaccuracies on a timely basis.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that through this, our society will grow to be more media-literate over time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But media literacy cannot be achieved just from this Bill alone.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All levels of society will need to partner one another to make this happen.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Social media sites must recognise that they owe a responsibility to ensure that their content is factually accurate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But that, in itself, is a big challenge as some of the existing models thrive on news virality.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The public must also arm ourselves with the necessary skills to decipher between what is real and what is fake.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government has done much in recent months on public engagement and I hope that such efforts continue unabated.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: History provides many examples of misinformation being used for malicious purposes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government should have the powers to take swift action.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And when that happens, damage, some of which may be irreversible, would have been done.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And that, to me, will, indeed, be chilling.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That aside, the ambit of this law has little to do with my Ministry.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But since I received a letter from concerned academics, I thought I should speak at this debate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is one signatory who is a foreign academic based in a local university.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: My colleagues from MCI and the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) have offered to meet with the academics who signed the letter.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The offer has not been formally taken up yet, but I understand many of them have attended the dialogue sessions with Minister Shanmugam, Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong as well as Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The three of them have been visiting universities and conducting talks and I hope that our three public officeholders have largely assuaged their concerns.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, I will first explain how hard, or rather, how impossible it is, for academic research to run afoul of POFMA.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, I will comment on what I think the academics, or at least some of them, are really worried about.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will end my speech with a summary in Chinese.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I have been sitting here listening to the debate, and I think we have, unfortunately, started to obfuscate what the core matter is about.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We started to come out with scenarios where we think falsehoods or truths are somewhat fuzzy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We talked about the balance between the Executive and the Judiciary, we talked about fast versus slow processes in the Courts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The issue is that we really have a serious threat from online falsehoods.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean, in the Members' lounge, was just telling me that when he was young, he remembered when the racial riots were happening, there was a big headline in The Straits Times saying "Stop Rumour Mongering" because that was fuelling the riots.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Just imagine today, with the tools in the hands of people with malicious intent, it is one thousand times easier to come up with a falsehood.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is what we are really dealing with.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One, what is put up online must be a statement of fact that is false.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When these two gates are crossed, then the falsehood may be corrected or removed by a "Direction". "Directions" are not criminal punishments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All that we are debating about concerning the powers of Ministers, it is the power to initiate a correction of an online falsehood that has gone viral and has public harm.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is for the Ministers and the Ministries to justify, prosecutors to initiate and the Courts to decide on the verdict.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What kind of online activities would pass the two gates?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I was thinking that I can cut down on the examples because I expected many Members to be citing many.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But given the examples I am hearing, let us get back to what are the examples we are talking about.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Two years ago, in Germany, there was a report that a mob of 50 "Arab-looking" men, assaulted women on New Year’s Eve in downtown Frankfurt.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But when the German police investigated, they found no evidence of this mysterious assault.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The newspaper eventually conceded that the attacks described in the article did not take place.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They apologised and took down the article from all its platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But more people had read and remembered the falsehood in the original article than the clarification.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Public sentiments shifted, society becomes more tense, political discourse altered.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The falsehood might have well affected the outcome of the referendum and the fate of the UK.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will get worse as technology continues to advance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You can now use artificial intelligence (AI) to make fake videos of a real person – "deep fakes".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Vikram Khanna wrote about it in The Straits Times today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You can just google "Obama deepfake" and you will find a video of the former US President – I tried, I found it – delivering a speech with swear words and all, which he, of course, did not make.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You can also find a deep fake video of President Donald Trump telling an audience in Belgium that they should withdraw from the Paris Climate Agreement, a speech which he did not make.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But you do not even need to deploy sophisticated technology to spread false information.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 1998, Dr Andrew Wakefield published a controversial study that linked the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, which protects against measles, mumps and rubella, to autism.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Although the study has been totally debunked, it helped fuel a dangerous movement of vaccine scepticism and refusal around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It was later discovered that Wakefield had falsified the data and had been paid by lawyers involved in an MMR lawsuit.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The paper was retracted only in 2010, 10 years after its publication.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The paper remains severely harmful as children who are unvaccinated could lose their lives.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is about experiments, gathering data, testing hypotheses, publishing findings, discovering how the world works and having work reviewed by peers and following a strict discipline and a strict process.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We should distinguish between two kinds of research.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The first kind is an empirical-based approach to understanding how the world and nature work.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is what researchers are doing in A*STAR, and in faculties, such as engineering and medicine, in our universities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are figuring out how the human genome works, finding new cures for diseases, ways to cut down carbon emission, developing new materials for building and bridges, inventing new models with new AI technology and algorithms to have sharper predictive powers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In all these fields, scientists are questioning truths all the time.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is an endless quest for knowledge, where our understanding of nature and life are constantly proven and then unproven.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Newton’s laws of motion, which used to be widely accepted, are proven now to be only partially true.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Scientists have also proven that time, which we used to believe it is constant, actually can be stretched, it can be compressed, it can be bent.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One branch of empirically-based research is data science.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I recently came across a book called Kiasunomics written by three National University of Singapore (NUS) researchers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a popular version of a series of papers they have published.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Households use more water when there was haze and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is very possible that, one day, someone may gather more data and refute their findings.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Does that mean POFMA will "criminalise" those researchers whose discoveries and theories were proven wrong or partially true?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, will Newton be caught by POFMA, because his laws are now only partially true?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Or the three authors of Kiasunomics will be persecuted, if one day, blue taxis have more accidents than yellow taxis?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Or will POFMA "criminalise" research that is trying to disprove a theory or a body of knowledge that is already well-established?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is simply not the business of POFMA.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Any attempts to apply POFMA to empirically-based, natural sciences research, will fail at the first gate I mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are two gates; it will fail at the first gate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Even if the data may not be accurate because the experiment was not well conducted, the data collected is not reproducible or incomplete, there is no falsehood as defined by POFMA.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One Member mentioned that 15 years ago, two labour economists got into trouble because they used partial data and concluded nine out of 10 jobs in Singapore went to foreigners.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, now, let us apply POFMA's two gates to this case.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I do not think there was any harm, such as riots or very heightened tensions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Incidentally, after I heard that speech, I did a check on the two academics, both of them are still teaching in the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy and I understand they are now both Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I do not believe good, honest research can cause public harm.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I have talked about the first type of research.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second type of research is based on opinion, philosophy, interpretation of history, cultural bias, geographical context and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is mainly practised as a strand of researchers in the humanities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Instead of empirical data, they use methods that are primarily critical and interpretive to substantiate their hypotheses and arguments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I enjoyed reading the books of an author called Yuval Noah Harari.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He is an Israeli historian and a tenured professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: His two bestselling books Sapiens and Homo Deus, I read both of them, he cites some empirical findings, but most of all, he describes his deductions, thoughts and opinions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He gave his take on the origins and purpose of religion in holding complex societies together.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He has an expansionary definition of religion that many will find offensive actually, and he postulated that humans will achieve near immortality and God-like powers, not too far into the future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some of the works of humanities scholars like Yuval Noah Harari can be controversial, highly debatable, even offensive to some.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, they would not even reach the two gates of POFMA.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Their conclusions are in the form of hypotheses, theories and opinions that are not covered by the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Those were the statements of facts that concern POFMA.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Actually, it is an excellent case study of how research upset conventional wisdom.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I want to talk about how he was treated then and how he would be treated today under POFMA should such research happen today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Of course, today, we know that the Earth goes round the Sun.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But at that time, the belief was that the Sun goes round the Earth and it was an important concept central to the power of the Church and the Roman authorities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He spent many lonely days and nights staring into the sky, collected data and proved that it is the other way round, that the Earth revolves around the Sun.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But despite his empirical methods, Assoc Prof Walter Theseira talked about the Inquisition, so his challenge was not kindly taken by the Roman authorities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Other astronomers came up with their observations and data to prove that the Sun, indeed, revolved around the Earth.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He was sentenced to indefinite imprisonment and kept under house arrest until his death.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What if something like that were to happen today, involving a question to which we have no answers, or we thought we had an answer, and a researcher comes up with something that challenges deeply held views or shared reality, as Assoc Prof Theseira mentioned?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have always been, sometimes to a fault.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And if it is an opinion-based research, we will have a vigorous public debate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In which case, such work I do not think it can pass the academic and professional standards of any decent university or research institute.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Quantum scientists have discovered that a very small particle can appear at two or more places at the same time until you look at it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You are not really there until I look at you.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The score of the football match is not four-zero until I look at it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is too simplistic a way to put it, but they are questioning reality as we know it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In economics, the post Global Financial Crisis debate continues on the efficacy of fiscal, monetary policies and quantitative easing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Researchers are questioning the causal relationship between unemployment and the skills gap, and if a nation’s success should also include measures beyond gross domestic product to include ecological sustainability and social equity.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These works challenge existing beliefs in far more profound ways than any memes, blog post, video, opinion piece in the newspapers shared online, which is the practical focus of POFMA.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If any of our researchers make such a breakthrough in our understanding of the world, rather than being persecuted, as Mr Cedric Foo said, they are more likely to be celebrated and maybe even accorded a National Day award!

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This Government will always honour empirical and evidence-based research.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I may be wrong, but I do not think it is about research.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are worried that POFMA will be used to stifle political discourse in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because not all researchers are just researchers; most researchers may also be activists.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But it is in their activist role that some of these academics are voicing their concerns about POFMA.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, there is a request for an explicit carve-out for opinions, criticisms, satires and so on in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I want to point out that we cannot conflate research with activism.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I read a Facebook post by Dr Derek da Cunha and I thought he put it very well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He observed that some academics "spend every other week banging away on the subject online and offline because his or her motivation is to effect change.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This isn’t even a case of any contentiousness over what is, or is not, the 'truth'." He added, "Instead, it brings up the question: what is the appropriate role of an academic?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Any contention that academics should not adhere to boundaries or parameters, but such boundaries or parameters should exist for everyone else, might be an unreasonable proposition." The same point was made by a Straits Times Forum letter writer who asked, "Where is the line between exercising academic freedom to pursue truth and wisdom, and hiding behind academic freedom to fulfil partisan political and socioeconomic agendas?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Does having academic freedom mean one has carte blanche to communicate irresponsibly and without credible evidence?" Let me put it quite plainly.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The law treats all activists equally, whether you are an academic or a man or woman on the street.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You are as free as an ordinary citizen to comment on current affairs or critique the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: POFMA offers no special shield to academics either.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the law aside, in this era of free-for-all communications and interactions, public discourse is becoming more rigorous.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Here is where things may get a little bit different for academics.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We hold academics to "conduct professorial" high standards of integrity in their teaching, research and the validity of their views put forward in public.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is especially so when they speak or make social media posts on current affairs while bearing the title of a professor in a publicly-funded university.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, you can put out an opinion that Singapore’s growth model has failed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You can say meritocracy in Singapore has failed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You can say the education system is elitist, our social welfare does not work and it does more harm than good.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: POFMA will not apply to you because that is your opinion.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But in the interest of open debate and given your stature in society and position in a publicly funded university, please expect Government agencies, if we do not agree with you, to put out the data and put out our arguments to convince the public otherwise.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If that has a chilling effect, please chill.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The same and, perhaps, even higher expectations apply to my Cabinet colleagues and I.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Whatever we say needs to be well thought out, set the tone for society, and be in the best interest of our people.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, if anyone of us puts forward a view in a speech, during a dialogue or in an Instagram or Facebook post, and if the public does not agree with us, they will speak up and give us a piece of their mind.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And we have to consider those views and re-evaluate our position.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The interaction will get more active and rigorous.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is part and parcel of modern governance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When it comes to our decisions and actions, the scrutiny will be even more intense.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We want this interaction and exchange of ideas and opinions to be free of malicious falsehoods which poison the atmosphere and mislead the discourse.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: (In Mandarin):   	Speaker, Sir, I shall continue my speech in Mandarin.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Fake news has been in existence since ancient times.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, during the Jin Dynasty in China, the Qin army from the north sent their troops south to attack Eastern Jin.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As the two troops battled at the Fei River, the troops from Eastern Jin suggested for the Qin troops to move back, to allow the Jin troops to cross the river, so that the two troops could battle to the death.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As the vanguards of the Qin army moved back, Jin soldiers who had infiltrated this group started shouting: "The Qin army has lost!

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Qin army has lost!" Amazingly, the Qin troops believed these words and thought that the command to move backwards was a sign of defeat.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This led to a sharp drop in the Qin troops' morale, eventually resulting in the Qin army’s defeat and retreat.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Qin army was filled with anxiety and panic, and every movement in the surrounding plants made them suspect that it was the Jin army lying in ambush.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That was how the Chinese Idiom "草木皆兵Cao Mu Jie Bing" (every plant is an enemy soldier) came about.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There can never be too much deceit in times of war.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This has been so since ancient times; falsehoods have been used to affect the emotions of societies and people.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Three years ago, during the UK's referendum on exiting the EU, that is, Brexit, the Internet was flooded with falsehoods, such as "Turkey is becoming part of the EU, which will cause large numbers of immigrants to enter the UK." Such intentional spread of falsehoods aimed to mislead the voters and affect the voting results.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Apart from politics, falsehoods can disrupt the everyday lives of people.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Eight years ago, when Northeast Japan was hit by a massive earthquake which damaged a nuclear power plant, there was a rumour circulating on social media that salt could guard against radiation exposure.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This caused people to rush to the supermarkets and buy all the available salt supplies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Nearer to home, in 2017, there was a rumour that a hawker in Geylang was selling satay made of dog and cat meat.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the same year, there were also accusations that some local supermarkets were selling rice made of plastic.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Fortunately, there were timely clarifications for these two incidents and they did not lead to more panic and hysteria.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In recent years, AI has developed the "Deepfake" capability, in which computers can be used to combine and superimpose existing images and videos and mimic a person's actions and speech.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: China has decided to ban the use of "Deepfake" technology.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We cannot stop the advancement of technology, but neither can we evade the problems that come along with it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For each of the examples I mentioned, the Bill can be used to request online platforms or media companies to issue corrections.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Legal action can then be taken against those who spread such falsehoods with malicious intent.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are academics who worry that the Bill will stifle freedom of speech or even hamper academic research.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Unless the research paper made use of falsified data or falsehoods, there is no need to worry.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, there is no need to worry about inadvertently sharing mistaken information.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, I hope that everyone can be vigilant at all times and verify the information they receive, before sharing them with family and friends.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In summary, there is actually nothing new under the sun.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But in this Internet era, strange things seem to be surfacing all the time.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This Bill may only have an effect on a small amount of falsehoods out there.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I believe that the falsehoods that it targets are those that pose the greatest danger and have negative impact.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Globally, falsehoods have already negatively impacted many democratic systems and the lives of people.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The greater reason for tabling this Bill is to safeguard the lives of our people against such threats.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A big worry of the modern world is whether democracy can withstand this onslaught.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And indeed, this is a major challenge of our times.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, the odds are stacked against those of us who are trying to uphold institutions, all of us in this House.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The balance of power is asymmetrical, heavily weighted in favour of those with malicious intentions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is far easier to make a sensational falsehood viral, than a technical correction.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is far easier to use bots to spread falsehoods than to use a speech and use traditional media coverage.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Let us juxtapose that video against the standards under POFMA.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Is there public harm, as a second gate?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Did the perpetrator possess knowledge of the harm, as a third gate?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the end, it was taken down, not by the force of law, but by Facebook itself under a lot of pressure.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Relative to the explosion of online capabilities that is now presented to those with malicious intent, the ambit of this law is not large.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And that is as far as executive powers of Ministers go.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is not the omnipresent, draconian, nuclear weapon, Infinity Gauntlet Snap that some people make it out to be.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira talked about the need for shared reality for any society and acknowledged the need for that.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For democracy and constructive discourse to work, there must be a common understanding of the underlying facts of the country – what happened and what did not.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I am glad that the Member acknowledged that.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some of these facts shape the character and common ethos of a nation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, the understanding of shared reality, with Science and History, is no longer like the 17th century.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think we have a large body of scientific evidence and we have a good record of history.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Germans had lived under a dark period of Nazism, and that is an undeniable fact.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In China, the May Fourth Movement happened 100 years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The US liberated the slaves and went through a devastating civil war.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In Singapore, we are a small, multicultural island state.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We faced Communist threats and were thrusted into independence.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, researchers continue to study and interpret those events: what caused them, what they represented, what is their impact today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But they cannot deny that they happened and continue to shape the character and psyche of societies today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A society that holds onto certain truths is a social necessity, a binding force in politics, and a prerequisite for civil discussions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Lose these and the country loses part of its soul.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Otherwise, democracy becomes a marketplace of merchants peddling forgeries.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Only by holding onto certain truths are we able to continue to collectively identify the issues that are important to us, the options and paths we can take, and decide the way forward, without the lies and without the manipulations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira said this is a vote of conscience.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is, indeed, a vote of conscience because look at the tectonic shifts that we are faced with.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Technology has fundamentally changed society, changed the political discourse.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is changing politics and modern society as we know it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All governments around the world need new rules, new laws and new mechanisms to deal with this tectonic change.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Earlier, in his speech, he referred to the case which I cited about the two economists 15 years ago.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And according to his analysis, he mentioned that in order to qualify as an actionable POFMA untruth, there are two gates to pass.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And his assessment was that in that scenario, gate one was not passed because there was no falsehood to begin with.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I am wanting some clarifications because when you look at that statement alone about job creation, it appears on one reading to be an assertion of fact, which later on, the Government came to correct and said it is not correct.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And one reading of POFMA, it could be argued that Gate 1 has been passed because there is an assertion of some facts which are not correct.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And Gate 2 possibly may be passed as well because this may diminish confidence in the Government in job creation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I would like the Minister to clarify again, which is very helpful, I think, earlier.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But I think we need more explanation about how the Minister sees the case and why POFMA would not apply.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Does it mean that if researchers conclude facts based on incomplete data, that would not come under POFMA even though, factually, it has to be corrected?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am prepared to explain this and have it recorded in the Hansard.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, there was no falsification and no falsehood involved.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: I just have one point of clarification as well as some feedback.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: In the first instance, the Minister mentioned the distinction between the empirical disciplines as well as humanities which he said is not so empirical but is interpretive and critical.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
