text: So, I do not think my Humanities and Social Science colleagues will forgive me if I let you get away with saying Humanities and Social Science research is not empirical.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: So, that would just be a point of clarification.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: The second point actually relates to the use of the term "public harm" which I think, at this point in the discussion, is somewhat confusing because we have actually been discussing the Bill which uses the term "public interest".

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: So, I think that may actually create more issues of contention because there is a great deal of academic research that, while being of public interest, may not necessarily generate public harm.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: The third point is actually to deal with hon Member Dr Intan Mokhtar's suggestion that we should actually set up in universities, possibly, committees that actually help us to review whether or not these are actually falsehoods that have been made by academics perhaps unwittingly, and that these committees can help to advise the Ministers.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: While on the one hand I am sympathetic to that argument as a fellow academic, on the other hand, I think the very establishment as well as existence of such committees will, in fact, seem to underline the lack of academic freedom which I think would be an unhealthy signal to send.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, being a quantitative economist myself, I very much welcome the Humanities to use more data and empirical evidence.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Two, the Member's point on public interest versus public harm is taken.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have given some illustrations of what I think is the measure of public harm before POFMA kicks in, and I am sure my colleagues will clarify the concept further.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Third, on committees to decide what are falsehoods within universities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think they already exist because the entire discipline of doing good research, comprising peer review, academic committees and so on, already make sure that all academics do their work properly using proper data, do not fabricate data, do not fabricate facts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When you stick to that, I do not see how POFMA will catch you.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am going to drag you back to the 2003 example.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reason why I am doing that is because I think it is still kind of fresh in the minds of many academics in Singapore about how we interface with society and with the state.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I should declare that I am an NUS professor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this particular case, the Nanyang Technological University (NTU) report, their findings are way off the mark.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And after that, there was a big controversy and the issue blew up and all the academics knew that these two academics were being corrected by the Minister.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That was the phrase that was used in the media article.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And my second clarification is that I can appreciate the Minister's more open view about academic research because he is the Minister for Education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But here, as in this case with the labour economists, they were commenting on something that has to do in terms of public interest and has to do with the Ministry of Manpower.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the Minister for Manpower reacts to their remarks, right?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, it is a different Ministry that is involved in evaluating the academic research.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, is this going to be a kind of blanket rule or norm within the Cabinet, that when it comes to academics, consult the Minister for Education first?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have no intention to reopen the 2003 case and go through the data to see whether there is any falsified data.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It cannot be that just because it is a research piece, we all have to shut up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not in the spirit of POFMA, nor the political discourse that we want.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the point that I am the Minister for Education so I am slightly more open whether all these cases concerning research will go through me.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think it should have my inputs, based on how the law is written today.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But based on the WP's suggestion, I am afraid the decisions will all go to the Courts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Speaker, first, let me congratulate the Minister for Education on that speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I think we should actually send it out to all our academics because I think it was a really good policy statement, besides POFMA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I think we all accept the need for the Government to rebut robustly research it does not agree with, whether from academics or activists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: What I am concerned about – which I talked a bit in my speech earlier – is that there has been a trend sometimes of Ministries using language in their rebuttal that implies falsehood.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I think when you look at the details of the case, it is not always the case for all of these that there is really a dispute about the facts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And we should be more disciplined in future.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The tabling of the Bill comes after regulatory moves around the world, such as Germany, France and, more recently, Australia.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill is comprehensive, well-considered, globally researched, and above all, publicly consulted and reviewed.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill commendably sets out to protect Singaporeans in a highly polarised world against the threat of online falsehood.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: As highlighted by the hon Minister, globally, we are witnessing countries grappling with the problem of online falsehoods which aims to do many things, including interfering in elections as well as democratic processes, undermining public institutions, exploiting fault lines, sowing discord amongst racial and religious communities and, ultimately, weakening countries through national security threats, both real and imagined.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, it is important that we do not politicise the Bill and make sure that we take an objective stand.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill is one that is of immense significance to safeguard Singapore's future, especially in today's world where there is an overload of information on a multitude of platforms that threatens to undermine much of our traditional forms of communication and reliable information sources.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Today, I wish to speak on two areas in relation to the proposed Bill: one, safeguarding racial and religious harmony; and two, on technological trends in disseminating online falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, I presented at the SC on Deliberate Online Falsehoods (DOFs), representing my interfaith non-profit organisation Roses of Peace.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I shared that given the destructive force of online falsehood in the digital age, it has the potential to exploit our social fault lines and can undermine our social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: If not countered, it can erode the multiracial and multi-religious fabric of our society and our forefathers who have fought to achieve this and preserve this.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: There needs to be a clear action plan involving a whole-of-nation effort to combat online falsehoods or fake news.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: As the hon Minister for Law and Home Affairs had described in his SC public hearing last year, tackling fake news will require a multi-pronged approach which takes into consideration effective legislation and Government policy, as well as efforts by corporations, non-profit organisations, religious organisations, civil society and ordinary citizens.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It is important for ordinary citizens to be equipped with the knowledge and tools to discern and deal with fake news.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Only when individuals are able to take ownership and understand the consequence of deliberate online falsehoods are we able to safeguard our social well-being and be a more resilient society.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The falsehood insinuated that the Muslim minority were trying to sterilise the Sinhalese majority.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: More recently, the tragic mosque shooting in Christchurch was socially engineered for virality and maximum reach via livestreaming.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The video was viewed just less than 200 times during the live broadcast.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: No users reported the video during the live broadcast.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Including the views during the live broadcast, the video was viewed about 4,000 times in total before being removed from Facebook.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: However, according to Facebook, in the first 24 hours, it was removed about 1.5 million times, copies of this video of the attack globally.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: More than 1.2 million of those videos were blocked at upload and were, therefore, prevented from being seen on their services.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: What I have just outlined above are serious and quick adverse consequences of viral and false information.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: We would be naïve to assume that Singapore would be immune to this.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, when one considers what is the right decision-making body to move quickly to counteract the effects and spread of false information, speed and effectiveness must be paramount.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: That is precisely what the SC, with representation from both sides of the House, had accepted.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe, in circumstances where false information is undermining Singapore's public interest, it is the Executive which should be empowered to act.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: They can do so swiftly and decisively to protect Singaporeans against such falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: A 2014 analysis by the Pew Research Centre found Singapore to be the world's most religiously diverse nation.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Despite our diversity, Singapore has enjoyed peace and religious harmony for over 50 years since Independence.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, we cannot take any chances and take the stability and security we enjoy for granted.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In today's world, online falsehoods are weaponised to be used against countries by state and non-state actors.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The online information space and the social media are a key battlefield in a new conception of warfare.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Now there is no need for war to be declared with the blurring of boundaries between wartime and peacetime.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: New dynamics brought about by technological advancements is an area of concern for any Governments looking to legislation to combat online falsehood.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: As technology is always ahead of regulations, we should develop the ability to respond swiftly and robustly before they can cause harm to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In an information-rich world, the most effective response to disinformation is literacy.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: As highlighted by the hon Education Minister, media literacy is essential for end users to be able to spot obvious fakes.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In future, AI-powered solutions may help us distinguish high-quality news sources and content from bogus ones, and even spot potential political motivations behind the propagation of certain news.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Political speech and even imagery can easily be manipulated at low cost and with professional quality.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It needs to be comprehensive and extremely well considered if we are to protect Singaporeans as well as their rights to freedom of choice in the digital age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It has been said that POFMA balances the right and utility of responsible free speech with the necessity for speedy action to prevent the subversion of society in the informational age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: In my view, this Bill is severely imbalanced.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Speed is distance over time, and the Government has chosen to maximise speed, giving itself great powers to cross vast distances in a short amount of time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: But this need for speed can have severe detrimental effects for the society, and the state itself, if it is not properly checked.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I shall deal with three issues: one, the problem with the definition of falsehoods in the hands of the Executive; two, the problem with the Government defending public confidence in the Government itself by force; and three, the Government choosing between a legacy and a Trojan Horse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The first issue concerns the definition of falsehoods in this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: First, a falsehood has to be a statement of fact.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Subsection 2(a) states that "a statement of fact is a statement which a reasonable person seeing, hearing or otherwise perceiving it would consider to be a representation of fact".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This definition rests on the figure of the reasonable person.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I just want to note a paradox here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: As elaborated by the Minister for Law in his opening speech, the problem we face today is that online falsehoods have undermined public discourse and eroded precisely this figure of the reasonable person.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Whether a statement is a fact or is an opinion goes to the heart of this piece of legislation, as it provides the scope for which statements would be covered by this law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: If the reasonable person does not quite exist anymore, how do we determine if a statement is, indeed, a statement of fact and not an opinion?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The fact that the Minister for Law had to go to great lengths to clarify with detailed examples on what are statements of fact and what are statements of opinion show that this distinction between fact and opinion has significantly blurred in public discourse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It is well and fine if a statement of fact is an established matter in jurisprudence, but we are talking about placing the powers in the Executive here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: If the reasonable person in the juridical definition of the statement of fact has, indeed, faded away, how would the Executive, specifically the Ministers, being not the Judiciary steeped in matters of jurisprudence, be able to distinguish between a statement of fact and a statement of opinion in a speedy manner?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This is an important issue, since a wrong application of a correction directive on a statement of opinion can be a miscarriage of justice and even affect electoral results.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Ministers have to be extremely cautious even at the first step of the process, to determine whether a statement is a statement of fact or a statement of opinion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The only resolution I can see is that Ministers will have to consult the Minister for Law on this determination and this would take time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Perhaps as much time as it would ought have taken to decide on a Correction order.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Sub-section 2(b) states that, "a statement is false if it is false" – that sounds a bit tautological but I think it can stand – "false or misleading, whether wholly or in part, and whether on its own or in the context in which it appears".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The definition of falsehoods should be simply based on fact.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: A fact is something that is known to be true because of existing information or proven to be so by current evidence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Conversely, a statement of fact is false when it can be shown to be not true by information or evidence, whether existing or new.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Furthermore, how can we justifiably and reasonably make people responsible for part of their statements and for statements taken out of context?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Public confidence is earned, not enforced by the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The second issue has to do with the meaning of “public interest” in section 4.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I have little quibble with the list of areas (a), (b), (c) and (e).

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Sub-section (f) is worded as "to prevent a diminution of public confidence in the performance of any duty or function of, or in the exercise of any power by, the Government, an Organ of State, a Statutory Board, or a part of the Government, an Organ of State or a Statutory Board".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Other than takedowns for posts that endanger our national security, foreign relations, racial and religious harmony, public safety, why is there a need for speed for all Ministers – all Ministers – to impose corrections on alleged falsehoods about the performance of the Government?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I am not saying that the Government should not act to clarify and correct widespread falsehoods that could undermine public confidence in our public institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I am saying that I do not see the need for speed to force a correction, as the current supposedly slow practices of correcting falsehoods already work to great effect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This arose from a misunderstanding arising from the setting of the automatic payouts at age 70 instead of 65.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I believe the automatic payouts should be set at the payout eligibility age, but that is my opinion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: But factually, it was false that the Government quietly raised the payout eligibility age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This was corrected by the Government by press statements and Parliamentary answers by the Minister for Manpower in response to questions from Members, which was then carried by the media.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This falsehood spurred the Government to redouble their public education efforts, producing good materials to educate the public on the policies, which effectively dispelled the falsehood.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This example was also cited by the Minister for Law in his speech moving the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: An objective press statement by the Police setting out the facts dispelled the falsehood.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: As a result, many were chastised by fellow online citizens for spreading baseless assumptions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: In these two examples, the Government is engaging Singaporeans as a partner in conversation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: In these two examples, the Government is not arbitrating truths ex cathedra, using its authority to force corrections and threaten mistaken citizens with punishment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Instead, it is calmly explaining the facts and issuing additional information so that public confidence can be restored and even improved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: In fact, timeliness and proportionality are key here, not speed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: In fact, the responses from the Government were not slow at all, and it was not hasty, too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The online public dwells in an information-rich environment and has its own norms and etiquette in engaging with debate and discussion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Trust in the Government is no longer built on the good performance of its duties alone, but on communication and public engagement by the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Educated citizens want to be engaged as peers by the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: As such, the Government acting as a party in contentious politics with the online public will erode public confidence in the Government in the long run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Giving the Ministers, and by extension the Civil Service, the powers to force corrections create an easy and speedy way out from the hard work they should be doing instead, which is earning their trust through time-consuming but ultimately fruitful engagement with the public.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I do not understand why the Government would want to protect their Ministers from the test of fire of public reason.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I now come to the third issue, which represents the WP's fundamental objection to the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: We believe that the Courts should be the place to arbitrate truths and correct falsehoods, because the Courts are the natural place to do this, since this is exactly the function of the Courts: the use of reason and objective tests to judge what is true and what is false.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The Executive of the Government works with truths, but it will have its blindspots.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: In other words, the Executive, like many other organisations in society and civic society as a whole, is an interested party in the determination of truths.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Of course, as the Executive of the Government upholds the general interest of society, the Executive has a lot more capacity to obtain information and generate knowledge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Though it does not have the monopoly on truths, the Executive is first among equals in knowing and working with truths.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It is the responsibility of the Executive to share its depositories of knowledge and truths with the public so that, together with the informed public, the Executive can correct falsehoods that could undermine our public institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It is not its place to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: If it does, it undermines our collective faith in truths in the long run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Should the Executive exercise the powers given in this law, it will short-circuit the process of co-correction with an informed public which I just described.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: In doing so, the Executive forces the truth, let me say it again, forces the truth unto the public, it does not arbitrate the truth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: If the Government can speed up the appeal process in this proposed regime, and for the POHA interim protection orders, then there is no natural obstacle to do the same for the alternative process of making the Executive apply to the Courts for corrections and takedowns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: But when it comes to public confidence in the performance of the Government, there is absolutely no need for speed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Heterodoxies, which may be extremely uncomfortable for the Government in the short term, are often useful and beneficial to public institutions in the long term.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Many times, the heterodoxies will not go away, and the more authorities tried to forcibly protect the orthodoxy, the stronger the heterodoxies grow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Sometimes, the heterodoxies turn out to be true, once the full force of information and evidence decide the matter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The only right approach is continued public engagement and public education by the authorities, the efforts of which in themselves will help to shore up public confidence in public institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: One strand of it grew from academic studies published in scholarly journals about possible association between the diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP) vaccine and Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) in the US in the 1980s.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: These studies, because of its sensational value, were reported in the media, creating alarm among the public and feeding the anti-vaxxers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Over time, medical scientists debunked many of the studies reporting possible association and produced studies that quite conclusively show no association between the DTP vaccine and SIDS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This enhanced scientific certainty made the public health system more robust and improved public confidence in public vaccination programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It could be said that society took one step back and then two steps forward, but if the authorities have intervened to suppress the heterodoxy in the name of protecting public confidence in the public health system in the first place, we would have been stuck with an orthodoxy, a believed truth, rather than one we have scientific certainty of.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The DTP-SIDS myth refuses to die till today, but this has spurred public education efforts that have enhanced public awareness of the benefits of vaccination.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This POFMA Bill undermines such a legacy and leaves us with a Trojan Horse instead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It is ironic that this Government is extolling the current public confidence in it to dismiss concerns of abuse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It is saying in a circular way, "Thank you for your trust in us, trust us then to use these draconian powers to protect that trust".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: What if future governments who do not deserve the trust of the public or even if this Government tomorrow, because they are not performing their duties well, seek to prop up the trust and deny public scrutiny using POFMA?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: There will be nothing to stop such irresponsible governments, for which corrections can pour out of POFMA as quickly as Greek troops pouring out of the Trojan Horse to seize the city of Troy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: What matters to us is not the assurances of the Minister for Law of restraint and reason on his part, but the substance of the law as framed in this Bill, whether it is a charming but fatal Trojan Horse or a true legacy of protection that deepens our trust and unity as a diverse society that goes online to discuss issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: In the same shadow of the Trojan Horse, the subsidiary argument that Ministers will face the public at the ballot box for wrong and heavy-handed actions is a terrible argument and poor justification for granting such far-reaching powers to the Executive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It is saying to the citizens, “If you are not happy with my decision, I dare you to vote me out”.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: If Singapore reaches this stage where the Ministers have to be tested at the ballot box in this manner, then we are already seeing the erosion of trust in Government and in the public institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It will be too late to turn back by then.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Truth and justice are not just ideals, but they are pragmatic values that pervade the performance of public institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Truth and justice are closely related, they imply each other.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The Executive acts on truths to accomplish justice.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I spoke to many residents and there is consensus that fake news has a profound effect on the world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The question now is how best to deal with this issue.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And it is this: how can our society best balance our individual desire to free speech, with our desire to be protected from the tremendous impact of irresponsible, or even worse still, deliberate falsehood, weaponised by the speed and reach of social media?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Many of us in this Chamber are aware that there is no single silver bullet to combat fake news, online or offline.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The best we can do is to create laws, so as to create an environment for responsible speech, anchored by an informed citizenry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, when the demand for fake news diminishes, no supply of fake news, no matter how large the supply, can seriously harm society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our desired outcome should not be just to weed out irresponsible speeches that diminish our society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We must also ensure that responsible speech thrives in society, because healthy private and public discourse is the means for people and society to reflect and move forward.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And that brings me to my main point today.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: After our robust debate today, we must do more to communicate to our people what constitutes responsible speech.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: A fair number of my residents have seen the various news articles, WhatsApp messages, and even Michelle Chong’s recent interview of Minister K Shanmugam.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But there is still a much-needed desire for clarity on what this entire framework of various laws means.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It is clear from what the various Government officials and Ministers have said.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But at the same time, certain offensive and divisive speeches are restricted using different laws.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Now that there is considerable public attention on responsible speech, let us ride on this wave of interest and share more on this topic.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: When people understand better how the different laws work, their powers and limitations, then they can see that the Government does not have blanket power to take down whatever news they do not like.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Only certain types of speech that are harmful to society can be dealt with according to the law.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: A good place for this to start is our schools, especially at our tertiary institutions, where there has been much discussion about this law today.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I have seen a deep conviction by MinLaw to create our overall framework for responsible speeches.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we can see a whole-of-Government effort, including MOE, to communicate that clearly to our people in a simplified manner.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like MinLaw to clarify on one matter.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I would like to end by suggesting that Singapore actively contribute to the global discourse on how we deal with deliberate online falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, there are many legislators all over the world watching our deliberations today.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Deliberate online falsehood is something that affects all societies and does not automatically and neatly stop at any borders.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In the long run, our best bet is to shape the larger environment in a positive way.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In my speech on the Motion on this matter last year, I quoted the Washington Post's motto, "Democracy dies from Darkness".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Democracy cannot survive and thrive without a public discourse informed by facts, truth and transparency because public discourse is the means for our society to reflect collectively.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It seeks to root out merchants of mistruths or special interests and, worse still, foreign influence that seeks to deliberately manipulate and destabilise our society through fake news.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But we must go beyond crafting this excellent legal framework.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We must communicate clearly and simply to our people what responsible speech entails, factoring our unique circumstances as a small multicultural, multi-religious and multiracial city-state.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: (In Malay):   	Fake news has adverse consequences around the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Often, it is an act of mischief that causes disruption, discord and panic.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Sometimes, it can generate serious consequences, such as interference in national elections in India and Thailand, and causing clashes between the people and the police as in Greece.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In the UK, the fake news aims to make people question the safety of using vaccine to prevent diseases.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: And we in Singapore also have our fair share of people who spread fake news.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: However, it is not surprising that there are those who are concerned about the POFMA Bill being tabled.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But having regulations in place is important to address falsehoods arising from cognitive biases.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Such falsehoods, built up over time via a drip-feed effect, can become something that is hard to overcome.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We have to nip the problem in the bud before it becomes a full-blown crisis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Falsehoods do not have to take the form of elaborate hoaxes that are detrimental to the public interest.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In fact, elaborate hoaxes are more easily recognised and debunking it is not difficult, because it can be easily traced.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: On the other hand, drip-feed falsehoods are dangerous because they do not have an immediate effect and are harder to detect.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: If it is a constant drip-feed of falsehoods, it is, in fact, more damaging in the long run.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is like a whispering campaign to poison minds.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The effect is comparable to the rain water dripping from a rooftop onto a walkway.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Eventually the tiny droplets will create a cavity on the cement floor.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Social media giant Facebook recognises this problem and took steps to reduce the impact in the lead-up to the French election, for instance.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: They targeted fake accounts, worked with newsrooms to debunk false claims, and ran full-page ads in the French newspapers to guide readers on how to spot fake news.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: According to the head of research at First Draft News, a non-profit coalition working to address misinformation online, which Facebook is also a member of, there was plenty of material sowing seeds of confusion and distrust.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: These come in the form of manipulated videos, photos and other misleading content.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is more insidious, compared to a major hoax.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: They are relentless in their attacks as they persisted in their line of thinking.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, it is crucial to note the intentions behind the creation of such content.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Not all exist with pure intentions of providing entertainment or an alternative voice.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Often, content creators seek to increase traffic and readership on their platforms which translates to financial profits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: They resort to sensationalising and manipulating news with intentions of generating so-called original content which they hope would go viral.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: These stories tend to spark strong emotional responses like anger.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: A common misconception is that drip-feed falsehoods do not have immediate impact on national security and so should not be investigated under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But if left unaddressed and allowed to manifest into something more threatening, that can lead to severe consequences.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Many violent conflicts around the world have occurred as a result of the spread of such drip-feed falsehoods, which feed on people's fears to instil mistrust and hate on a gradual but regular basis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In 2018, a terrible lynching happened in Mexico because of some rumours of child abduction when, in fact, no children were kidnapped.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The incident made waves globally and many major news outlets cited it in their commentaries about the dangers of fake news.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Yet, in 2019, child abduction rumours are causing violent attacks on the Roma people in France.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In other countries, religious institutions are destroyed, innocent people injured, even killed in protests, while outcomes of political elections and major referendums are manipulated through falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It will be too late if we wait until the harm reaches a severe level to take action.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, my question then is how will the Minister for Home Affairs or Minister for Law react to seemingly inconsequential lies and misrepresentations, especially when the perpetrators use the drip technique to slowly feed poison into the minds of readers, for example, a personal account about how the Police have mishandled a case, which may or may not contain some personal bias, or a photo edited in a way that misrepresents local authority figures, or a post about an ethnic stereotype, perhaps made in jest?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Ethnic memes are popular in the west, and I have no doubt that some Singaporeans use them in a tongue-and-cheek manner with no real intention of promoting hate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I agree that swift action is necessary to prevent seeds of discord from growing into something more threatening.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This would not only assure Singaporeans that the Government only targets false statements with evidence, but it will also give more strength to the correction.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Corrections must be carefully crafted and they must be detailed, with the purpose of refuting each and every false claim.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The Minister has said that this will be done, and it will be prescribed through law.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This Bill should not be deemed as an end-all and be-all to shut down fake news.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I also note that some netizens have been comparing POFMA to the Anti-fake News Bill by our Malaysian counterparts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But I tried to read the Bill to my understanding the example, illustrations of actions that would be prosecuted under the Anti-fake News Bill in Malaysia, are indicative of outright defamation, quite a different type of falsehood from what POFMA seeks to eradicate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Moreover, the punishments are harsh for perpetrators and abettors, involving astronomical fines and long jail terms.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: For example, they may be issued to intermediaries, primarily.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The Directions are not even focused on punishment but on remedying the impact and thus the correction is an important element.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Both Bills, in Singapore and Malaysia, have different intents and it is unfair to compare them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The main levers in the POFMA Bill are targeted at the intermediaries, through the various Directions that can be made.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: That is different from Malaysia's Anti-fake News Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Education must continue to play an important role, too, to impart critical thinking skills and help Singaporeans to discern whether something is a falsehood.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: There must be more trusted avenues for Singaporeans to do fact-checking.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: There are some international websites which do fact-checking and publish corrections of fake news.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Unfortunately, there are also hoax websites that impersonate fact-checking websites!

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What other efforts are there to complement the legislation in countering online falsehoods?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In prosecuting perpetrators of fake news, we must maintain transparency of the process, allowing the public to understand why it is deemed a falsehood.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We must reflect on why many people believed in a particular piece of fake news, and how we can get to the root of the problem.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We must also persist to encourage Singaporeans to adopt the correct attitudes and values when gathering information on the Internet.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Deliberate disinformation has been part of statecraft for centuries.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore has experienced our own tragic effect of disinformation in our early days.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Early propagandists like Tan Malaka who hailed from Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Arriving in Malaya in the 1920s, he invited the Chinese Communist Party to send agents into Malaya in 1925.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That marked the beginnings of the early stages of the Malayan Communist Party (CPM).

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The CPM grew by leaps and bounds during the Second World War.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We launched the Communist struggle at the end of the Japanese Occupation and thus began the Malayan Emergency.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Subsequently, they went underground but continued to destabilise the young nations of Malaya and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is a tragic yet pivotal moment in our history, one seared into our psyche.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, though we call it a race riot, it was the weaponisation of political narrative that led to the unfortunate incidents.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many have studied it, key of which was the political disagreements between the Alliance Federal government in Malaysia and the PAP Government in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) at that time led the campaign through Utusan Melayu, which was a Jawi-based newspaper.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Very soon, the fall, the riots took place.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It established facts that were untrue about our leaders, it spoke about Singapore leadership intentions to oppress Malay rights.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Clarifications were made by Singapore leaders, but clarifications were not published by the paper.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A series of leaflets were issued calling for Chinese to be killed in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In one paragraph, it said, "We should wipe out all the Chinese from Singapore to prevent them from making fools of us." Materials like that inflamed tensions between the communities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On top of that, you have further inflammatory speeches by people, such as the Secretary-General of UMNO, Syed Jaafar Albar.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One thing led to another and created a climate of fear and distrust.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What would have been a small incident during the procession on Prophet Muhammed's birthday became that spark on the entire pile of tinder that exploded.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Deaths, injuries, destruction, not just of lives and infrastructure but society itself.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But will we be as lucky the next time?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But when lives depend on accurate information that needs to be out there urgently, we will be and would not want to be philosophical about it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is subjected to a daily barrage of disinformation to destabilise the country, further divide the Russian-speaking population, the minorities there, and the majority Ukrainians.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As an example: a pro-Russian fake news site circulated an article that the press service of the Ministry of State of Security in the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR) reported that Ukrainian forces were preparing a provocation in Donbass.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This was when an EU delegation was due to visit.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The DPR Ministry claims to have uncovered Ukrainian forces’ plans to use a missile to shoot down the delegation’s helicopter and blame it on the DPR's rebels.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is just one example of the daily barrage that they have to go through.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The SC has reported on how falsehoods have been weaponised by some countries.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Minister, in his opening speech yesterday, spoke about "non-kinetic warfare" to harm the sovereignty and social resilience of other nation states.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Dr Shashi Jayakumar of the Rajaratnam School of International Studies presented before the SC and shared on how disinformation operations involve, and I quote: "spreading rumours to discredit politicians, and playing up themes like the negative portrayal of immigration policy have been aimed at undermining public trust towards democracy, and systematically influencing populations to become less trusting of mainstream established news networks and more trusting of fringe news sources (backed by foreign powers) and conspiracy narratives." We must realise that this is not a theoretical possibility.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is not one that is far removed from our shores.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are a nation that is open and connected and diverse and, therefore, is the perfect target for disinformation operations as part of larger influence operations to wear down our people.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I return to my earlier starting point that disinformation is not new.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Then what makes it so different now that we require new and robust laws?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Traditional vectors in traditional warfare are physical weapons, but they have limitations of reach and cost.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Falsehoods, however, as weaponised narratives and disinformation, are unconstrained by physical bunkers of hiding spots.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It has a global blast radius that self-propagates after launch.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Vulnerability traditionally meant how much of a bombardment you can take before physical resistance succumbs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, it is easy to get past cognitive resistance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The scope and speed by which falsehoods spread (a) when digital technology costs so much less than bullets; (b) ammunition that self-replicates through bots and online armies; and what some refer to as a firehose of falsehood, the deluge that comes towards you.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And, of course, synergy when disinformation builds up one on another, confusing first, confounding and then eventually convincing the population.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I think we can all agree that against such state-sponsored disinformation campaigns need speed, accuracy and clarity, wide distribution and inoculation to combat.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And therefore, the Executive is best placed in this situation to make the call for national security.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There will be some who say, why not let us take a middle ground.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While some falsehoods will require swift action, the same urgency should not extend to other kinds of falsehoods, for example, drip-feed falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this line, I wish to make a point on the final limb that is proposed in this legislation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That of undermining public confidence in the Government and other agencies and some say the definition of "public interest" is far too wide.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, given the expert evidence on disinformation operations, especially those that are already apparent in Singapore, it is clear why this ground is needed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is important that the exercise of power remains subject to clear check and balance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But this Bill does provide for it and has been emphasised by the Minister and many others who have spoken about it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Disinformation campaigns, weaponised narratives, all served as this new front, and we must all be prepared.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To better inform the public on why POFMA is of particular importance to combat such foreign campaigns, I ask that the Minister share more on how the Bill serves as a counter to state-linked campaigns run against us and to prepare and inoculate our people against such disinformation that seeks to divide our population.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Coming back to my example on the Communist threat in the early years, some younger residents that I spoke to recently asked what will be the status of academic research, for example, historians writing papers on research into Operation Coldstore, research that asks if there was ever a Communist threat, if there were ever any Communists in Singapore at all.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I think these are honest questions and I am thankful that Minister Ong Ye Kung, as Minister for Education, has spoken succinctly on this, what the Bill encompasses and what it does not, especially when it comes to academia.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Much has also been said about the directions by the Minister or Ministers, whether to correct or to take down.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some say that the direction is like a beheading.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It serves as a tool to permanently silence the discussion.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This, I think, grossly misconstrues what the directions set out to do.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Far from silencing discourse, I submit that it adds to it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In fact, as it stands, even after a correction, the original poster can still comment on it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So can journalists, so can academics, so can any man in the street.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When the Minister gives a correction or takedown direction, he is required to give reasons on why a statement of fact is false.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, far from reducing the discourse, it adds to it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In fact. after a takedown, the person is free to continue posting on any other matter.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To say that the directions will silence discourse ignores that the discourse will now be more complete because it will have both viewpoints.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We should never allow such people to propagate their vile ideologies in any form or manner.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This world has no place for sick people with no love and respect for life, happiness and basic human decency.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: If this Bill is also to hold those big, powerful online businesses accountable and responsible to stop the spread of such vile messages, by all means, let us go after them, too.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: These money‐minded companies cannot have the cake and eat it at the expense of our social order, racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: And if this Bill is drafted solely to protect our way of life, our love and respect for one another, regardless of race, language or religion, I am all for it.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But this Bill is way more than that.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This Bill will also give a “big brother” government considerable latitude to silence the voice of the common man in a community where he can be at ease to express his views, opinions, arts, music, political beliefs and more, without inhibition.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This Bill will strike fear into the hearts of these Singaporeans who are vocal and passionate about the issues they care about most because they can be issued with a Part 3 Direction even if they do not know or have no reason to believe that the fact of what they have shared in their community could be wrong.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This Bill will arm the Minister with a nuclear option to act as judge and jury to obliterate critics and opponents of the Government in a flash.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This Bill, if abused, will turn Singapore into a repressive state in no time.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: One cannot shout fire in a crowded place and cause panic and mayhem in the name of free speech.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I also subscribe to the fact that we are living in a very different world now.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We do need to protect the society at large from being torn apart by the rise of racial and religious tensions fanned by bigots, extremists and racists.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, this Bill should be scoped with the sole purpose to protect the society from harm espoused by people with vile intentions.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It should be scoped to hold companies which allow hate ideologies and messages to propagate in their systems accountable.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It should not be scoped with ambiguity to protect a “big brother” government from critics, political opponents, civil societies, non-government organisations (NGOs) and online communities, in the name of tackling online falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This Government has already amassed an arsenal of legislation to block or take down undesirable materials to protect the community at large.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Does it really need a nuclear option to send a shiver down the spines of men in the street, uncles and aunties, academics, critics and the society at large in the name of protecting them from online falsehood and manipulation?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The nuclear option, if abused, will actually allow the Minister to influence the outcome of an election, something which this Bill is designed to prevent in the first place.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Who can vouch that an incumbent party, when faced with multiple battles on all fronts, will not resort to desperate measures to avoid losing power in a critical election?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We are all against foreign intervention in our electoral process.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The powers that be in this world may want to influence the outcome of elections for whatever reason and we should not allow them.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But we are not alone and we should work with the social media giants to stop these foreign agents from trying to influence the outcome of our elections.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But the biggest fear of someone making a false statement of fact knowingly to influence the outcome of an election may not come from an individual or from an outside source, but from an incumbent party with ample resources to shape public opinion and perception at will.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The biggest contributor of misleading propaganda may come from the incumbent Government itself.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, where is the protection against the incumbent from influencing the outcome of an election under this Bill?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Take, for example, at the last General Election.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What if, during an election, some insiders were to publish serious personal allegations against the top leadership of the incumbent party, questioning their integrity and character to lead the country?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Under this Bill, the Minister, Competent Authority or Alternate Authority, can easily order a takedown of the allegations in the name of public interest, knowing very well that no one, apart from the Ministers, the affected Minister and insiders themselves, would know who was telling the truth.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, would this Bill be used to silence such information which could be material to help voters decide whom to support in an election?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The nuclear option would be able to silence anyone instantly at a critical time with no immediate recourse.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Minister for Law was reported to have said, and I quote, "The Courts decide ultimately what is true and what is false and they will be the final arbiters." But under this proposed Bill, if a Minister opines that it is in the public interest to issue a Part 3 Direction on a statement made against the Prime Minister, for example, that opinion would be taken at face value as the gospel truth, and justice would have to be served immediately.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: How is that even right to begin with?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: How it is not wrong in any sense of the laws that one is judged and prosecuted for something that the Courts must decide ultimately if it was indeed false in the first place?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This Bill will assume the Government is always right all the time until the Courts say otherwise.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As the Minister had cleverly put it, the Court is the final arbiter of truth, and the key word is "final" because, in reality, the original arbiter of truth had already spoken and issued the decree for punitive action to be taken immediately.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: And what if the alleged false statement of fact was not false after all and it could have influenced the outcome of the election?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What if the Minister were to decide to cancel a Part 3 Direction on his own initiative, days after the elections are over?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In both cases, no final arbiter of truth would be required.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Can the results of the general elections be declared void then?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But if we knew that there is a nuclear option in the Bill, which could be abused in the future, why are we, as legislators, not doing anything about it now?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Why would we want to leave a nuclear option for a future dictator to silence all dissenting voices with a snap of his fingers?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As stated at the beginning of my speech, I am all for the protection of our way of life, our racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am also all for making the online businesses accountable for the spread of ideologies that threaten the social fabric of our society.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What I cannot support is for this Government to slip a nuclear option into this Bill to protect itself in the name of tackling online falsehood, especially in the context of conducting a fair election.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: When we enact Bills that chip away our basic rights and freedoms in the name of protecting the society at large, we have to be wary about the added power we would be giving to the state in the process.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: That power, in the wrong hands, may kill the dreams, imaginations, laughter and creativity of the people.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This Bill, in the hands of a despot, will kill democracy over time.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: My views are informed by my Ministry and its agencies' experience in administering current content-related legislation, in dealing with tech companies across a spectrum of issues, working with industries on the digitalisation of our economy and nurturing digital readiness in our society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: A recent Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI) study found that while broadcast and print media remain relevant, there has been a pronounced shift towards online news consumption.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Most consumers of online news typically access at least four or more digital sources.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These sources are of varying reliability, ranging from the online version of mainstream media like Channel NewsAsia (CNA) and The Straits Times, to international news media like Cable News Network (CNN) and the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), and social media platforms like Facebook and Twitter.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Closed messaging services like WhatsApp and WeChat have also become prevalent with more than 50% of Singapore residents using them to communicate and share information.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These trends will only gather pace and intensify, in tandem with the growing reach and accessibility of technology.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our mobile population penetration rate, at about 150%, is among the highest in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As for Internet broadband, the wireless penetration rate for our population is over 200%.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And the wired household penetration rate is 93.5%.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, simply put, Singaporeans are highly connected and voracious consumers of data.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Connectivity and data are also essential to our digital economy.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The major global technology companies (FAANGs) have a significant presence in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We also have a vibrant news and media ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: More than 60 media organisations are accredited in Singapore, and large media organisations, including BBC, Bloomberg and Thomson Reuters, have their regional offices in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, it is unambiguous and undeniable that the flow of data and information, like the flow of goods, services and capital, is vital to our economy and to our society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And that is why any suggestion that this Bill is aimed at curtailing the online flow of information, or that it will be used by Ministers to make arbitrary decisions, is wholly unfounded and completely off the mark.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Any action to do so would be ill-advised and inimical to our interests.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Why would any Minister want to put in jeopardy, jobs for Singaporeans and opportunities for our businesses?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: That just does not make good economics nor good politics.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Moreover, these kinds of decisions would also be subject to intense scrutiny and it will be called out by a highly connected citizenry, as well as the tech and media organisations who have a substantial presence in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, we have an ecosystem that relies or derives great value from the flow of information and data.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And that ecosystem itself is going to be a natural check against any tendency to act or overreach.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As Minister Shanmugam has explained in detail and many Members of this House have agreed, this surge in the flow of information is a double-edged sword.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It can be used to educate, foster understanding and build trust.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But it can also be abused to spread falsehoods, sow discord and harm society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: At the same time, technology companies' algorithms, policies and design features have made it easier for echo chambers to be created and exploited.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We face the most serious challenge in the digital realm because advances in technology have greatly increased the volume, reach and impact of online information flows.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In the past decade alone, global cross-border data flows have risen 64 times.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: A further three-fold increase in Internet traffic is forecast from 2017 to 2022, and global mobile data traffic will increase seven-fold.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, against this backdrop, we need new modes of engagement with the digital information landscape to ensure that our citizens are well-informed and equipped to navigate the vast and diverse online terrain, discern truth from falsehood and engage in meaningful discourse and make informed choices.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Some Members have asked how today's tools fall short.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our present laws, which were mainly conceived in the era of print and broadcast media, were not designed to address the issue of online falsehoods.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For example, there are powers under the Broadcasting Act (BA) which regulates all broadcast content to issue takedown notices and block websites for public interest or security reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: However, in administering the Act, IMDA has found these to be blunt tools.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It would mean blocking an entire online platform for a single falsehood, which Mr Low Thia Khiang may think it is all right.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But it runs completely contrary to our desire for proportionality and calibrated regulatory interventions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: That is why this POFMA legislation is necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It is an essential and important addition to our regulatory architecture that introduces a calibrated set of measures to deal with the virulence and virality of online falsehoods.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Within this spectrum of measures, our preference, in the main, is to issue correction directions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The merits of juxtaposing the facts with falsehoods should be self-evident.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It will allow readers to make informed judgements, draw their own conclusions about the arguments that are being made and promote a more vigorous online discourse.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As we have explained, the Disabling and Stop Communication Directions will only be used in extreme cases where there is a threat of serious harm.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Some have expressed concerns whether the powers under the proposed legislation will be used judiciously.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I would cite for Members' reference our experience with the BA about which there were similar concerns.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: There has been much debate over who should wield the powers under this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is important, especially because online falsehoods can occur in domains as diverse as healthcare, finance or security.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Minister, supported by his Ministry's officials and resources, would have the requisite domain expertise to make an assessment and act quickly to stem the potential harm arising from an online falsehood.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Accountability is ensured as aggrieved parties can take action in Court against the Minister's decision.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Therefore, in assigning the powers under the Bill to Portfolio Ministers, the Bill, I humbly submit, appropriately and correctly locates authority with accountability, supported by the requisite knowledge and expertise to make expeditious decisions, which are essential when you are dealing with the virality of online falsehoods.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I am, therefore, somewhat surprised by the allegations, bordering on the melodramatic, of some WP Members of Parliament who suggested that this Bill allows Ministers to arbitrarily decide what is true, to impose penalties on individuals, and to suppress any commentary.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: First, the primary focus of this Bill is not individual per se; it is actually the larger tech platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Having said that, content often originates because of individual action and, therefore, you cannot completely exempt it from the focus of this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, assume someone puts up something online that is a falsehood.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Minister – the Portfolio Minister – has to decide if it is false and if it is in the public interest to act against it.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: If so, he has to then decide to issue a Direction, whether it is a correction or takedown, depending on what is the appropriate course of action.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The individual – since we decide to focus on individuals, taking up the case made by Mr Low Thia Khiang and other Members of the WP –then has a choice: you comply with the Direction, or you disagree and you appeal to the Minister.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: You apply to the Minister for either a cancellation or a variation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: If the Minister decides a Direction is still valid, then the individual can still appeal to the High Court within the prescribed period.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Now, what then on the part of the Executive?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: If the individual does not comply with the Direction, the competent authority will commence investigations, or may commence investigations for non-compliance with the Direction under section 15 of this Act.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Reasonable excuse is a defence to the criminal offence of not complying with the Direction.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The outcome of the investigation will be presented to the Public Prosecutor in the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) for decision on prosecution.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: If the Public Prosecutor decides to proceed, the matter will be brought to the Courts, and the Court will then decide on guilt and penalties.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, this process is one where there is very clear due process.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I fail to see how one can jump to the conclusion that Ministers are judge and jury, or indeed exercise nuclear options.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Also, the Courts decide on the penalties, not the Ministers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And, the right to comment, that is the right to free speech, continues in the course of this process until and unless it is subjudice.
