speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In other words, the individual can, and other interested parties can, put up online commentary to say that: I am the subject of POFMA action, or as Prof Lim Sun Sun put it, "I am being POFMA-ed", and you can take it up as a commentary and discussion.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I fail to understand how this encroaches on the rights of the individual, how it has this purported chilling effect that many Members of the Opposition claim.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Certainly, given the safeguards and the due process that I have outlined, I do not see how this can be seen as Ministers having excessive powers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Png Eng Huat also talked about the Election period.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, the Member's entire speech about conflicts of interest during the Election is addressed by that section because, during the Election period, the Ministers from different Ministries will appoint their Permanent Secretaries or the equivalent senior officials to act and exercise the authorities under this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: There is nothing in the Bill that prevents Ministers from consulting and seeking views from experts outside of their Ministries, where necessary and the circumstances permit.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In addition, certain broader powers, such as those to block funding and access to online locations under part 5 of the Bill, are given only to the Minister for Communications and Information as these decisions have broader implications, beyond individual Ministries, for Internet users, the industry and the digital infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Under section 6(1), the Minister may appoint a Statutory Board or senior official as the Competent Authority.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As enumerated in section 6(2), a key function of the Competent Authority is to give effect to the instructions of the Ministers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: IMDA's experience in administering BA and other content regulation policies, and its regular interaction with the media and technology companies will be relevant to the administration of this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This POFMA Office will support the Portfolio Ministers with technical advice on the precedents, the types of levers available, the feasibility and the effectiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Competent Authority will thus help provide consistency across the Government in the implementation of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This office will also work with technology companies on the Codes of Practice and monitor compliance with the directions and Codes.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Apart from the measures proposed in the legislation, there is also a need to address issues upstream.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Upstream safeguards like authenticity of users and transparency of advertising are issues that technology companies are also trying to address in different ways.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The more we can work with tech companies on such upstream systems and processes, the less we will need to take action downstream.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These Codes will apply only to prescribed digital advertising and Internet intermediaries, and we are now developing them in consultation with these intermediaries.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Codes aim to, first, prevent and counter the misuse of online accounts where malicious actors act behind online anonymity.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Among other things this would require intermediaries to use reasonable verification measures to prevent inauthentic accounts or bots from being created or used for malicious activities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Second, these Codes will enhance the transparency of political advertising.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This encompasses Election advertising and advertisements on issues of public interest or controversy in the Singapore context, including those pertaining to race or religion.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This will ensure that credible content is given prominence and/or falsehoods are prevented from gaining prominence.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Ms Joan Pereira has asked about the Codes and how they were being developed.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The scope of these Codes of Practice takes reference from international norms, including the EU Code of Practice on Disinformation, as well as, we have been having consultations with companies and international experts.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: All of these will inform the final formulation of the Codes of Practice.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The implementation of the Codes will be targeted and graduated, and the focus will be on ensuring that intermediaries have adequate systems and processes in place.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: When breaches occur, the Competent Authority will consider factors, such as the seriousness of the breach, whether there has been a pattern of similar breaches, and whether it reflects systemic deficiency in processes, and whether intermediaries' efforts to remedy the breaches are adequate.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: There has been a question, and some Members have articulated this: how or whether this Bill will affect Singapore's attractiveness as a technology hub and our relationship with the tech companies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The tech companies are an important part of Singapore's business ecosystem, especially our digital economy.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our value proposition to tech companies is anchored on several factors and that includes our political stability, our rule of law, conducive business environment, international connectivity and our skilled workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is why the major tech companies have continued to expand their operations in Singapore in the past years.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We continue to have regular engagements with the technology companies on a broad range of issues pertaining to investments, research and development, talent development and other collaborations of mutual interest.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: With respect to this Bill, our officials have been working with the tech companies that are most affected to incorporate their comments and feedback and, where possible, work together on solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Because these Annexes will clarify how each intermediary will operationalise the broad outcomes, principles and objectives of the Codes, taking into account the unique characteristics of each intermediary’s platform, its existing systems and measures to combat disinformation, technical capabilities, as well as effectiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In other words, some of these will have to be customised because of the nature of the different intermediaries, and those will be captured in the Annexes to these Codes of Practice.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Prof Lim Sun Sun said that we should approach these tech companies under a "collaborate framework".

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Where there are falsehoods that affect the public interest, defensive action should and must be taken and we need to have regulatory tools to deal with the problem.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And that is why we have sought to deeply engage the tech companies throughout this process.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Neither is it necessarily even in the interest of the tech companies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Faced with broad demands and heavy penalties, companies would be compelled to be excessively cautious.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For example, it has been reported that following the passing of the German law, one in six of Facebook moderators is now based in Germany.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Left to independently interpret Government objectives, companies would be accused of being politicised and biased by their users.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Since 2018, Twitter and Facebook have been dogged by accusations of "shadow-banning" conservative opinions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: They will issue unambiguous and detailed directions for the companies then to carry out.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Seah Kian Peng asked quite eloquently yesterday whether we are asking too much of the proposed legislation and too little of ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Amid the heat and dust generated by this vigorous debate on this Bill, we must not lose sight of the larger point and, that is, legislation is necessary but it is by no means sufficient in the fight against online falsehoods.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Ultimately, our first and most important line of defence against online falsehoods is a well-informed and discerning citizenry, equipped with tools to combat online falsehoods.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The SC highlighted the role of trusted fact-checking initiatives in combatting deliberate online falsehoods, and recommended that different media organisations, and partners from other industries, consider establishing a coalition in Singapore to debunk falsehoods swiftly and credibly, as well as to provide support to such fact-checking initiatives.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Government agrees that it is important to have such fact-checking initiatives in society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: However, such initiatives should go beyond fact-checking to ensure that the discourse is authentic and responsible, and citizens are well-informed of the principles of engagement.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Over time, through the collaborative efforts of different parties and agencies, we envisage a tighter nexus between the different entities, including academia and journalists in Singapore, so that high-quality information can reach the general public to engender greater understanding of current affairs and complex issues.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These efforts will also be aligned with the Government’s commitment to support the growth of a robust and vibrant information ecosystem, with a variety of entities contributing to the overall effort.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To do so, we will continue to support ground-up efforts by interested members of the community and student groups and invest in resources and efforts to build up digital literacy.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: There have been many community efforts already in this regard.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Dr Intan Mokhtar spoke about the need for media literacy for the young, and digital literacy for the elderly.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Various Government agencies, such as the National Library Board, Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Defence, provide information literacy resources to students, adults and seniors.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Government also launched Digital Defence as the sixth pillar of Total Defence this year, with the call to be secure, alert and responsible online.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Media Literacy Council runs the Better Internet Campaign and provides seed funding for youth-led initiatives to address digital literacy and cyber safety and security.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: There are also collaborations among our local universities, tech companies and media companies to enhance media and information literacy, such as the hackathon called, quite dramatically, “Fake News Must Die” and it was held in late 2017 supported by Google, our institutes of higher learning and mainstream media.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Over time and taken together, these measures will empower citizens to make informed decisions on their consumption of information and to be more discerning on multifaceted issues, thereby helping to grow an informed citizenry.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We also continue to have constructive discussions with the tech industry on a broader range of issues of mutual interest.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I hope that all Singaporeans will join us in this important effort, give their full support to the intent of this legislation and the impact it seeks to have in raising the quality and integrity of discourse in the digital realm and help to raise the digital readiness and strengthen the Digital Defence capabilities of our society.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And I hope that this also illustrates why I feel that the approach this Bill takes is, indeed, the right approach to protecting us all from online falsehoods.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It was not too long ago that healthcare professionals and ordinary citizens alike hailed the Internet as the great equaliser by helping to reduce information asymmetry between healthcare providers and their patients.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While many doctors were initially apprehensive when their patients became so much better informed due to the amount of medical information available online, healthcare professionals gradually learnt to welcome this and appreciate how this made the doctor-patient relationship more equal and more participative.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But it soon became apparent that the Internet, like any powerful tool, can be a double-edged sword.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Medical misinformation and outright falsehoods began gaining a larger and larger footprint in the datasphere, and it was exasperating to many healthcare providers that such falsehoods online were significantly impacting the health-seeking behaviour and ultimately the health of their patients, so much so that life and limb were at risk.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In an op ed piece earlier this year by Dr Haider Warraich, with the byline “Fake news threatens our democracy.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But fake medical news threatens our lives”, he notes that and, I quote, “While misinformation has been the object of great attention in politics, medical misinformation might have an even greater body count.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As is true with fake news in general, medical lies tend to spread further than truths on the Internet – and they have very real repercussions”.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   	I am sure that Members of this House are aware of the many examples of fake health news online that have led to very real harm.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is also a lot of false information online about the dangers of various types of vaccines.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In recent months, some residents have approached me with their concerns about the safety of vaccination programmes that we have been advocating for public health reasons.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some expressed their belief that vaccination could lead to serious mental or neurological damage, others were convinced that many vaccines contain poisons.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When asked about the source of this information, they all indicated articles they had read on the Internet, or information circulated via WhatsApp or short message services (SMS).

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is unsurprising, because such untruths cannot be circulated in print or other physical media as there are regulations against the promulgation of such false information.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Prof Heidi Larson, who is a public health expert at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, wrote in the journal Nature that: "The next major outbreak of a fatal strain of influenza or something else will not be due to a lack of preventive technologies.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Instead, emotional contagion, digitally enabled, could erode trust in vaccines so much as to render them moot.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This deluge of conflicting and manipulated information on social media should be recognised as a global public health threat." Like other Members before me, I do not think that this Bill will be an impediment to free speech, nor should it have any chilling effect on public discourse or creativity.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I believe it will actually accomplish the opposite.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The problem we have now is that in the online arena, those that shout the loudest, trumpet that which is sensationalist, novel or frightening regardless of its veracity, will garner the most attention and drown out other voices, leading to an imbalance which actually prevents equitable and meaningful discussion.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A lie is a lie, no matter how much you may wish it to be true, and no matter how you paint it, and the distinction between truth and falsehood is simple where it counts, in matters of life and death, and of sickness and health.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Particularly in issues of healthcare, there is really no need for committee after committee, council after council, or for the Courts to decide what is true and what is not.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This yardstick does not apply to truth in advertising or standards in claims about medical treatments offline, so why should offline or online untruths be spared?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, I feel that the same should apply to online information and also misinformation about healthcare.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Much of this information online is deliberate and carefully crafted and cultivated.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This new disease on online space, as hon Member Ms Sun Xueling has so eloquently put in her speech yesterday, needs a targeted yet calibrated response with legislation, such as the one we are debating today, or these bad actors of the social media space will gain the upper hand to the detriment of us all.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is, of course, important that we continue to invest in public education, but the general public cannot be always relied on to tell what is fake news and what is not.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If there is a physical threat to public security or public health, an Executive decision needs to be made as to how to counter this threat, and certainly decision by committee or by prior application to the Courts would not work.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is because like most situations in healthcare, prevention is always better than cure.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Once a medical lie has entered the public domain, it takes root very quickly and becomes very hard to eradicate, if not impossible.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Posting the real facts alongside the falsehood will probably be of little use.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is so much more powerful and engaging to read a snippet of alarmist fake medical news, and believe it to be true due to the strong human element, than to believe the reams of boring but rigorous scientific and medical evidence that can be posted alongside it.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, there is news circulating online about how a promising young person was reduced to a cripple some weeks after receiving a vaccine, and how the vaccine was responsible for her horrific condition.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Imagine if we were just to post alongside this untrue article the links to the many scientific papers showing it to be untrue, I wonder how many would think otherwise or have their opinions changed as a result of this corrective posting.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Way back during the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) epidemic, for instance, what if there was fake news online that going to a quarantined area or to a hospital would lead to loss of life, or maybe things like eating white salt would be able to cure you of SARS?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If this was allowed to spread unchecked on the Internet, how many lives would have been lost?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In fact, it is very far from the nuclear option that hon Member Mr Png Eng Huat just spoke about.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: From the perspective of an academic, which I think in some areas of my job roles I do consider myself as an academic, it has always been the case that when we do research or publish papers about various aspects of science or research, these are already subject to many rules and regulations.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And the veracity of such publications, if there are erroneous conclusions or problems with the data, this is subject to very real scrutiny and there is already a due process for corrections or even retractions.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, such avenues do not exist if such papers are published online, which is one of the criticisms for the emerging breadth of so-called research articles that are sprouting online.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, if I were to take some data that had been rejected by all of the highly regarded and respected medical journals, and decided to take it in my own hands and publish it online, and many people could read it, there is actually very little recourse for the scientific community or for various agencies to be able to correct such falsehood.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have had some rather bizarre images ranging from decapitations to usage of phrases like "nuclear", "chilling", "afraid", "fear" – it makes you wonder sometimes whether we are watching a very disturbing B-grade, post-apocalyptic movie.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have also heard some very compelling, logical and rational arguments as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I do have some points of clarification I would like to raise in my speech.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A key tenet of POFMA is that deliberate online falsehood and misinformation campaigns will undermine social trust among communities, lead to the diminution of confidence in our public institutions and inflict harm on public interest.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, clause 4 of the Bill clearly spells out instances where public interest will be compromised and that the Act can be invoked when such instances occur.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While clause 4 spells out these instances, it also provides the Government some discretion to act under POFMA.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, I would imagine that while falsehoods that deliberately promote ill-will among different communities would warrant the Government to invoke POFMA to "prevent feelings of enmity, hatred and ill-will between different groups of persons", other forms of falsehoods and manipulations might be less clear cut.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, it is stated in point (f) in clause 4 that POFMA could be exercised "to prevent diminution of public confidence in the performance of any duty or function of, or in the exercise of any power by the government”.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another point I would like to raise pertains to the appeal mechanism that goes via the Courts.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The present Act provides an eventual avenue for appeals against the Government’s decision to be made to the Courts, after an appeal to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There has been some criticism that this might result in an appeals process that is too overwhelming and even financially prohibitive.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I realised that this would then raise the issue of who would appoint the members of this tribunal, as if the tribunal was appointed and approved by the Executive branch of the Government, then it would ultimately be handling an appeal on a decision made by that same Executive branch.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nevertheless, I do appreciate the fact that the Minister for Law has stated that the appeals process via the Courts will be kept as affordable and simple as possible, and I trust that the Government will do periodic reviews of this process to ensure that it always remains so.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to be cognisant about the slow-drip effect of deliberate online falsehood on our social fabric and how it could erode trust between communities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, I believe that the Government has the responsibility to nip deliberate attempts to undermine social cohesion before these attempts can take root.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I also feel that we need to get the balance right between making the right decision when it comes to curtailing deliberate online falsehoods, and being judicious in how those decisions are made.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: From developing to developed countries, they have seeded distrust, sparked violence and shaped elections.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore is right to take a proactive stance against the spread of online falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we do so, I hope we can take a measured approach that balances the urgency of combating falsehoods with the costs to society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As the Minister has already addressed many of my concerns I was going to raise, and as many Members have raised many of the points I was going to raise – that is the luxury of being the last speaker – I just have three quick points for further clarifications.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would we also direct that the appeal be heard within a certain timeframe?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that it might be difficult to provide an estimate, but would be grateful for a rough estimate of cost and timeline.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the Ministry has said that the Bill does not cover satire or comedy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this exclusion is nowhere to be found in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not uncommon for satire or comedy to exaggerate or invent facts by intention.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, online falsehoods have sometimes been perpetuated, for instance, by state actors in the guise of comedy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, Sir, the fight against the spread of falsehood must also be the fight for the spread of truth.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The battle against falsehoods demands not only the stick but also the carrot.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Having the tools to react promptly to falsehood is important.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the Government cannot constantly be on the backfoot playing whack-a-mole whenever another falsehood pops up.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we want people to present the truth, we must demonstrate readiness to give the truth and then the data they need.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Instead of being reactive, we can be proactive in spreading the truth by helping people who would like to report on the truth, to obtain Government data needed to verify their facts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It can do so by sharing data and information more frequently and in greater detail.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Other countries have done so through the freedom of information laws.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These include those closest to us, such as China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Thailand.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While Hong Kong has not legislated on the freedom of information, it has a Code of Access to Information.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is the formal framework for access to information held by government departments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Code requires civil servants routinely, or on request, to provide information unless there are specific reasons for not doing so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, there are procedures for review of complaint if the provisions of the Code have not been properly applied.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our concern may be that excessive openers may compromise national security.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, there are common exceptions in freedom of information laws around the world, including national security, public safety, prevention of criminal activities and personal privacy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The freedom of information laws has been implemented to varying degrees of success and effectiveness in these countries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With more than 80 case studies available, there are ample lessons that we can learn from both the successes and the failures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The SC has suggested that the Government should study the experiences of countries with freedom of information legislation and ombudsmen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of the points raised by Members have also been addressed by Minister Ong Ye Kung and Minister Iswaran.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Vikram Nair and Mr Henry Kwek asked some questions relating to other parts of the Bill that were not covered in the opening speech, either by myself or Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But let me take Members briefly through these other provisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Such a website can be "declared" by the Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The owner or operator of the website will be required to put up a notice warning users that the website has been declared and the website cannot then be promoted using digital ad tools.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Henry Kwek asked about the defence of "reasonable excuse" and how it would work in practice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Clause 27, in particular, sets out factors that the Court must consider when deciding if the defence is available to an intermediary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are the state of the art at that point in time, the cost of complying with the Direction relative to the means available to the Internet intermediary, and any other relevant factor.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The bigger an intermediary is, the more it can be expected to invest in keeping its systems safe for those who use it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This also ensures that regulation does not become a barrier to entry for new entrants, thereby further cementing the dominance of the large incumbents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it should not be seen as licence for non-compliance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An intermediary that does not currently have the technical features to comply with the Direction, does not automatically have reasonable excuse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If that were so, an intermediary can just deliberately refrain from adopting product features that are needed, so that it does not have to comply with the Directions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that would subvert the intent of the defence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why the Bill spells out these relevant factors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the Court will look at all the circumstances and decide what would be reasonable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Vikram Nair asked if this Bill will cover past statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Any statement after the Act, assuming it is passed, comes into force, will be covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It could also cover future statements that may be made by reference to something said in the past, or statements which repeat past statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Irene Quay asked about the relationship of this Bill with the Defamation Act and the Internal Security Act (ISA).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Defamation Act deals in the private law sphere, with damage to reputation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, if someone says you are corrupt, then if it is not true, you can sue to clear your name.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Internal Security Act (ISA) deals with threats to national security.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This Bill deals with falsehoods, to mitigate the impact and deter those who deliberately peddle in falsehoods, with the specific framework that is different from ISA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prof Lim Sun Sun agrees with the need for legislation but refers to a "collaborative framework" within the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will be Codes of Practice for upstream regulation of tech companies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think I can refer Prof Lim to the SC's findings on the question of regulating tech companies, and it was quite unequivocal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I can give the Member the paragraph references – paragraphs 406, 436, 476, 536.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the SC looked at the evidence that was presented and it was quite clear that regulation was necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we look at what the UK Digital Secretary Jeremy Wright said, and I quote, "The era of self-regulation for online companies is over.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Voluntary actions from industry to tackle online harms have not been applied consistently or gone far enough." And, of course, Mr Zuckerberg himself, one day before this Bill was tabled said, and I quote, "I believe we need a more serious active role for governments and regulators ...

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I believe we need new regulation in four areas: harmful content, election integrity, privacy and data portability." Assoc Prof Walter Theseira articulated what the three Nominated Members of Parliament accept – the definitions of falsehood and of public interest in the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They accept that the Executive must have the power to act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And they accept that trying to introduce judicial or independent oversight first, risks harm in the event of an imminent threat.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think Ms Anthea Ong said that the Independent Council proposed by the Nominated Members of Parliament was not meant to intervene with the decision-making process set out in the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As for the actual points in the Notice of Amendments, I do not think Members want me to repeat the points I made yesterday.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, a number of comments were made on the definition of falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Mr Pritam Singh asked, fact and comment divisions not so clear; false or misleading, in whole or in part, is very wide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng talked about satire and comedy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked about efforts to educate Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Dennis Tan talked about "misleading" according to whose standards.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I say something according to my own views, but what if the Minister or Court interprets your meaning differently?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why should I be subject to corrections or takedowns?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us say, Mr Dennis Tan, you put out a statement that three Chinese Police officers raped a Malay girl and the Police are covering it up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, you refuse to put a correction on the basis that it is not misleading according to your standards.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There have got to be objective standards in these things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think, as a lawyer, you will understand that quite easily.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or for that matter, an actual case, Mr Nicholas Lim, that he was not charged because his parents were influential.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think you know who his parents are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if you continue to insist your statement that his parents were influential and that is why the Police did not take action, I think there must be some objective standards.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The law deals with objectivity in all these areas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Anthea Ong gave an illustration about an NGO that has evidence from a sexual assault victim, was unwilling to disclose the same details to the authorities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And Mr Chen Show Mao made a similar point as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the definition of what constitutes a "statement of fact", I have gone through in some detail and so have others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has been laid down by the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I will quote the Court of Appeal which has said the test for distinguishing between "comment" and "statement of fact" is an objective one.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I quote here, "whether an ordinary, reasonable reader on reading the whole article would understand the words as comment  or   statements of fact".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts are equipped to apply the legal test and have regularly done so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Nominated Members of Parliament, for example, in their Explanatory Note, have said they do not propose amendments to the definition of a "statement of fact".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And before the SC, law academics gave evidence about the law, including professors from NUS and the Dean of the Singapore Management University (SMU) Law School.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam's question about education, about what is covered and not covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Yes, of course, that will continue to be done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And Mr Louis Ng's question on satire and comedy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I gave some examples yesterday about how parody can be converted and put out as fact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think the Member is talking about that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Dennis Tan also asked about falsehood in general.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said "diminution of public confidence" is not found elsewhere in the world and will prevent bona fide criticism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would put this point in the same league as the earlier point and would ask what the Member means by "bona fide criticism" when falsehoods are generated and pushed out by bots, trolls, fake accounts and all the other mechanisms that I spoke about yesterday.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As a lawyer, Mr Dennis Tan will understand what is bona fide criticism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Certainly, this will not be considered by any Court, by anyone reasonable Court, as bona fide criticism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this debate, this Bill, I hope it is clear that we are not dealing with bona fide criticisms; we are dealing with falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh has some points about clause 4(f) on public confidence and cited as an example the recent discussion involving permits that Nas Daily obtained to hold a fan meet in Botanic Gardens.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think because his speech came immediately after Mr Edwin Tong's speech, he may not have had the time to look at the illustrations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I specifically referred to it in my speech as well yesterday precisely about this incident, and I gave various illustrations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I will just refer Mr Pritam Singh to that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I will also caution generally against taking statements issued before this Bill comes into force and trying to compare and take them as if they come within the rubric of this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those statements were issued without reference to the terms of this Bill for several years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You should not take those statements and say, "Ah!

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Therefore, this comes within this Bill." They are different.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh also takes issue with clause 4 being non-exhaustive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I had set out the existing legal position in considerable detail in my opening speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And there are many statutory provisions, including the BA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And there are very practical reasons for keeping the list non-exhaustive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The SC report states that as falsehoods appear in a broad spectrum of circumstances, if you look at paragraph 538.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we provide a closed list, then people will know precisely what the parameters are, and can work around them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we talked about foreign actors, other bad people, and the point really is, public interest is a second limb.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have got to prove the falsehoods in the first place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think once you say it is false, there is really not much argument if it impacts on public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you have got to prove public interest in some way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the Courts will have the final say on the matter, if challenged.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Darryl David has asked for clarity of what would be considered a diminution of public confidence in our institutions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Yesterday, I referred to the Yellow Vest movement trying to erode trust in the police.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The letter suggested that Sweden was prepared to do so, to make people believe their governments were not above interfering with justice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is a serious diminution of public confidence and ultimately eroding trust.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Swedish police had said no such thing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The effect was to suggest that the police did not have things under control, that they cannot be relied on to protect society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can make those comments, but if you want to refer to facts, then you should get your facts right.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if you were to make a comment, "Swedish police do not have things under control" or "Singapore Police do not have things under control", you are welcome to say that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That would not be covered by the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if you say, by specific reference, that these are "no go" areas, and that is either true or it is not true.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Darryl David again spoke about Advisory Council, but I hear his latest remarks, and I think Prof Lim Sun Sun also said something similar.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Prof Lim's suggestion was Advisory Panel to Minister who makes a final order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are many examples of how quickly these things move.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Nominated Member of Parliament Mohamed Irshad spoke about what happened in Myanmar.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This led to two days of violence, and left people dead.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Within 24 hours, 14 Buddhist temples were burnt and destroyed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another was the falsehood which Mr Pritam Singh referred to – the cryptocurrency's founder had died in a car crash.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If it was on the stock exchange, and say, it relates to a bank in Singapore, and such a rumour, then there would be some public interest in going to deal with it, in terms of how stock exchanges and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) deal with these issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are things where immediate Executive action will be necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not mean that the Ministers will move or act without consideration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The amount of consideration depends on the time that they can take, but it has to be quick.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is one of the reasons why it is different Ministers, because, one day it could deal with Finance, one day it could deal with Health, one day it could deal with the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF), and another day it could deal with the Police.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the domain experts, Ministers advised by civil servants, will have to decide quickly and open themselves up for challenge, if there is a challenge and it has all got to be done in public, quite apart from questions in Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Other Members, including Mr Christopher de Souza, Mr Cedric Foo, Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Saktiandi Supaat, have mentioned the need for speed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some Members have suggested some other alternate third party to have the power to decide whether to allow falsehoods to carry on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have a third party, the Government deals with the consequences often times of the falsehood.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you then separate the responsibility of dealing with the consequences, from the power to stop the falsehoods in the first place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the Executive exercises a power and makes itself accountable to the Courts and to Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a completely defensible, open system that places no great power within the Executive and, in that context, I think all the nine WP Members of Parliament's speeches are remarkable for the fact that they do not deal head-on with the point I made, which is that the powers here are narrower than the powers that currently exist.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the Armageddon that we were threatened with if this Bill comes into law, I am still trying to see the logical flow of that argument.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng spoke about cost and Mr Dennis Tan asked about judicial review applications and costs, and Mr Murali Pillai talked about parallel procedures providing for judicial oversight.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Quite a lot of the points I wanted to make about the speeches by the WP Members of Parliament have already been made by Mr Murali Pillai in a very lucid way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng's concerns about the cost of appeals, I have already set out in some detail the process and what will happen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But when we talk about judicial review, that is quite a separate exercise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Appeals on question of fact should be fairly straightforward.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And after that, for normal fees to be paid to Court and for the Court to have ultimate discretion to decide who should pay the cost.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because if someone carries on and on and on for several days of argument unreasonably, that is something the Court should take into account, for example.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked about the cost regime for judicial review and an expedited process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think these are very different processes for appeal on truth versus falsehoods versus a judicial review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a whole body of administrative law, principles, and that has to be dealt with – judicial review – in the usual way, and could involve very detailed arguments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about the risk of inconsistency in parallel tracks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think this is not the only area of the law where that occurs and there are procedures that the Courts can adopt to resolve that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Leon Perera, I think they have conflated Directions with criminal punishments, if I am not wrong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Directions simply require you to put up corrections, or take down the material as appropriate, in an appropriate case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said yesterday, it could appear in your article, "Look, there is a correction required on this because this article contains untruths or inaccuracies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And for the truth, go to such and such a website".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Chen Show Mao had suggested that penalties under this Bill are harsh.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would say the existing penalties are comparable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Mr Melvin Yong asked for clarification on what consequences there will be for those who inadvertently forward falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You may receive a Correction from the platform to inform you.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a falsehood that has travelled to 20,000 people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does it make sense for the Government to go and look for 20,000 people and ask them to do things?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Bill is primarily aimed at tech platforms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the tech platforms are to carry the Corrections and push it down to the people who have received the original falsehood.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will be questions on what technology allows and does not allow.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is the primary, in essence, focus of the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And in some cases, the tech platforms could be asked to "take down" and ensure the "take down" applies across the board.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It simply does not make sense to go and find and look for thousands of people and individually go to each one of them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It makes sense if there is one creator of falsehoods, deliberately creating and sitting somewhere and pushing out falsehoods, that person can be dealt with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Irene Quay and Dr Intan Mokhtar asked about other legislation and how they apply.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar also asked about academics and assurance that academics and researchers can continue to enjoy academic freedom.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about plans to assure well-meaning members of society that they would continue to contribute to meaningful civic discussions, and Mr Alex Yam said some of the constituents he has spoken with have asked if the Bill will cover academic research.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My colleague, Minister Ong Ye Kung, gave a comprehensive response on academia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think I really have much to add.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On your specific question, Mr Alex Yam, you asked about historians and mentioned a specific example, Operation Coldstore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us say a historian says, "Communists did not intend to conduct armed insurrection in Singapore" and he relies on some documents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He interprets them one way; that is his opinion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But supposing that there is no such document, and he says that there is such a document, and that he manufactured his claim.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But say, he refers to figures in the documents and there are no such figures and he just invented it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is false, so the Courts will easily be able to deal with all of these.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or say, he gave an interpretation of a document but on oath he subsequently admits that his interpretation of the documents was misleading, and that he had given an untrue characterisation and inaccurate reflection of the documents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In such a situation, of course, the academic's reliance on the underlying documents, based on his own admission, would be false.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The remedy in such situations – put up a clarification, for example, that he has admitted that his statements were misleading, an untrue characterisation, inaccurate reflection of the documents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ultimately, it depends on an objective interpretation, as I said earlier about the Courts, but that does not preclude challenging conventional wisdom, challenging established thinking.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira asked about the scope of his review of statements that the Government has made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not have the precise figures, but he said that there was a small number of cases where the interpretations were based on facts, rather than facts themselves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But also, as I said just now, we must not assume that all those statements in the past which have referred to a variety of things, as if this Bill has been drafted with those statements or those statements had anticipated this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Quite a few of those statements may well not come within the rubric of this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Anyway, public interest has got to be established, and it does not mean that each time the Government responds, automatically, public interest was involved or had been involved in the past.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That could have been made with a number of considerations in mind.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it does not mean that, automatically, the standard for public interest set out in the Bill would have been invoked.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have not looked at it but these are sort of commonsensical points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And there was a question on Government transparency and Freedom of Information Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Irene Quay asked about this and Mr Louis Ng asked about it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is one of my favourite topics – Freedom of Information Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Mr Louis Ng said that a number of countries, including China, Pakistan, Zimbabwe, they all have a Freedom of Information Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would say we should consider and this is a serious issue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Who uses the Freedom of Information Act and what has it been used for?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I am making some serious points here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You first start looking at the requests and I will tell you what sort of requests have been made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Going to the UK, these are some of the requests that were made: (a) total amount spent on Ferrero Rocher chocolates in UK embassies; (b) how many toilet rolls were used during Tony Blair’s administration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Imagine the civil servants would have to go and calculate that across all government agencies in the 10 years that Tony Blair was Prime Minister; (c) what kind of tea is drunk at the Ministry of Defence?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was the Deputy Prime Minister; (e) registration numbers of all vintage lorries held by local authorities; (f) eligible bachelors in the police force between the ages of 35 and 49 by someone who said that she liked men in uniform; (g) statistics of reported sex with sheep and any other animal in Wales, if possible, since records began.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If it can be shown that it improves governance, we should have it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I quote you Francis Fukuyama: "Legislators and officials must preserve deliberative space, just as families need to protect their privacy when debating their finances, or how to deal with a wayward child.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And they need to be able to do so without donning a straight-jacket of rules specifying how they must talk to each other, and to citizens.” So, you will get a lot of requests which are very odd, to say the least.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Civil servants will have to deal with all these requests at taxpayers’ expense.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if you look at the countries and you look at who uses them, it is not the average man in the street.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, the average man or woman in the street uses it some of the time but, mostly, it actually ends up privileging and giving more advantage to those who are better organised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Businesses go to the Freedom of Information Act to find out lots of information to help their business.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Lawyers, lobbyists, journalists – these are the people who put in the bulk of the requests.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And when I give you the examples, it is immediately clear to you why.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is that the best way of improving governance?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You are all representatives who are elected by the people, some of you are appointed as Nominated Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But you are here in a representative Parliament which is sovereign.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if you look at the questions that have been raised in this Parliament just in the last two sessions, February to May, we debated since the Budget Debate two Private Members' Motions, one Adjournment Motion by Mr Pritam Singh, data security, election procedures, CPF payouts, racial and religious harmony, regard for women, including protection, development of the Malay/Muslim community, long-term care financing, mental health, bilateral relations with Malaysia, foreign policy positioning, safe use of personal mobility devices, management of stock exchange, power failures, NUS.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Anything that is happening out there, we are discussing them here, month by month.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you look at the number of questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you cannot have time, you do not have enough time for the oral Parliamentary Questions, you convert it to Written question, it has to be answered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, again, if it is not answered, there has got to be a good reason.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Questions have been raised about Mr Pang – Committees of Inquiry have been held, Government has been questioned on the findings; it is held accountable, it has provided information.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, if your residents have questions, or anybody else has questions, they can approach the Members of Parliament, they can approach the Nominated Members of Parliament. "Representative democracy" means that at your level, you go through those questions and if somebody comes and asks you, "I want to know who are all the eligible women in SAF?", I do not think "representative democracy" means you will come here and ask that question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if you did, I doubt very much if you will remain a Member of Parliament for very long after that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there is a certain responsibility on you to mediate the questions that your residents ask and then come here and ask sensible questions, ask questions that matter for governance, ask questions that matter for society at large and ignore the frivolous questions and, indeed, explain to your resident why those questions ought not to be asked.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That makes a lot of sense, rather than an Act and legislation which has, firstly, tied up resources.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us not talk theory, let us talk reality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have given you examples in the UK from the Head of Civil Service and very senior people in Australia about how civil servants have started behaving, how discussions within government have been tied up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And second, the kind of requests that are being made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can you imagine any Member here asking about how many toilet rolls the Ministry of Home Affairs may have used up?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why should it take up my civil servants' time?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if you did, if you did ask me, I will ask you to explain why you are asking it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, let us have some faith in representative democracy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have the institutions and we are using them well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do not need to run after new institutions just because the UK, Australia, China, Pakistan and Zimbabwe have them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, there were questions about what if Government itself spreads falsehoods?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is some argument about how that legislation ought to be.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But then to say, "Oh, well, what about other aspects, what about Government?" It is not really an answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And assuming the Government puts out a falsehood, are there no remedies?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if there is no credible explanation, what happens to the Minister or Ministry that puts out that falsehood?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is what a debate in Parliament means.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is equally important to see what he did not say.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The report sets out the problem and it made recommendations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government and Parliament have spent the last 18 months considering the problem.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang, I think, first does not disagree that this is a serious problem.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I did not hear him disagree with that either.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Nevertheless, he says the Government will amass more powers under the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will say, "How so?" It is directly contrary to what I have said and contrary to what he seems to accept, that the powers under the Bill are narrower.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He knows also that the current powers are quite broad.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, he said today, the Government can shut down Facebook.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, he knows the current powers are very broad.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has also suggested that making an order under the Bill is like chopping off a head first and then reporting to the Emperor.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is typical of Mr Low Thia Khiang, it is very colourful.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is an original article, a correction is carried.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The head on the shoulders continues to be there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even the hands are there, they are not cut off.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the hands can be on the computer to continue to type.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And they can complain in public and the person can go to Court and the Minister will have to defend himself in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even takedown, the same process, even if there is a takedown.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, of course, proportionality has to be shown as to why it is a takedown, as opposed to corrections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is like shining a torchlight, a flood light, on falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Minister is given the torchlight to shine.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The person who is upset can decide to go to Court and nobody's head is chopped off, nobody's hands are chopped off.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is the problem when we ask for transparency – I mean, it is one of the key tenets of the WP – is this not transparency?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You put up an article, the Government says this is not correct, you carry a correction, let your readers judge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would say a First-World Parliament should deal with the evidence and facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is the elephant in the room that nobody has answered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang says this Bill is going to have a chilling effect and he makes a passing reference to a coffee shop – I do not think he meant it in this context – he said speech is no longer confined to coffee shops.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That immediately reminded me of another speech by Mr Low.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have a great deal of respect for him, in particular, his political skills.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has been in the House for almost as long as me and perhaps we both immediately think in terms of coffee shops, which is, of course, a key node of local community and talk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I think it will be useful to look at what he had said previously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think he will remember three years ago, the debate on the Administration of Justice (Protection) Act (AOJPA) Bill in this House.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Low said, "This Bill" – referring to that Bill – "covers talk at coffee shops, makes the Government the sole decision-maker of public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Elements are similar to the Internal Security Act (ISA)"; all actually completely inaccurate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said, and I quote, "I stand by what I say, based on my understanding of the effect and implication of the Bill if passed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For instance, there is a definition of publication and according to clause 2 of the Bill, a person is said to have published something when he communicates even orally or even if it is just one member of the public, so that I think it applies to people who talk, discuss at coffee shops." And then he said, "Madam, what I am most uncomfortable with is clause 3(4) of the Bill that gives the Government the right to make statements and allows the Government to become the sole interpreter and decision-maker of what constitutes public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And this, I smell a similar element in the ISA." My response at that time, I said this is a strange case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A Minister for Law who puts up the Bill after extensive consultation with the Courts, I kept saying ad nauseam that the law was the same as before it was – common law – and it is intended to be the same on those clauses that you referred to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said the law is different in respect of the clauses that you referred to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But he was unable to explain how, why the Bill changed the law, as Mr Low claimed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There were other clauses where there was a change and I explained in that long debate what the changes were and where it was the same.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I had said during AOJPA, how does a person sitting in a coffee shop in Hougang, saying that something is wrong in the Courts, how does that statement impact on either the Judge, the witnesses or the proceedings?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You are trying to frighten people unnecessarily saying that people in coffee shops now cannot talk after AOJPA was passed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And they cannot sit there and have their coffee and talk about Court cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Coffee shops, I think, have grown louder since then.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think it has prevented talk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, after all that talk of chill and fear, I can tell you coffee shops in Yishun do not even think of AOJPA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I am sure it is the same in Hougang and Aljunied and everywhere else in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Quite vibrant and we want it to be so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, what Mr Low says about this Bill amassing power is not quite right and Mr Low must know that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just as he would have known that what he said about the AOJPA actually was not accurate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, what is the purpose of saying this?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because people listening to Mr Low might be misled?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said that if one says the Government introduced the PGP and MGP to buy votes, that may be covered by the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or to say that older Singaporeans are unable to accept a non-Chinese Prime Minister would be covered and can be used selectively by the Government to target statements by the Government's opponents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I say to Mr Low, come on, you must know, everybody here knows, none of these are covered by the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, let us have a debate that deals with the terms of the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us not try and get people misled by using examples which have nothing to do with the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are all comments, even under the Telecoms Act which was in existence all this while.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It really should not have been made without basis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Low is not a lawyer, so maybe please bear with me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: POHA has got, primarily, provisions on harassment, people getting harassed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Low, sit back and think about it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How can the Government be harassed in the context of POHA?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How is it possible for the Government to be harassed?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the Government has never claimed that it can be harassed, nor has it brought a single action on the basis of it being harassed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we had tried it, we would have been laughed out of Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There was a subsequent exchange between the Law Ministry and the WP where we said harassment provisions cannot apply to the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But POHA, the Act, also contains section 15, which does not have anything to do with harassment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has got to do with statements and refers to statements and persons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked me, does this Bill apply to corporates?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I said, the Interpretation Act will apply.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Interpretation Act has got to apply and, depending on the context, it can apply to corporates or it may not apply to corporates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Obviously, when it comes to harassment, it cannot apply to the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is public, it is transparent, this is rule of law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We intended and we believed, but if the Court disagrees with us, we just accept it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we have never suggested or tried to rely on any of the harassment provisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It would be absurd for us to try and rely on the harassment provisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On taking people to Court, Mr Low Thia Khiang and Mr Pritam Singh said Ministers can make decisions but how often will people take Ministers to Court?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The first point, I said orders are, as a matter of looking at the framework, likely to be made primarily against tech companies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second point, there is a very serious logical fallacy at the heart of this point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, each time the Government wants to do something, somebody has to be sued whether or not the person wants to go to Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People, they put up a falsehood, maybe they did not really, after getting the notice, they just want to accept it, they really do not want the fuss of having to go to Court, but you will require them to be sued and brought to Court, every single time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is the difference between your proposal and the Government's proposal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government's proposal – we intervene, we ask for clarifications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In some cases, we ask for a takedown.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The person who is on the other end will decide, "Am I going to challenge?" And he knows he has got three days free in Court, he knows that on the issue of falsehoods, he does not even need a lawyer, so it is very low cost and he has got to decide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If he wants to challenge, he can challenge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If he does not want to challenge, he does not have to challenge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Which is better for the citizen do you think?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, how does your proposal make sense if your true objection is, well, you know, people are reluctant to go to Court?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then you should be supporting the Government's position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Leave it to the people who want to go to Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And do you know we are talking theory here?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I told Members yesterday a large number of these people would not be found.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What Mr Lee said is very relevant here and was in many ways an inspiration for the central thinking.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When people say things which are false and hide, what is the best remedy?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You shine a powerful light, the light of truth, to show up the falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People then can decide for themselves what is true and what is false.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is that not a good thing to have?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Surely, you do not want these people who put out falsehoods to hide and mislead others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you want to shine a powerful light.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That power already exists and broader powers exist now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I explained why we are putting up this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is primarily to shine a light on the various falsehoods that circulate so that people can understand the truth, so that the infrastructure of fact would be powerful, so that democracy itself is protected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think that has got to be read together with Mr Leon Perera's clarifications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You will have to bring a person to Court every single time, and that is even without considering other issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How long will it take to find the originator?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Supposing you have rules which deal with parties and service, and ex parte and inter partes hearing, and when you look for the originator and when you do not, it gets very complex.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Are you sure that it can be done within a matter of hours?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No real explanation from the WP on an important point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not as if the Court is ousted in one approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the Government's approach, you get certainty of speed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The respondent can decide if he wants to go to Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, how is your proposal better than what the Government has proposed?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh made the point about fact and opinion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said Ministers make the decision but, not accustomed to applying jurisprudence, would they all come and consult me?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ministers make their decisions, Ministries make their decisions based on the law and there is maybe advice by inhouse counsel, which there are in some Ministries, and by AGC, where necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It all depends on the speed with which they have to act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
