text: They have to weigh the importance of acting immediately, the amount of advice they need, and they will be advised by their civil servants.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they get it wrong, they get overruled by the Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh gave two examples, of CPF and Mr Nicholas Lim.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said the corrections have helped; he asserted it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does he know for a fact that the corrections have helped completely cure the original falsehoods?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does he know how many people continue to believe the falsehoods without knowledge of the clarifications?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People who believe in the falsehoods exist in different universes from people who read the clarifications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If everyone was like you, Assoc Prof Goh, we would not need a lot of the laws we have in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But unfortunately, there are people – well-meaning people, highly educated people – who do not keep up with current affairs to the level that you do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You cannot blame them; people lead busy lives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I had explained yesterday, the SC Report goes into some considerable detail – heuristic tendencies, shortcuts, depends on who you get it from, how authentic the source looks, and nowadays things can be made to look very authentic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It looks as if it is from CNN, Washington Post.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I gave you examples like New York Times and Washington Post who were themselves misled and published some fake stories as real.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh did not explain what is the problem with carrying the clarifications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Helps transparency rather than putting in terms of Armageddon.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in the first place, you got to show that it was a falsehood.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if it is a falsehood, 4(f) is the second gate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What do you stand to gain by protecting falsehoods?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You expressed a lot of concern that, well, pushing this down may not be useful.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Leave that to the judgement of the people who want to push it down.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You may not agree with it philosophically but that is not a point of principle.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The point of principle is that it is a falsehood that needs to be clarified.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we believe it is necessary, then the next question is proportionality and the Courts, if necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are not seeking to force down orthodoxy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we are debating at two different levels.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are talking about whether Mr Nicholas Lim's father was influential.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is not a question of orthodoxy; it is a question of fact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You bring in arguments of public health – how do they apply?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I repeat myself – is it true, is it false, is it an opinion?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh also suggested there is no need for speed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It may not look urgent but if it sinks in, that is difficult to dislodge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, even when it does not look urgent, you know the virality of falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You need to intervene quickly to break the virality because the people who read the falsehoods may not necessarily read the corrections or the clarifications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have seen this happen over and over again.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a well-known saying, and I quote, "A lie can travel halfway around the world while the truth is still putting on its shoes".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is the difference between truth and falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why you need to intervene quickly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong spoke yesterday about the different universes that saw the truth and falsehoods on the Macron campaign.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All the WP Members pivot in their speech very quickly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They pivot very quickly to the broad points on free speech and that, with respect, overlooks completely the point that what we are talking about is falsehoods, turbo-charged by bots, trolls, fake accounts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, unfortunately, this debate, for all the rhetoric, there has been no engagement on the key issues on why there should be free speech in this area.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why are these things entitled to free speech?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That, in essence, is the only difference and I have dealt with that earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It comes down, after these two days, to that one difference, really.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Png Eng Huat's speech, I listened, and I was a little bit astonished as to whether he had read the same Bill that I have.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He starts with the "big brother" government; it gives "big brother" government considerable latitude to silence the common man; catches opinions, comment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have been listening to the debate, you have read the statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think you did not want the Bill and its provisions to interfere with the flow of the rhetoric.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you also referred to what happens during elections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that is why I said I do not know which Bill you are referring to, and whether you are interested in dealing substantively with the Bill we are dealing with, with a proper debate, or just came with a prepared speech which has no relevance to the debate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I would suggest that the hon Member stop misquoting what I said in the CNA interview.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The point is simply this: every time you elect the government, you vest them with a whole lot of powers, including the power to declare war in extremis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How they should use their powers is not something I can vouch for.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What a future government will do with that power is not something I can vouch for.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I can only say we look at these problems, we need this legislation in place, and we have to deal with them, just like we deal with a whole variety of issues, just like all the other legislation that we have.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Any legislation, any legislative power, any government in place for five years can abuse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The rest of the WP Members' speeches repeat the points about chilling effect, it conflates opinion with facts, overlooks having a correction does not necessarily mean the original post is censored and the author can continue to post and give new viewpoints.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Really none of them bothered to deal with the current position and the important points I have made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Listening to the speeches, one phrase struck me – Mr Leon Perera and his reference to "industrial freezer".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not free speech which will go into deep freeze.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It strikes me that some stock phrases are kept in deep freeze by Mr Perera and his colleagues and brought out of the chiller once in a while and dutifully repeated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the AOJPA, Ms Sylvia Lim said, and I quote, "Such a spectacle if applied to this Bill will clearly have a chilling effect on public discourse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Are we not using a sledgehammer to kill an ant?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It would be intimidating not just to persons on the receiving end of such investigations but to society at large.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The upshot of reducing the role of the Courts and vesting draconian powers in the Executive...", none of that is true, by the way, "...is to leave Singaporeans at the mercy of administrative discretion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We would be one step closer to being a police state".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Since 2016, I ask Members, have Singaporeans been suffering at the mercy of an administrative discretion?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, not to be outdone, I quote, "As an ordinary person who relies on the law to protect my family, I find this proposed law cast too large and a fearful shadow on the whole of Singapore and diminishes my sense of security for my family.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Reading this Bill as an ordinary person sends a chill down my spine".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the last three years, fearful shadow over the whole of Singapore, chill down his spine every day as he goes to NUS, despite my clarification that before and after the Bill the law was largely the same.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, I would take a bet with you.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With the passage of the years, it can be seen, all of these statements were quite unconnected with reality and quite extreme.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Meanwhile, the standing of our Judiciary has been going up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Lawyers, including Mr Dennis Tan, make money partly because of the good standing of our Judiciary which was sought to be protected by that Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leon Perera also said, by reference to other countries, "Why are we taking a tighter approach when they are going the other way?" I would say, in the last three years, would he have preferred the trajectory of the UK versus our trajectory, whether in the Courts or in general?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think there comes a time – we were a colony of the UK – but there comes a time when we have to learn to think for ourselves what is good for us and stop being colonised in our minds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The year 1988 does not sound right because I am not sure Mr Low Thia Khiang was in Parliament in 1988.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I will say this but maybe I will have to change the date.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I quote: "...Bill further deprives the Opposition of their right to make use of other media to reach out to the people in order to express their views on the nation, society and the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The PAP introduces this amendment Bill just as the people of Singapore are beginning to avail themselves of some different views and comments from SCV.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government has been telling the people of Singapore that our information is open.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our people tune in to foreign TV programmes through SCV.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, after this Bill is passed, if Singapore Cable Vision (SCV) is to telecast any programme that contains unfavourable comments on the PAP which are considered to be biased and the office in charge is accordingly found to be guilty of an offence, then is this what the PAP Government means by saying our information is open?" It has been many years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Has there been any rampant prosecution of SCV officers?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I leave Members to judge for themselves and, if I have gotten the dates wrong, I apologise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you were in Parliament, Mr Low Thia Khiang.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, really, I think it is good for us to have the debate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Really, I was hoping yesterday and I had made this point in a very deliberate way that there is no profit of any sort, including political profit, in trying to allow these lies to proliferate and damage our infrastructure of fact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will damage the institutions and, frankly, no mainstream political party will benefit from this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will damage any party that wants to consider itself mainstream and credible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have seen what happens in the US, you have seen what happens to the UK.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is an exercise to maintain our society and the values and have a set of honest debates on what should be the way forward – honest debates on social policy, honest debates on economic policy, honest debates on how we should structure society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it should be based on a foundation of truth, foundation of honour and foundation where we keep out the lies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is not about the WP or the PAP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think, firstly, in general, we had an exchange about the proposal that the WP put forward with the Courts as the first arbiter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second point, I think the Minister raised it a few times in his speech and I believe the remark was also made by hon Member Mr Seah Kian Peng about the word "narrow", that the POFMA Bill actually narrows the Government's powers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Well, I can understand why that word was used.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I think very reasonable people, both inside and outside this House, may suggest that the word ought to be "sharpened".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: He looked at the Telecommunications Act, Penal Act, Sedition Act, ISA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Do they all cover online falsehoods? "Yes", they do.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Under "Additional requirements", in the case of the Telecommunications Act – Knowledge of falsity and fabrication, does it deal with the falsehoods itself? – "No." Under the Penal Code, knowingly spread falsehoods that concern race and religion, does it deal with the falsehood itself? – the answer was "No".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The other point – it is unfortunate that I did not come to this House prepared to debate the freedom of information (FOI) and the points that the Minister made about freedom of information.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I will try to provide some responses from—

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We can do it at some other point in time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I think there are certain things which I can probably cover at least in a cursory, or slightly more than a cursory manner.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In some cases, there have been successes, in some others there have not.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But the FOI cannot be seen as a silver bullet.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But it is one part of an ecosystem, one part of citizen engagement which, I submit, is actually very important and I think it helps in this building of trust and not just from one government to another.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It also raises the standard of conversation amongst members of the public.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: When I was actually studying for my juris doctor postgraduate programme in SMU, there was a requirement for students to undertake 80 years of—sorry, I beg your pardon, 80 hours – thank you, Prime Minister – that is too long   – 80 hours of internship experience.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I got in touch with some friends and I did an internship at the Central Information Commission in New Delhi.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This Commission actually looks into the right to information issues.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That experience, yes, it was only for a short three to four weeks, but it was very revealing because you had ordinary members of the public actually coming up with not ridiculous requests but serious requests about why certain commitments made by the government were not followed through or what happened in certain cases where certain information was actually supposed to be given but was not given.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I saw another side of FOI, granted only four weeks.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, while there is certainly a case to be made for some ridiculous requests which, of course, under most right to Information Acts can be dealt with separately and —

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Pritam Singh, could you please be brief with your points?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Yes, yes, I am rounding up, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The fact is that exemptions are not out of the question in freedom of information legislation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Of course, there is also the issue of questions that can be answered and cannot be answered and the Government can just put down its reasons why certain matters cannot be answered.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I do apologise for having to go through this very quickly but I thought it deserves a reply.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the first point, Mr Singh, I think we understand each other.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is something that you can look at the Bill and the current legislation and work out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not a matter of, I think, opinion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I will just leave it at that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the freedom of information, I do not think we want to go into a lengthy debate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I answered because two Members of Parliament, maybe more than two, raised it as fairly substantive points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I suppose one example that you highlighted is the Member of Parliament's expenses' scandal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The main point I made is that Parliament is the representative.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I can understand why maybe they did not raise that issue themselves because it is related to themselves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I assume on every other issue, Parliament is in a position to raise and, thankfully in Singapore, you know, we do not do any special favours for Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Mr Singh would have followed the news as to how much fake news is in vogue, particularly in the current period.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Yes, what you have quoted me, those were concerns that I had expressed in Parliament and not only my concerns, but concerns also from outside the Parliament.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I have also articulated in the process of studying the provisions of the Bill what possibly the Government can abuse some of the provisions in the Bill which I have articulated, which you have quoted me, and I stand by what I said.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I will clarify certain points that the Minister made.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Some of the legal points, my colleagues will help to clarify those as well.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: First, he referred to the part in my speech on coffee shops.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I talked about the coffee shop discussion on politics in relation to the advancement of new media.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: What I am saying is that, today, political discourse is not restricted to coffee shops alone.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: People can go to the Internet and so on.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: So, it is a progress rather than whispering around.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I do not know why he took issue with that.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Okay, he said I talked about chopping off heads.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: It is the same as chopping off heads!

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: You decide what you are going to do.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Later on, of course, the person can go to the Courts.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: But the fact is that the person would have to abide by the Direction of the Minister first.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: That is why in Chinese, we say "先斩后奏", so you chop off the head and decide what to do, you take action and you have to act.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: That is what I meant by chopping off heads.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Thirdly, the Minister is taking issue with me about me mentioning ISA.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: My view about POFMA and how I compared it with ISA before this House, basically, is that I see some fundamentals in there.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Detention without trial, without going through the Court." Similarly, you can also appeal to the Court.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: So, the Executive decides what action to be taken and the action is effected.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: He looks at the circumstances and decides what is in the public interest, what is statement, and decides, "Okay, this is the action to be taken", without having to go to Court.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: So, to me, there are some fundamental similarities here.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: It can be sometimes not very sure what is factual or not.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I gave those examples; the Minister said those are opinions, not facts.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I am not sure in some interpretation or saying in a different way, it can be interpreted as facts and thereby, comes under falsehood.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: These are some things which are not very clear.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Of course, the Minister said that he would assure this House and there would be subsidiary legislation, but the question is, there is a grey area which we are worried about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said the Member's reference to coffee shop triggered in my memory a previous reference to "coffee shop".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, on facts, I accept in good faith that Mr Low has some lack of clarity on what are facts and opinions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But then, he has got to rely on the law and what the Courts have said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I think we can leave it at that.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Deputy Speaker, in the analysis of Government actions against misinformation over the past few years, I found that sometimes, Ministries were imprecise in their language.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: They would label, for example, differences of opinion as false.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: What I am suggesting is would the Minister consider working with the whole-of-Government to ensure that once the Act is in place, Ministries do not label differences of opinion as false, because I think it has real meaning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: If you call it false, the public will expect that you should be using the Act against it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: And if it is not at that level, maybe just call it a misrepresentation or what you wish, instead.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Theseira, I thought you were my friend.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second point is, you can have false opinions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not make sense to use it against individuals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You think the tech companies would not challenge?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, when the challenge comes, the Minister will have to justify and it is going to be something that Ministers would have to think carefully about, take proper advice and act only when it is really something that he can stand on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why we have not sought to, as I said yesterday, over-egg the pudding in terms of trying to define "fact" and what is not fact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have relied on existing jurisprudence and leave it to the Courts, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Okay, I think I will allow three more.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The Minister referred to what I and some others have said in the 2016 debate on the AOJPA Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Of course, I do not want to belabour the House with that debate, which is over.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But the fact is that those concerns that we had about how codifying the law has changed the common law by making contempt an arrestable offence, bringing the Police in, giving the Minister immunity, I think those points have been made and I leave the public to judge what was said in that debate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: First of all, the Minister earlier referred to what Mr Low Thia Khiang had mentioned regarding the Court case where the Government tried to use POHA.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And Justice of Appeal Andrew Phang, if I am not wrong, said that if the Government had intended to use POHA for any relief, it should have been made clear during the Second Reading of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: He mentioned in his round-up that during an appeal under POFMA, proportionality would have to be shown.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, is it actually under judicial review and not at the appeal?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the Court can look and substitute its view for that of the Minister; that is what I meant by straight appeal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, proportionality is more the traditional exercise of government powers; and that would be judicial review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, thank you for asking for that clarification.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The other point that Ms Sylvia Lim made, in terms of section 15, I have not looked at the Court of Appeal judgment recently or the Hansard, but based on memory, what I had said in Parliament is, the word "persons" in POHA must be interpreted in accordance with the Interpretation Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is, I think, on the record and that is what we stand by.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you go to the Interpretation Act, it sets out how "persons" are defined.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the Court of Appeal had to look at the context of the Act and look at who it applied to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it took a different interpretation from what I had thought was correct, or what we had intended.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that is the Court and we are bound by the Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They did go through the Hansard and they applied the Interpretation Act, but they looked at it and they said "persons", applying it here, does not include corporate entities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is not as if we misled Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has got to be decided in accordance with the Interpretation Act, and they decided according to the Interpretation Act, except that they took a different view from us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For the rest of POHA, there is no question that the Government could have relied upon — As I have said, it is absurd to suggest that the Government could be harassed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Legally, it does not make any sense, if I could say that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I note the Member's points on the Contempt Act.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Leon Perera and Mr Png Eng Huat.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, I just wanted to ask for the Minister's comment on that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Here, I am not talking about defamation action that could be taken against individual Ministers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I am talking about fake news that may originate from a Ministry, from a Government agency.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I know the Minister said that this does not happen very much, it is a question of scale.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It could happen, it may happen more in the future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: POHA is apparently not a recourse, defamation may not be a recourse.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The third and last one, the Minister mentioned that compared to some of the existing remedies, the penalties and the powers are actually a scoping down.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think clause 45 of the Telecommunications Act (TA) and the BA were mentioned.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The Telecommunications Act just says that he knows to be false; so, he must have knowledge, not reason to believe.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The BA, and I refer to Prof Goh Yihan's submission, does not apply to non-licensees, it does not apply to websites run by individuals, persons communicating via closed platform groups like WhatsApp, Telegram and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The first point on falsehoods and public interest, that an investigative journalist is prevented from publishing something that is embarrassing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think I would say this: it could be embarrassing, it may not be embarrassing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It could additionally be embarrassing, but that is an irrelevant consideration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Member's point, I think really, if I understand it, is, it may not be false, and it may not be of public interest, but because it is embarrassing, a Minister tries to stop it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think that is the point the Member really makes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, a journalist can go to Court and say, "Why am I being stopped?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is false?" because the Minister's Direction has got to set out what is false.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the face of it, you can tell whether it is credible or not credible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If on the face of it, it is not false, you think the journalist will keep quiet?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have said in nine days, you can be in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because not only did he try to suppress something embarrassing, but now he would be shown to have used and abused his powers and overruled by a Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is far worse for a Minister to do that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not many Ministers in many countries will survive that kind of action.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If a Minister had tried to suppress and the Court says this was neither in the public interest, nor was it false, I think not many Ministers will survive that, particularly if it comes out that it was for an extraneous purpose.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the Ministers put their personal reputations at stake every single time a decision is made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, what recourse does one have if the Government is the originator of fake news?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have dealt with it fairly extensively in my round-up speech; I am not going to repeat it again.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leon Perera said compared with section 45 of the TA, the definition is actually broader because it is misleading.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Here the Bill, it is both misleading and false.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I explained it in some careful detail yesterday how the current BA can, through class licensing scheme and through subsidiary legislation, be made to apply to all.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If what this Government really wanted was just to amass powers, why do we put up a legislation for debate that gives the Courts greater oversight?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not just this Government, it is the future governments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a system; it is an institution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we want to set in place more judicial oversight as these powers get exercised, but that does not mean that the powers are being expanded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh said sharper, but they are narrowed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to introduce a New Clause entitled "Principles of Act".

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The "Principles of Act", I referred to them in my Second Reading debate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The purpose is to provide guidance to the proportionate and limited exercise of powers under the Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I accept the Minister believes that these guarantees are already provided in the existing Bill or will be provided in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Nonetheless, I think this debate has shown us that it is not easy for non-lawyers to understand or interpret the appropriate scope of the Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: So, I think it is important to provide a plain language set of the principles in the primary legislation that cannot be changed by a future Government without returning to Parliament.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: In performing any duty or exercising any power under this Act in relation to the communication of online Falsehoods, any Minister and any Competent Authority must have regard to the following principles of this Act: (proc text)]   [(proc text) (b)	as facts can be contentious and difficult to establish, and because the advancement of knowledge often depends on contesting apparent facts, the disputation of a fact does not imply that one or more contested facts are falsehoods by that virtue alone; (proc text)] [(proc text) (c)	while an authority may have higher quality data or more accurate means of determining the facts, given the variety of legitimate means by which facts can be established, a statement of fact that differs from a fact established by an authority does not imply a falsehood by that virtue alone; (proc text)]   [(proc text) (e)	the executive powers in this Act may be regarded as, from least to most restrictive: A Correction Direction, a Targeted Correction Direction, a General Correction Direction, a Stop Communication Direction, and a Disabling Direction; (proc text)] [(proc text) (f)	regard must be had to whether the public interest for which the duty is being performed or the power is being exercised can be achieved in the way that is the least restrictive on the rights of the public to speak and debate freely; (proc text)] [(proc text) (g)	in all matters relating to the administration or application of this Act, the aim is to target material online falsehoods that are against the public interest, and not opinions, comments, critiques, satire, parody, generalisations or statements of experiences.”.
